2027-07-03.title: Dukhrana of Saint Thomas the Apostle
2027-07-03.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: God plants a garden in Eden, in the east
Keep hold of instruction, for she is your life
The household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles
It is to peace that God has called you
What God has joined together, let no one separate
2027-07-03.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. This is the last weekend of the season: the Season of Kaitha begins on Sunday 4 July. Today is the Dukhrana of Saint Thomas the Apostle, an important feast and a day of obligation in the Syro-Malabar calendar, and also the Seventh Saturday of the Apostles, the last day of the season. Both sets of readings printed in the calendar are shown: the four readings of the feast and the weekday readings. The calendar's headings for the feast: “God put the man whom He had formed, in Eden”; “Keep hold of instruction, for she is your life”; “The household of God, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets”; “My Lord and my God”. For the Saturday: “Wife should not separate from the husband”; “God created them as man and woman”. Verify locally the times of the Holy Qurbana. Many also mark today as Syro-Malabar Church Day and as Indian Christian Day (verify locally). The Latin Church keeps the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle today, and in India with special joy; tomorrow the Season of Kaitha begins.
2027-07-03.verse: Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”
theo: “Dukhrana” is a Syriac word that means remembrance. Each year on 3 July our Church remembers Mar Thoma, the Apostle Thomas, whom we call our father in faith. According to the East Syriac tradition, this is the day on which his relics were solemnly brought to Edessa, and so the day became his memorial; in the Syro-Malabar Church it is an important feast and a day of obligation. It is also the last day of the Season of the Apostles, and the season could not close with a better name. Thomas is the apostle whom the Gospel of John knows best after Peter and the beloved disciple. Three times he speaks. When Jesus decided to return to Judea, where his enemies were waiting, it was Thomas who said to the others, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.” At the Last Supper, when Jesus said “you know the way”, it was Thomas who said what the others were thinking: “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?” And on the second Sunday of Easter he spoke the greatest words in the Gospel. We have been unfair to Thomas by calling him only the doubter. He is the brave one, the honest one, and the one who confessed.

The Gospel is one of the most loved passages of John. Thomas was not with the others on Easter evening when Jesus came, and the ten told him, “We have seen the Lord.” He answered, “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the mark of the nails and my hand in his side, I will not believe.” Thomas asked for no more than the others had already received, since Jesus had “showed them his hands and his side” on the first evening. And Jesus did not refuse. “A week later his disciples were again in the house, and Thomas was with them.” The Lord came again, “Although the doors were shut”, and said, “Peace be with you.” Then he turned to Thomas by name and gave him what he had asked: “Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.” The Gospel does not say that Thomas touched. It says that he answered, and what he answered is the climax of the whole book: “My Lord and my God!” The Gospel began with “the Word was God”; now a disciple says it to the face of the risen Jesus. The Catechism notes that even in the presence of the risen Lord some disciples doubted, and that the Lord's patient dealing with their doubt is part of the Church's faith (CCC 644). Then comes a blessing for us: “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.” That is the Indian Church, and every church after the apostles: “Although you have not seen him, you love him; and even though you do not see him now, you believe in him and rejoice with an indescribable and glorious joy.”

The Epistle tells us what the apostles are to the Church: “So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone. In him the whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in whom you also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God.” The Church is apostolic because she is founded on the apostles, and because the teaching they handed on is kept in her by their successors, the bishops (CCC 857). For us in India this is not abstract. Our community has always said that it received the faith directly from an apostle. According to tradition, Thomas came by sea to Muziris, near Kodungallur, in the year 52, preached to Jews and others on the Malabar coast, baptised, and founded communities at Kodungallur, Palayoor, Kokkamangalam, Kottakkavu, Niranam, Nilackal and Kollam, and then travelled further to the east coast, where he was martyred at Mylapore about the year 72; his tomb is venerated in the San Thome Basilica at Chennai. Historians weigh the sources with care, and the tradition has been held with unbroken love by the Thomas Christians for nearly two thousand years: in the ancient Acts of Thomas, in the memory of the Church of the East, in the songs and customs of our families. The Orthodox, Mar Thoma and Malankara Churches honour the same apostle, and today we rejoice with them in the one Lord whom Thomas confessed.

Why does the Church read Genesis on this day? The calendar chooses a passage about a garden in the east: “And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden, in the east; and there he put the man whom he had formed.” In the middle of the garden stands “the tree of life”; “A river flows out of Eden to water the garden”; and “The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and keep it.” The Bible ends where it begins: in the last book, “On either side of the river is the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit… and the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations”, and the risen Lord promises, “To everyone who conquers, I will give permission to eat from the tree of life that is in the paradise of God.” Our East Syriac fathers, above all Saint Ephrem, loved to sing of this paradise, and of the Church as the garden that God plants again. On Easter morning Mary Magdalene thought the risen Lord was the gardener. Thomas was given a garden to till and keep: a garden in the east, watered by rivers, where the tree of the cross would stand and where the leaves of the tree would heal people. The rivers of the Malabar coast meet the sea near Kodungallur, and by tradition the preaching of the apostle there was the first stream of the river of the Gospel in our land.

The second reading is from the book of Proverbs, the voice of Wisdom speaking to a child: “Hear, my child, and accept my words, that the years of your life may be many. I have taught you the way of wisdom; I have led you in the paths of uprightness.” And: “Keep hold of instruction; do not let go; guard her, for she is your life.” The Thomas Christians have done exactly this. For centuries, without a ruling power to protect them and often without many books, they kept hold of the instruction handed down to them: the Qurbana, the Creed, the sign of the cross, the fasts, the family prayer, and the memory of Thomas, whom they called the Way of Thomas, Mar Thoma Margam. The sage's last verse is the promise for those who keep to the path: “But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day.” Thomas once asked, “How can we know the way?” and Jesus answered, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” We owe to the honest question of Thomas one of the greatest sayings of the Lord.

The weekday readings of the Seventh Saturday also have something to say on this feast. Paul, in the first letter to the Corinthians, speaks to the married and the unmarried about the practical shape of Christian faith in a household. “To the married I give this command, not I but the Lord, that the wife should not separate from her husband… and that the husband should not divorce his wife.” Where one partner is not yet a believer, he says that the believing partner should not cast the other aside: “For the unbelieving husband is made holy through his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy through her husband.” The Catechism uses this verse for the task of the Catholic spouse in a marriage with a person of another faith (CCC 1637). Paul's last word is a gentle one: “It is to peace that God has called you. Wife, for all you know, you might save your husband. Husband, for all you know, you might save your wife.” The Gospel takes us back to the beginning, to the same Genesis: “Have you not read that the one who made them at the beginning ‘made them male and female,’ and said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’? So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” Jesus names the hardness of heart which made Moses permit divorce, and says, “from the beginning it was not so”; the Church holds the indissolubility of marriage as a gift of Christ and also accompanies with mercy those whose marriages have been wounded (CCC 1614–1615, 1640). Faith came to India through families, and it is handed on by families still. The garden of Eden was a home before it was a Church, and the Church has always been a household.

On this feast the Church prays that the faith of Thomas, tested and then confessed, be ours. Many Syro-Malabar people today go on pilgrimage to the churches that tradition links with the apostle, or sing the old songs of Mar Thoma. But the best Dukhrana is a daily one: to say at the elevation in the Qurbana, in our own heart, “My Lord and my God”, and then to carry the same Lord to those who have not yet seen. Thomas is the apostle of India and of the Church of the East; the Syro-Malabar Church today carries his mission to every state of India and to many countries of the world. May the Apostle who said “Let us also go” make us willing to go.
conn: Let us also go.
“Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, ‘Let us also go, that we may die with him’” (John 11:16).
The way.

“Thomas said to him, ‘Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?’ Jesus said to him, ‘I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me’” (John 14:5–6).
The wounds and the peace.

“After he said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. Jesus said to them again, ‘Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so I send you’” (John 20:20–21).
Written that you may believe.
“But these are written so that you may come to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that through believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31).
The twelve foundations.
“And the wall of the city has twelve foundations, and on them are the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb” (Revelation 21:14).
The tree of life.
“She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her; those who hold her fast are called happy” (Proverbs 3:18); “the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:2).
To the ends of the world.
“Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Romans 10:18); “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation” (Mark 16:15).
outline: Opening
Dukhrana, remembrance: the apostle who said “Let us also go”, “How can we know the way?” and “My Lord and my God!”
Point 1 · My Lord and my God
Thomas asks for what the others had been given; Jesus comes again for him; the highest confession of the Gospel; the blessing on those who have not seen.
Point 2 · The foundation of the apostles
The Church is apostolic; the Thomas tradition in India, held “according to tradition” with love; Mylapore and the seven communities.
Point 3 · The garden in the east
The planted garden, the river and the tree of life; the Church as God's garden; the Gospel as a river in our land.
Point 4 · Keep hold of instruction
The path of the righteous like the light of dawn; the Way of Thomas kept for two thousand years; I am the way.
Point 5 · What God has joined together
Peace in the household; the family as the first church.
Take-home line
“My Lord and my God!”
live: Confess in your heart (John 20:28)
At the elevation of the Holy Qurbana this Sunday, say quietly in your heart, “My Lord and my God.” Say it also whenever you see a crucifix this week.
Let us also go (John 11:16)
Choose one place or person you have avoided because it is hard to go there, a sick relative, a quarrel, an old friend, and go this week.
Hand on the faith (Proverbs 4:13)
Tell your children or grandchildren the story of how the faith came to your family, and teach them the prayer of Thomas.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

Thomas's unbelief helped our faith more than the faith of the disciples who believed at once. When he touched the wounds, our own hesitation was healed. The Lord allowed him to doubt so that the doubt might be cured by touch and that we, who come later, might be strengthened.
St Augustine (in substance)
Thomas saw and touched a man, and confessed God, whom he neither saw nor touched. What he saw and touched removed every doubt, and his confession reaches beyond what his eyes and hands could reach.
magis: Catechism 644 (in substance)

Even before the risen Lord, the disciples still doubted. Thomas himself met the test of doubt, and when Jesus showed him the wounds in his hands and side he said, “My Lord and my God!” The Church's faith in the Resurrection is built on these witnesses.
Catechism 857 (in substance)

The Church is apostolic because she is founded on the apostles, in three ways: she was and remains built on their witness, she keeps and hands on their teaching, and she continues to be taught and guided by them through their successors, the bishops.
saints: Dukhrana of Saint Thomas the Apostle, an important feast and a day of obligation in the Syro-Malabar calendar; also the Seventh Saturday of the Apostles. The Latin Church keeps the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle today, and in India with special joy. Indian Christian Day and Syro-Malabar Church Day are marked on this day (verify locally).

Sun 4 July: First Sunday of Kaitha, Feast of the Twelve Apostles. Mon 5 and Tue 6: the first Monday and Tuesday of Kaitha; Tue 6 also St Maria Goretti. Fri 9 July: First Friday of Kaitha, St James of Nisibis.
2027-07-03.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you came through closed doors and showed the wounds of your love to your disciple Thomas, and he answered, “My Lord and my God!” Give us the faith of Thomas: courage to go with you even to death, honesty to ask the way, and humility to adore. We thank you for the apostle who, according to tradition, brought the Gospel to our land, and for all the parents, teachers and ancestors who have handed it on. Keep us on the Way, make us strong in your peace, and send us as witnesses to those who have not yet seen. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Church does for us what the Lord did for Thomas: after the consecration the priest shows us the Body and the Blood, and we answer with our whole heart, “My Lord and my God.” The doors are shut, the Lord stands in our midst and says, “Peace be with you”, and he gives us his wounds as the food of life. Thomas touched, or was invited to touch, a body that had been wounded; at the altar we receive that same Body, now glorified. “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”

The altar is also the foundation stone of the household of God. Built on the foundation of the apostles, with Christ as cornerstone, the Church gathers round the altar, and the whole structure “grows into a holy temple in the Lord”. Here the faith that Thomas brought, the Qurbana in the East Syriac tradition, is celebrated as our fathers celebrated it, and here the family that God has joined together learns to be one.

2027-07-04.title: First Sunday of Kaitha: Feast of the Twelve Apostles
2027-07-04.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Elijah builds an altar of twelve stones
Many signs and wonders through the apostles
Be united in the same mind and the same purpose
Take the lowest place; invite the poor
2027-07-04.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which opens on the Sunday after the Dukhrana of St Thomas: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church contemplates its growth and harvest, in the apostles, martyrs and saints who watered the Church with their blood. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. Today is the First Sunday of Kaitha and the Feast of the Twelve Apostles, which opens the season. The calendar's own headings: “Elijah builds an altar with twelve stones”; “The Apostles heal many”; “Be united in the mind”; “The mentality of the disciple”. The calendar's longer forms are Acts 5:12–32; 1 Corinthians 1:9–16 with 2 Corinthians 1:8–14; Luke 14:1–14. In the Latin calendar today is the Fourteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time. Verify locally the times of the Holy Qurbana and how the feast is kept.
2027-07-04.verse: For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.
theo: After yesterday's Dukhrana of Mar Thoma, our Church turns today to all twelve. “He called his disciples and chose twelve of them, whom he also named apostles”, Luke says, after a night on the mountain “in prayer to God”. Their names are given in the Gospels in four lists, and the first is this: “These are the names of the twelve apostles: first, Simon, also known as Peter, and his brother Andrew; James son of Zebedee, and his brother John; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, the one who betrayed him.” Mark gives the purpose: “And he appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, to be with him, and to be sent out to proclaim the message.” First to be with him, then to be sent. The number is deliberate: twelve, like the tribes of Israel, because Jesus was gathering the whole people of God anew. “You who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” After the betrayal of Judas, the apostles prayed and “the lot fell on Matthias; and he was added to the eleven apostles”: the Twelve is a college that the Church keeps whole (CCC 880). In the last book of the Bible the holy city has “twelve foundations, and on them are the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb”. Today we keep the feast of all the names, including those about whom the Gospels tell us almost nothing; they too are foundation stones.

Today also opens the Season of Kaitha, the summer of the Church's year. After the apostles have sown, the Church looks at the growth and the harvest. The first reading chooses a very fitting beginning: a prophet builds an altar. In the days of King Ahab, Israel was “limping with two different opinions”, between the Lord and Baal, and the altar of the Lord on Mount Carmel “had been thrown down”. “Then Elijah said to all the people, ‘Come closer to me’; and all the people came closer to him. First he repaired the altar of the Lord that had been thrown down; Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the Lord came, saying, ‘Israel shall be your name’; with the stones he built an altar in the name of the Lord.” Twelve stones, one altar: the divided people is gathered again, and the Lord's name is the name above the whole. Elijah has the sacrifice soaked with water three times, so that whatever follows can only be the Lord's doing, and his prayer is short and humble: “Answer me, O Lord, answer me, so that this people may know that you, O Lord, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back.” Then “the fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and even licked up the water that was in the trench.” The people fall on their faces: “The Lord indeed is God; the Lord indeed is God.” The Church has always seen in the twelve stones the twelve apostles, on whom the new altar of the Church is built; and in the fire from heaven the fire of Pentecost, which made the same twelve a witness.

The Acts reading shows what the fire did. “Now many signs and wonders were done among the people through the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico.” They stayed in the Temple, as faithful sons of Israel; the Church did not begin by leaving the house of the Lord but by praying in it. The people held them in high esteem, and “more than ever believers were added to the Lord, great numbers of both men and women, so that they even carried out the sick into the streets, and laid them on cots and mats, in order that Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he came by. A great number of people would also gather from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, and they were all cured.” This is harvest. Then the high priest and the party of the Sadducees, “being filled with jealousy”, arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison. We see here one group of leaders, the high priest and his party, and not the Jewish people, who held the apostles in high esteem. “But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out, and said, ‘Go, stand in the temple and tell the people the whole message about this life.’” An open prison door and a command to go back to the very place of danger: the Church is sent, again and again, to speak the whole message and not only the parts that are welcome.

Paul, writing to Corinth, shows what can happen to a Church that forgets the one Lord. “God is faithful; by him you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord. Now I appeal to you, brothers and sisters, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you be in agreement and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same purpose.” The Corinthians were each saying, “I belong to Paul,” or “I belong to Apollos,” or “I belong to Cephas,” or “I belong to Christ.” The apostles, great as they were, are never meant to be the names of parties. Paul answers with three questions: “Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” The Twelve are many, and the Lord is one. This is also a prayer for our own day: for the unity of our parishes and our Church, and for the unity of all who are baptised into Christ, with the Orthodox, the Mar Thoma and the Malankara Churches, who also honour the apostles and share much of our heritage. “There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to the one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:4–5; CCC 813).

The Gospel is set at a meal. Jesus is at table in the house of a leading Pharisee, and he sees how the guests choose the places of honour. He tells them a parable: “When you are invited by someone to a wedding banquet, do not sit down at the place of honor… But when you are invited, go and sit down at the lowest place, so that when your host comes, he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher’; then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at the table with you.” The principle is the one that should rule the Church: “For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.” The apostles themselves had to learn it. At the Last Supper “a dispute also arose among them as to which one of them was to be regarded as the greatest,” and Jesus answered, “the greatest among you must become like the youngest, and the leader like one who serves… I am among you as one who serves.” Then he turns to the host: “When you give a luncheon or a dinner, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, in case they may invite you in return… But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind. And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you, for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.” In Kerala this is the parish feast, with its nercha meal: let the first to be served and the best seat be for the one who cannot give anything back. In this season of the harvest the rice-ears that are full bow their heads, and the empty ones stand straight. The Twelve, humbled by their failure and lifted by the Spirit, are the ears that bowed.
conn: Chosen after prayer.

“Now during those days he went out to the mountain to pray; and he spent the night in prayer to God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose twelve of them, whom he also named apostles” (Luke 6:12–13).
With him and sent.
“And he appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, to be with him, and to be sent out to proclaim the message” (Mark 3:14).
Sent to the nations.
“Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).
Fruit that lasts.
“You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last” (John 15:16).
Sowers and reapers.

“May those who sow in tears reap with shouts of joy. Those who go out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm 126:5–6); “so that sower and reaper may rejoice together” (John 4:36).
The greatest as servant.
“whoever wishes to be great among you must be your servant” (Matthew 20:26); “Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10).
Unity.
“that they may all be one. As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me” (John 17:21).
outline: Opening
The Twelve and the opening of Kaitha: from sowing to harvest.
Point 1 · Twelve stones, one altar
The names of the Twelve, chosen after prayer; Elijah's altar; the fire from heaven.
Point 2 · Go and tell the whole message
Signs in the Temple; Peter's shadow; the open prison door; the harvest of the Church.
Point 3 · Has Christ been divided?
Not I belong to Paul or Cephas, but all belong to Christ; unity with one another and among the Churches.
Point 4 · The lowest place and the empty chair
Humility at the banquet; the apostles who argued and learned; the parish feast and the poor.
Take-home line
“All who humble themselves will be exalted.”
live: Learn the Twelve (Matthew 10:2–4)
Learn the names of the Twelve this week and say them with your family at evening prayer; add the name of Matthias.
Take the lowest place (Luke 14:10)
At the next parish gathering, a feast, a meeting or a meal, take the last seat and serve someone else first.
Invite the poor (Luke 14:13)
If your family keeps a feast this month, invite one person who cannot invite you back, and sit with them.
fathers: St Cyprian of Carthage (in substance)
The other apostles were what Peter was, sharing an equal fellowship of honour and power; but the beginning starts from unity, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one.
St Augustine (in substance)
Do you want to build a great tower of holiness? Think first of the foundation of humility. The higher you intend to raise the building, the deeper you must dig the foundation.
magis: Catechism 880 (in substance)

When Christ instituted the Twelve, he made them a college or permanent assembly and put Peter at its head. The college of bishops, with the Pope as its head, is the continuation of the college of apostles.
Catechism 813 (in substance)

The Church is one because of her source, the unity of the Trinity; because of her founder, Christ; and because of her soul, the Holy Spirit. Her unity is a gift, and we must keep it with every effort.
saints: First Sunday of Kaitha, the Feast of the Twelve Apostles. In the Latin calendar, the Fourteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
Mon 5 and Tue 6: the first Monday and Tuesday of Kaitha; Tue 6 also St Maria Goretti. Fri 9 July: First Friday of Kaitha, St James of Nisibis.
2027-07-04.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you prayed all night and chose twelve to be with you and to be sent. We thank you for Peter and Andrew, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew, James and Thaddaeus, Simon and Matthias. As you built an altar of twelve stones in the days of Elijah, build your Church on the foundation of the apostles, with yourself as cornerstone. Send the fire of your Spirit on us at the opening of this season; keep us one in mind and purpose; teach us to take the lowest place, to invite the poor, and to bring a rich harvest for your kingdom. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the altar is the place where the fire of heaven falls on the offering. Elijah's altar of twelve stones is a sign of ours: the altar of the Church rests on the apostles, and the Lord himself is the cornerstone. When the priest calls down the Holy Spirit on the bread and wine, we ask for the fire that fell on Carmel and on the Upper Room, and the people answer as they did on Carmel: “The Lord indeed is God.” The words of the Last Supper, handed on by the apostles, are the words we hear at every Qurbana.

And this altar is a banquet table where the first places belong to the poor: the Lord who made himself the servant of the Twelve at the Last Supper serves us with his own Body and Blood. Those who come to this table as beggars leave as brothers and sisters, and take their seat with the lowest and the last.

The parable of the prodigal son
2027-07-11.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church looks at its growth and fruit. This is the season of the apostles and martyrs who watered the Church with their blood, and of watchfulness for the coming of the Lord. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints of the East Syriac tradition. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar gives longer forms: Isaiah 3:16–4:6; 2 Corinthians 3:4–18; Luke 15:4–32. In the Latin calendar today is the Fifteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time; St Benedict (11 July) gives way to the Sunday.
2027-07-11.verse: But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him.
theo: The first reading is part of Moses' last sermon, and it begins with a question that reaches across the whole history of the world: “For ask now about former ages, long before your own, ever since the day that God created human beings on the earth; ask from one end of heaven to the other: has anything so great as this ever happened or has its like ever been heard of?” Moses asks whether any people has ever heard the voice of a god speaking out of a fire and lived, and whether any god has ever gone to take a nation for himself “by trials, by signs and wonders, by war, by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm”, as the Lord did in Egypt. Then the reason is given in one sentence, which the calendar rightly calls the eternal love of God: “And because he loved your ancestors, he chose their descendants after them.” Israel was not chosen because it was great, but because it was loved. The commandments that follow, “for your own well-being and that of your descendants after you”, come after the love, as a father's rule comes after the father's embrace.

In Isaiah the prophet looks beyond a time of judgment: “On that day the branch of the Lord shall be beautiful and glorious.” The Church has always heard in the word Branch the promised king of David's line (compare Jeremiah 23:5), and in the survivors in Zion, “everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem”, the holy people he gathers. God cleanses Jerusalem “by a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning”, and then, as in the Exodus, he creates over Mount Zion “a cloud by day and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night”. The last verse is a picture for every monsoon in Kerala: over all the glory there will be “a canopy. It will serve as a pavilion, a shade by day from the heat, and a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain.” This is the Church in the season of Kaitha, which begins in the heat and the heavy rains of July: a tent that God himself spreads over his people. (The longer reading begins with the woes on the proud daughters of Zion, and the calendar's heading remembers only the promise.)

Paul's Epistle is about confidence. “Not that we are competent of ourselves to claim anything as coming from us; our competence is from God, who has made us competent to be ministers of a new covenant, not of letter but of spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” He compares the ministry of Moses, whose face shone with a glory that Israel could not bear to look at, with the ministry of the Spirit. Paul does not despise the first: it “came in glory”. He says that when a greater glory appears, the first looks pale beside it, as a lamp beside the sun. This is not a rejection of the Jewish people or their covenant; the Church teaches that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29), and Paul himself was a son of that covenant. His point is that what Jeremiah promised has come: the law written on hearts by the Holy Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33). And so, he says, “we act with great boldness”. The minister of this covenant does not shine by himself; he lets the Spirit give life.

Then comes the Gospel, the most famous of all parables, which the calendar calls the parable of the prodigal son, though it is better called the parable of the father. It is the third of three: a lost sheep, a lost coin, a lost son. St Luke tells us why Jesus told them: the Pharisees and scribes were grumbling, “This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them.” The younger son asks for his share while his father is alive, which is as good as saying, I wish you were dead. He goes to a distant country, spends everything, and ends up feeding pigs, the lowest place a Jewish young man can imagine, wishing he could eat what the pigs eat. Then comes the turning: “when he came to himself.” He rehearses a speech: “I have sinned against heaven and before you.” But before he can say it, the father, who has been watching the road, sees him “while he was still far off”, is “filled with compassion”, runs (an old man does not run in an Eastern village), embraces and kisses him. The robe, the ring and the sandals are the signs of a son, not of a servant; the fatted calf is for a feast. “For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!”

The parable has a second half, and Jesus meant it for his critics. The elder son, who has stayed, comes in from the field, hears the music, and is angry and will not go in. And the father goes out again, as he went out to the younger, and pleads with him: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.” The elder son says “this son of yours”; the father answers “this brother of yours”. The parable ends without telling us whether he went in. That is not an accident: the open door is held out to everyone who ever thought of himself as faithful and cannot bear the joy of mercy. Many Kerala families know both sons: one who went to a distant land and came home, and one who stayed and carried the house. Both are loved. The Church answers the father's call in the sacrament of Reconciliation, where the robe is given again, and in the Holy Qurbana, which is the feast of the fatted calf.
conn: Love before law.
“When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 11:1); “I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you” (Jeremiah 31:3).
The Branch.

“The days are surely coming, says the Lord, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land” (Jeremiah 23:5).
Cloud and fire.

“The Lord went in front of them in a pillar of cloud by day, to lead them along the way, and in a pillar of fire by night, to give them light” (Exodus 13:21). “For you have been a refuge to the poor, a refuge to the needy in their distress, a shelter from the rainstorm and a shade from the heat” (Isaiah 25:4).
The covenant of the Spirit.

“I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Jeremiah 31:33); “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).
The Father's welcome.
“As a father has compassion for his children, so the Lord has compassion for those who fear him” (Psalm 103:13).
Joy in heaven.
“Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance” (Luke 15:7).
altar: At every Holy Qurbana the Father runs down the road to meet us. Words of repentance and prayers for forgiveness are said in the Qurbana, and the answer is the table: the robe of the Spirit, the ring of the covenant, and the fatted calf, the Body and Blood of Christ, the feast that the Father makes for those who were lost and are found.

The elder brother is at the altar too, with his questions and his good deeds. The same Lord who gives himself to the sinner comes out to plead with the one who is angry at mercy; he says to each of us: all that is mine is yours. Whoever receives the Qurbana is asked to go into the house and sit at the table with his brother.
outline: Opening
A father at the gate, looking down the road.
Point 1 · He loved your ancestors
The eternal love that chooses before it commands; the question of Moses.
Point 2 · The canopy over Zion
The Branch, the holy remnant, and the shelter from the heat and the storm.
Point 3 · The Spirit gives life
The ministry of the new covenant; boldness without pride; the gifts irrevocable.
Point 4 · The running Father
Lost sheep, lost coin, lost son; the younger son comes to himself, the robe, the ring, the feast.
Point 5 · The elder son
The father goes out again; this brother of yours; the open door.
Take-home line
“This son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!”
live: Return to the Father (Luke 15:18)
If you have been away from confession or the Qurbana, rehearse a short prayer, ‘Father, I have sinned’, and go this week.
Go out to the elder brother (Luke 15:28)
Is there someone at home or in the parish who is angry about mercy shown to someone else? Go out to them and listen.
Wait at the gate (Luke 15:20)
Pray every evening for one person who has gone away from the Church, and keep a lamp on in your heart.
Give thanks for the covenant (2 Corinthians 3:6)
Read one page of the Gospel this week and ask the Spirit to write it on your heart.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)
You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.
St Ambrose of Milan (in substance)

The father saw him from afar and ran, because mercy is quicker than the sinner's footsteps. The robe is the grace that was lost, the ring is the seal of the Spirit, the shoes are the readiness for the Gospel, and the feast is the Body of the Lord.
magis: Catechism 218–220
God chose Israel because he loved it; his love is everlasting and faithful, and Scripture compares it to the love of a father for his child.
Catechism 1439
The process of conversion and repentance was described by Jesus in the parable of the prodigal son, whose centre is the merciful father.
Catechism 839
The Jewish people are the first to hear the Word of God; to them belong the covenants, and the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable.
saints: Second Sunday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar, the Fifteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time; St Benedict, whose memorial falls on 11 July, gives way to the Sunday.
Mon 12: Second Monday of Kaitha. Thu 15: Sts Kuriakose and Julitta. Fri 16: Our Lady of Mount Carmel and Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai.
2027-07-11.prayer: Father of mercies, who chose your people because you loved them, and who watch the road for each of your children, we thank you for your Son, who has told us what you are like. Bring home all who are far away, and give us the courage to say, ‘Father, I have sinned.’ Clothe us again with the robe of your Spirit, put on our hand the ring of your covenant, and seat us at the table of your Son. Teach those of us who have stayed at home to share your joy, and to welcome our brothers and sisters without grudging. Spread over your Church the canopy of your protection against the heat and the storm, and write your law on our hearts. We ask this through Jesus Christ, your Son, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever. Amen.

2027-07-15.title: Second Thursday of Kaitha · Saint Kuriakose and Saint Julitta, Martyrs
2027-07-15.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The testing of faith produces endurance
Have faith in God; pray and forgive
Sts Kuriakose and Julitta · First Reading
Azariah prays in the midst of the furnace
Sts Kuriakose and Julitta · Second Reading
Stephen, full of grace and power, before the council (the calendar gives 6:8–7:10)
The faith of the ancient patriarchs (the calendar gives 11:3–10, 32–40 and 12:1–2)
Bear witness to the Lord before the people
2027-07-15.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which follows the Season of the Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when we remember the apostles, martyrs and saints who sowed the Gospel and watered it with their blood, and keep ourselves ready for the coming of the Lord. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar gives the weekday readings of the Second Thursday of Kaitha and the readings of the commemoration of St Kuriakose and St Julitta, an Ordinary Feast of the Oriental tradition; both sets are shown here (verify locally which are read). The calendar's own headings: “The testing of the faith produces steadfastness”; “Faith makes everything possible”; “Praising the Lord from the furnace”; “Martyrdom of Saint Stephen”; “Faith of the ancient patriarchs”; “Bear witness to the Lord in front of the people”. In the Latin calendar, St Bonaventure, bishop and Doctor (a memorial).
2027-07-15.verse: “Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven.
theo: The Church today keeps the memory of a mother and a child. According to the ancient Acts of the martyrs, which come down to us with some details we cannot verify, Julitta was a noble widow of Iconium who fled from the persecution of the emperor Diocletian, about the year 304, with her small son Cyricus, whom we call Kuriakose, who was about three years old. They were seized at Tarsus in Cilicia, the city of St Paul. The governor questioned the mother, and she confessed Christ. The little boy, taken up in the governor's arms, is said to have repeated after her, in his child's voice, “I am a Christian.” In anger the governor threw him down the steps of the tribunal, and he died. Julitta was tortured and beheaded. The details may have grown in the telling, but the memory of the Church has been steady: the faith of a mother and the faith of her child were stronger than the sword. Churches of the East and of the West honoured them early, and the name Kuriakose is cherished by Christians in Kerala to this day.

The readings for the day are chosen to help us understand them, and the seasonal readings of Kaitha speak to the same courage in ordinary life. James begins with a surprising command: “My brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of any kind, consider it nothing but joy, because you know that the testing of your faith produces endurance; and let endurance have its full effect, so that you may be mature and complete, lacking in nothing.” Joy here is not a pleasant feeling. It is the steady confidence that nothing God allows is wasted. And James knows that we are not strong: “If any of you is lacking in wisdom, ask God, who gives to all generously and ungrudgingly, and it will be given you.” The only condition is “in faith, never doubting”, for the doubter is like a wave tossed by the wind. A person under trial does not first need a plan; he first needs to ask, and to keep on asking, with a heart that holds to God.

Mark's Gospel gives the same lesson in a hard scene. Jesus is hungry and sees a fig tree in leaf, but it has no fruit. He says to it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again,” and the next morning the tree is withered to its roots. This is a sign in the manner of the prophets, who often pictured Israel as a tree that should have borne fruit (Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1). Mark places the tree on either side of the cleansing of the Temple, and the message is for every believer and every community: leaves without fruit, religion without justice and love, cannot stand before God. Peter notices the tree, and Jesus turns the moment into a lesson on prayer: “Have faith in God. Truly I tell you, if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and if you do not doubt in your heart, but believe that what you say will come to pass, it will be done for you.” The mountain is whatever stands before the work of God and looks immovable. Then the surprise: “Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone; so that your Father in heaven may also forgive you your trespasses.” Faith that moves mountains cannot live beside a grudge.

The readings of the martyrs carry us from prayer to witness. In Daniel the three young men walk in the middle of the furnace: “They walked around in the midst of the flames, singing hymns to God and blessing the Lord.” Then Azariah stands in the fire and prays. His prayer, which the Church reads as the Prayer of Azariah, confesses the sins of the people, asks God not to abandon them for the sake of his name, and offers what remains when every sacrifice has been taken away: a contrite heart and a humble spirit. They had already said to the king what the martyrs would say after them: “If our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the furnace of blazing fire and out of your hand, O king, let him deliver us. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods and we will not worship the golden statue that you have set up.” That “but if not” is the faith of the martyrs: they trust God whether he rescues them or not. In the Acts of the Apostles Stephen, “full of grace and power”, is dragged before the council by false witnesses, and “all who sat in the council looked intently at him, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.” The first martyr shows that witness shines before it bleeds.

The letter to the Hebrews gives the root of it all: “By faith we understand that the worlds were prepared by the word of God.” Abel, Enoch, Noah and Abraham each lived by what they could not see: “And without faith it is impossible to please God, for whoever would approach him must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.” Abraham “set out, not knowing where he was going”, and lived in tents, for “he looked forward to the city that has foundations, whose architect and builder is God.” Jesus's own words in Matthew complete the picture and give a mother and a child their strength: “See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.” “When they hand you over, do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say; for what you are to say will be given to you at that time; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” A three-year-old could say no more than “I am a Christian”, and that was exactly what the Spirit gave. “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. And even the hairs of your head are all counted. So do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.” And the promise on which all martyrs rest: “Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven.”
outline: Opening
A mother and a three-year-old at Tarsus: the courage of the smallest believer.
Point 1 · Trials and wisdom
Joy that knows nothing is wasted; ask God in faith, never doubting.
Point 2 · Faith, prayer and forgiveness
Leaves without fruit; the mountain that moves; a grudge that blocks the prayer.
Point 3 · Witness in the furnace
“But if not”; Stephen's face like an angel's; the Spirit speaks in the hour of trial.
Take-home line
“Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven.”
live: Ask for wisdom in faith (James 1:5–6)
Name one decision you are struggling with. Each morning this week ask God for wisdom in one short prayer, and take the next honest step without second-guessing.
Say it plainly and kindly (Matthew 10:32)
This week, when you are asked about your faith, whether at work, in the bus or in the neighbourhood, answer simply, without apology and without anger.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)
It is not the punishment but the cause that makes a martyr.
St Cyprian of Carthage (in substance)

He who is at odds with his brother cannot pray in peace. God does not accept the sacrifice of one who is in discord; he bids us first to be reconciled to a brother, and then to come and offer our gift.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
Christ did not say that we would never meet wolves; he said that he was sending us among wolves. Yet the sheep conquer, because the Shepherd is with them.
magis: Catechism 2474
The Church has carefully gathered the records of those who persevered to the end in witnessing to their faith. These are the official Acts of the Martyrs.
Catechism 2609–2610
Jesus asks for faith in prayer: “all things are possible to him who believes”. The prayer of faith is not only saying “Lord, Lord”, but a heart ready to do the will of the Father.
Catechism 2843
It is not in our power not to feel or to forget an offence; but the heart that offers itself to the Holy Spirit turns injury into compassion and purifies the memory.
saints: Second Thursday of Kaitha. Saint Kuriakose and Saint Julitta, martyrs (an Ordinary Feast of the Oriental tradition; martyred about 304, according to the ancient Acts). In the Latin calendar, St Bonaventure, bishop and Doctor of the Church (a memorial).

13–18 July: the second week of Kaitha. Tue 13 and Wed 14: Second Tuesday and Wednesday of Kaitha. Thu 15: Sts Kuriakose and Julitta, an Ordinary Feast of the Oriental tradition (in the Latin calendar, St Bonaventure). Fri 16: the Second Friday of Kaitha, Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai, and Our Lady of Mount Carmel, an Important Marian Feast. Sat 17: Second Saturday of Kaitha. Sun 18: Third Sunday of Kaitha. Looking ahead: St Mary Magdalene on Thursday 22 July, and St Alphonsa, the first woman of India to be raised to the altars, on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-15.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you called a mother and her little child to confess your name before the judge and you made them stronger than the sword. Give us a faith that rejoices in trials, that asks you for wisdom without doubt, and that forgives before it prays. When we are asked who we are, let your Spirit speak in us; when we are afraid, remind us that no sparrow falls without the Father. By the prayers of Saint Julitta and Saint Kuriakose, keep our children in your faith and bring us with them to the city whose builder is God. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Church stands with the martyrs, “the great cloud of witnesses”, around the altar where the Lord who was faithful unto death gives himself in his Body and Blood. In the same bread that strengthened Julitta and her child we receive the strength to forgive, to pray in faith, and to say plainly whose we are.

2027-07-18.title: Third Sunday of Kaitha
2027-07-18.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: I rejoice because you felt a godly grief
A man born blind receives sight and faith
2027-07-18.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which follows the Season of the Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when we remember the apostles, martyrs and saints who sowed the Gospel and watered it with their blood, and keep ourselves ready for the coming of the Lord. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar gives longer forms: Deuteronomy 5:1–16 and John 9:1–38. In the Latin calendar today is the Sixteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time. Looking ahead: St Mary Magdalene on Thursday 22 July, and St Alphonsa, the first woman of India to be raised to the altars, on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-18.verse: As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.
theo: On the Third Sunday of Kaitha the Church opens with the Ten Commandments, but the first word is not a command. “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” Before God asks anything, he recalls what he has done: the rescue of a people of slaves. The commandments are the way of life for people already saved, the house rules of a father for the children he has carried out of Egypt. “You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not make for yourself an idol.” The jealous God is the lover who will not share his beloved with anything that cannot love her back. The text speaks of the damage of sin that passes from parents to children, and sets beside it the greater truth that God shows “steadfast love to the thousandth generation of those who love me and keep my commandments”; the prophet Ezekiel teaches clearly that each person answers for his own sin (Ezekiel 18:20). Then come the Name and the Sabbath: “You shall not make wrongful use of the name of the Lord your God.” “Observe the sabbath day and keep it holy, as the Lord your God commanded you.” Deuteronomy gives the Sabbath a reason of mercy and of memory: rest for the worker, and “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the Lord your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm.” The Church keeps the first day of the week, the day of the Lord's Resurrection, in the same spirit: rest for all, especially for those who work for us, and thanksgiving to the God who saves. The reading ends with the commandment that opens the second table of the law: “Honor your father and your mother, as the Lord your God commanded you, so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you.”

Isaiah sings what sounds like a love-song: “Let me sing for my beloved my love-song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it; he expected it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes.” Every verb is a work of love: digging, clearing, planting, building. Then the singer turns to the listeners and asks them to judge: “What more was there to do for my vineyard that I have not done in it? When I expected it to yield grapes, why did it yield wild grapes?” The question is the cry of a God who has done everything and whose love has been met with fruit that tastes sour. Then the verdict, and the meaning of the song: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the people of Judah are his pleasant planting; he expected justice, but saw bloodshed; righteousness, but heard a cry!” In Hebrew the words sound alike: mishpat (justice) and mispach (bloodshed), tsedaqah (righteousness) and tse'aqah (a cry). Wherever people use their power to hurt the weak, the cry of the wronged goes up. Isaiah speaks to God's own people, and the Church hears it as addressed to herself. Anyone who has tended pepper vines or paddy in Kerala knows the labour and the waiting for the harvest; the Lord waits in the same way for the fruit of our lives. And in John's Gospel Jesus names himself the true vine and says, “Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit.”

Paul's letter shows how the vineyard bears fruit. He begins with the promises, “Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and of spirit, making holiness perfect in the fear of God,” and then he opens his heart: “Make room in your hearts for us.” He tells of his own trial in Macedonia: “disputes without and fears within.” “But God, who consoles the downcast, consoled us by the arrival of Titus.” The center of the reading is a distinction every Christian must learn: “Now I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because your grief led to repentance; for you felt a godly grief... For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret, but worldly grief produces death.” Worldly grief is sorrow that looks at itself: it is shame at being found out, regret for what it cost me, and it ends in bitterness or despair. Godly grief looks at God and at the harm done to others; it ends in a turning back. The Church's tradition has seen the two in the two apostles who failed: Judas, who was filled with remorse but did not turn to the Lord, and Peter, who “went out and wept bitterly” and was restored. Saint Ambrose said of Peter (in substance): I do not find what he said in his defence; I find that he wept. Paul lists the fruits: “what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what zeal.” This is the vineyard's grapes. The Church offers the sacrament of Reconciliation, our confession, as the place where godly grief becomes joy.

The Gospel is a story of sight. “As he walked along, he saw a man blind from birth. His disciples asked him, ‘Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?’” People then, and now, ask where to put the blame. Jesus refuses the question: “Neither this man nor his parents sinned; he was born blind so that God’s works might be revealed in him.” Suffering is not always a punishment; it can be the place where the work of God will be seen. “We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming when no one can work. As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” Then the strange action: “he spat on the ground and made mud with the saliva and spread the mud on the man’s eyes, saying to him, ‘Go, wash in the pool of Siloam’ (which means Sent).” The Fathers saw here the Word made flesh using earth, like the creator who made the first man from the clay, and they saw in the pool of Siloam, “Sent”, the baptism that Jesus, the Sent One, gives; baptism was long called “illumination”. The man does what he is told: “Then he went and washed and came back able to see.” His neighbours cannot believe it: “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?” He says simply, “I am the man.” When they ask who healed him he says only, “The man called Jesus made mud, spread it on my eyes, and said to me, ‘Go to Siloam and wash.’ Then I went and washed and received my sight.” “Where is he?” “I do not know.” His sight is real, and his faith has hardly begun.

The reading then skips what follows, the questioning by those who disliked what had happened and the man's growing courage, and returns at the end: “Jesus heard that they had driven him out, and when he found him, he said, ‘Do you believe in the Son of Man?’” The Lord goes looking for the one who has been cast out. The man answers, “And who is he, sir? Tell me, so that I may believe in him.” Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.” Then the whole journey comes to rest in one sentence: “He said, ‘Lord, I believe.’ And he worshiped him.” First he called Jesus “the man called Jesus”; now he says “Lord”. The eyes opened first; the heart is opened later; and the first sight of his life ends with worship. Put the four readings together and the shape of the Season of Kaitha appears: the law of the God who has saved us, the vineyard that must bear fruit, the grief that turns us back, and the light that lets us see the Lord and say, “Lord, I believe.”
conn: Out of the house of slavery.
“I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2); “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15).
The Lord's Day.
“The sabbath was made for humankind, and not humankind for the sabbath” (Mark 2:27); “I was in the spirit on the Lord’s day” (Revelation 1:10).
The vine and the branches.
“I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).
A broken and contrite heart.
“The sacrifice acceptable to God is a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17); “And he went out and wept bitterly” (Luke 22:62).
For God's glory.
“But when Jesus heard it, he said, ‘This illness does not lead to death; rather it is for God’s glory, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it’” (John 11:4).
The light of the world.

“I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness but will have the light of life” (John 8:12); “Sleeper, awake! Rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” (Ephesians 5:14).
altar: Every Sunday at the Holy Qurbana the Church hears the law, the song of the vineyard, the voice of the apostle and the Gospel, and then goes to the altar, where the Lord who is the true vine gives his own Blood as the fruit of the vineyard. As we come to Communion we can say, with the man born blind, “Lord, I believe”; and the bread and cup are the light that opens our eyes to know him.

The Sunday itself is the first of the commandments' gifts: the day of rest and the day of the Resurrection. When we come to church, rest from our work, and receive the Body of the Lord, we keep the Sabbath in its full meaning: not a rule that weighs us down, but the day on which God saves us again.
outline: Opening
Grace before law: the God who brought us out of slavery gives us the commandments.
Point 1 · The Ten Words
Love before law; the Name and the Lord's Day; honouring parents.
Point 2 · The vineyard
What more could God have done? Justice and righteousness are the fruit he looks for.
Point 3 · Godly grief
Worldly grief and godly grief; Judas and Peter; the fruits of repentance.
Point 4 · Sight and faith
The man born blind: mud, Siloam and the Sent One; “Lord, I believe.”
Take-home line
“As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”
live: Keep the Lord's Day (Deuteronomy 5:12–15)
This Sunday, rest from unnecessary work, give your household and those who serve you a real day of rest, and spend time with God and your family.
Turn back with godly grief (2 Corinthians 7:10)
Examine one habit that has borne wild grapes. Go to confession this month, and do one act of reparation to someone you have hurt.
fathers: St Irenaeus of Lyons (in substance)

The Lord did not abolish the commandments of the law, but extended and fulfilled them: he did not loosen the bonds of love; he asked for a greater obedience and a nearer love, so that we might follow him with a whole heart.
St Ambrose of Milan (in substance)
I do not find what Peter said in his defence; I find that he wept. I read of his tears, not of his excuses. Tears wash away what shame cannot say.
St Augustine (in substance)

Siloam means Sent, and who was sent but Christ? He anointed the eyes of the blind man with clay, and then he sent him to the pool; the clay was the Word made flesh, and the washing was the baptism in which we are enlightened.
magis: Catechism 2060
The Decalogue must first be understood in the context of the Exodus, the great event of God's saving intervention at the centre of the Old Covenant.
Catechism 2174
Jesus rose from the dead on the first day of the week. As the day of Christ's Resurrection, Sunday is the Lord's Day, the foundation and kernel of the whole liturgical year.
Catechism 1431
Interior penance is a radical reorientation of our whole life, a return to God with all our heart, and an end of sin.
Catechism 1216
Baptism is called “enlightenment” because those who receive it are enlightened in the mind.
saints: Third Sunday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar, the Sixteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
Mon 19, Tue 20 and Wed 21: Kaitha weekdays. Thu 22: St Mary Magdalene, apostle of the apostles. Fri 23: Third Friday of Kaitha. Sun 25: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha. Wed 28: St Alphonsa.
2027-07-18.prayer: Lord our God, you brought your people out of slavery and gave them a law of love; you planted your vineyard with the care of a lover and looked for justice. Give us the grief that turns us back to you and the fruit that pleases you. As you opened the eyes of the man born blind, open ours to see your works and to worship you. Teach us to keep your Sunday with joy, to honour our parents, to love our neighbour, and to say with our whole life, “Lord, I believe.” We ask this through Jesus Christ, the light of the world, who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.

2027-07-25.title: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha
2027-07-25.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The law given through Moses: honour your father and mother
A people who did not turn to the one who struck them
Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord
Do not make void the word of God through your tradition
2027-07-25.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, summer), which began on 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when she remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her with their blood and waits in readiness for the Lord's coming. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “The law is through Moses”; “Punishment to Israel for false doings”; “Be proud in the Lord Jesus”; “Do not reject the word of God to keep your tradition”. The calendar gives longer forms: Deuteronomy 5:16–6:3; Isaiah 9:8–21; 2 Corinthians 10:1–18; Mark 7:1–23. St James the Apostle (25 July) gives way to the Sunday. Today is also the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly (instituted by Pope Francis in 2021, kept near the feast of Sts Joachim and Anne). In the Latin calendar today is the Seventeenth Sunday in Ordinary Time (the feeding of the five thousand, John 6).
2027-07-25.verse: You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.
theo: The Fourth Sunday of Kaitha puts side by side two things that people often think are rivals: the commandment of God and the traditions of men. The Gospel opens with a scene any Kerala household would know. The Pharisees and some scribes who had come from Jerusalem notice that the disciples eat without first washing their hands. Washing before meals, and washing cups, pots and bronze kettles, was a devout custom of pious Jews, and in itself a good one; Jesus himself does not condemn the custom. What he condemns is the use of such a custom to set aside what God has plainly said. Their question, “Why do your disciples not live according to the tradition of the elders?”, is answered with a sentence from Isaiah, who prophesied that this people “honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me.” We should hear this as a debate among the people of God, in which Jesus speaks as a Jewish teacher to other Jewish teachers, and as a warning to every community that has traditions, including ours.

Then Jesus gives a precise example, and it is about parents. “Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother.’” That is the fourth commandment of the first reading: “Honor your father and your mother, as the Lord your God commanded you, so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land.” Some, however, had arranged that whatever support a son might have given his parents could be declared “Corban,” dedicated to God, and so withheld from the father and mother who needed it. It looked pious, and it killed a commandment. The lesson is plain: no offering, no donation, no ornament on the church and no vow can replace the daily care of an old father or mother. “Then you no longer permit doing anything for a father or mother, thus making void the word of God through your tradition.” On this Sunday, when many parishes and families remember grandparents and the elderly, the Gospel asks a very practical question: who is sitting alone in the back room of our house?

The first reading takes us to Horeb, where Moses recalls the ten words and the fire. “These words the Lord spoke with a loud voice to your whole assembly at the mountain, out of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness, and he added no more. He wrote them on two stone tablets.” The people were afraid, and said: “Today we have seen that God may speak to someone and the person may still live.” God's law is not a burden placed on us to catch us out. It is the voice of the living God out of the fire, spoken so that people may live. The commandment about parents stands at the head of the second table because the family is where every child first learns to hear a voice that asks for love and gives life in return.

Isaiah shows what happens when a people hears no voice at all. “The people did not turn to him who struck them, or seek the Lord of hosts.” The leaders led them astray, and the prophets who taught lies were the tail; the orphans and widows found no compassion; wickedness burned like a fire; “Manasseh devoured Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh.” Brother devours brother, and the fire of the sin of a people finally burns the people. It is a hard reading, and it is not a prophecy about other people only. Wherever a family fights over land and inheritance, wherever relatives stop speaking for years, we are in the world of Manasseh and Ephraim. The Lord's hand, says the prophet, “is stretched out still”: stretched out in judgment, and, as the Church reads it, still stretched out to call us back.

Paul's short passage in the second reading supplies the remedy: measure yourself by the Lord and not by one another. The Corinthians' rivals commended themselves and compared themselves with each other, which, says Paul, “does not show good sense.” He will boast only within the field that God has assigned to him, and he will not boast in the labours of others. The whole passage closes with a sentence from Jeremiah that he also uses in his first letter: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For the Church in Kerala the sentence is a good guard against the pride of old families, rich parishes, big feasts and fine buildings. “For it is not those who commend themselves that are approved, but those whom the Lord commends.” The Lord commends the one who honours a father and a mother, who keeps a clean heart, and who listens when God speaks from the fire.
conn: Honour father and mother.

“Honor your father and your mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the Lord your God is giving you” (Exodus 20:12); “Honor your father and mother” is “the first commandment with a promise” (Ephesians 6:2).
Care in old age.

“My child, help your father in his old age, and do not grieve him as long as he lives” (Sirach 3:12); “Listen to your father who begot you, and do not despise your mother when she is old” (Proverbs 23:22).
Lips and heart.

“The Lord said: Because these people draw near with their mouths and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their worship of me is a human commandment learned by rote” (Isaiah 29:13).
What defiles.

“It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but it is what comes out of the mouth that defiles” (Matthew 15:11); “For it is from within, from the human heart, that evil intentions come” (Mark 7:21).
The fire of God.
“Our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29); at Pentecost “divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them” (Acts 2:3).
Boast in the Lord.

“Let those who boast boast in this, that they understand and know me, that I am the Lord; I act with steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth” (Jeremiah 9:24); “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).
altar: The word Qurbana comes from the same root as Corban, the gift that is brought near to God. At the Holy Qurbana nothing is withheld from God and nothing is taken from the poor: what we bring is bread and wine, and with it our work, our care for our parents and our children. Christ the true Offering gives himself to us, and the heart, not only the lips, is nourished.

The altar and the family table are not rivals. The Lord who gives his Body and Blood at the altar sends us home to wash the feet and share the meal of the father and mother, the grandfather and grandmother, who are waiting there. Whoever goes from the Qurbana and forgets the old person at home has taken the Corban and left the commandment.
outline: Opening
Washed hands and clean hearts: what do the traditions of our homes and parishes serve?
Point 1 · The voice out of the fire
The Ten Words are God's own voice, given for life; the fourth commandment opens the table of love.
Point 2 · Corban and the commandment
No offering replaces the care of parents; the word of God must not be made void by our tradition.
Point 3 · The fire that devours and the one who boasts
Manasseh and Ephraim: families that devour each other; boast only in the Lord.
Take-home line
“You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.” Let us return to the commandment.
live: Honour your parents (Deuteronomy 5:16)
Visit, telephone or sit with a parent, a grandparent or an elderly neighbour this week, and ask them to tell you a story of their faith.
Weigh your offerings (Mark 7:11–12)
Ask whether any gift you give to the Church or a charity is a way of avoiding a duty at home. Meet the duty at home first.
Wash the heart (Mark 7:15)
Before going to the Holy Qurbana this week, say a short prayer: “Create in me a clean heart.” Then name one bitter word you will not speak.
Make peace in the family (Isaiah 9:21)
If two relatives are not speaking, try to bring them together this week, or at least pray for them by name.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Honour of parents is the first lesson of love. Do not think that you have done enough when you have given gifts at the altar and left your father to want. The one who is cruel to the parent who bore him cannot be pleasing to the Lord whom he has not seen.
St Augustine (in substance)

What makes a person unclean is not the food that goes in but the heart that is evil. Wash the heart, and you will have washed all. The Lord looks first at the inside of the cup, and the inside is the heart.
St Gregory the Great (in substance)
Those who boast in the Lord boast in what is true, since they know that whatever good they have is a gift. The one who boasts in himself builds on sand; the one who boasts in the Lord builds on rock.
magis: Catechism 2197

The fourth commandment opens the second table of the Decalogue. It shows us the order of charity: after God, we are to honour our parents, who have given us life and handed on to us the knowledge of God.
Catechism 2218
Respect for parents shows itself in obedience while children live in the home, and in later years in gratitude, care and company when parents are old, ill, lonely or in distress.
Catechism 83

The Tradition that comes from the apostles hands on what they received from Jesus' teaching and example. It is to be distinguished from the theological, disciplinary, liturgical or devotional traditions born over time in the local Churches, which the Church's authority may keep, modify or abandon.
Catechism 2060
The Ten Commandments belong to God's Revelation. At the same time they teach us the true humanity of man, and they are given as a covenant in which God and the people are bound together.
saints: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha. St James the Apostle (25 July) gives way to the Sunday. World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly. In the Latin calendar, the Seventeenth Sunday in Ordinary Time.

Mon 26: Sts Joachim and Anne. Wed 28: St Alphonsa. Thu 29: St Martha. Sat 31: St Ignatius of Loyola. Karkidakam, the heart of the monsoon, begins in mid-July: many families read the Bible and pray the rosary together at home in the long wet evenings.

25–31 July: the fourth week of the Season of Kaitha. Sun 25: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha (St James the Apostle gives way to the Sunday; World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly). Mon 26: Sts Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Wed 28: St Alphonsa, the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised, an important feast. Thu 29: St Martha. Fri 30: Fourth Friday of Kaitha. Sat 31: St Ignatius of Loyola. In the Latin calendar the same days keep Sts Joachim and Anne (26), St Alphonsa (28, a memorial in India), Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus (29) and St Ignatius (31). Looking ahead: the month of August and the later weeks of Kaitha.
2027-07-25.prayer: Lord God, you spoke to your people out of the fire and gave them your commandments that they might live. Teach us to honour our fathers and mothers, to care for them in their old age and to respect the elders of our parish and of every family. Keep our worship from becoming a habit of the lips while the heart is far from you. Heal every family in which brother is set against brother, and make us boast in you alone. Through the prayers of Sts Joachim and Anne, grandparents of your Son, bless the old people of our homes. Amen.

2027-07-01.title: Seventh Thursday of the Apostles
2027-07-01.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The light of the Gospel shines in the face of Christ
Woe to the teachers who lock people out and play with oaths
2027-07-01.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations.
