The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. This is the last weekend of the season: the Season of Kaitha begins on Sunday 4 July. The calendar's own headings: “Treasure in clay jars”; “Hypocrisy of the Pharisees and Scribes”. In Matthew 23 the Malayalam Bible numbers the verses a little differently from the English: the English verse 13 is the Malayalam verses 13–14.
2027-07-01.verse: For it is the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
theo: On the last Thursday of the Season of the Apostles the Church sets two kinds of preaching side by side: a preacher who has nothing to hide, and teachers who have forgotten why they speak. Paul begins with a sentence of quiet courage: “Therefore, since it is by God’s mercy that we are engaged in this ministry, we do not lose heart.” He writes to the Corinthians, who had heard from other teachers that Paul was unimpressive and unreliable. He does not answer with an attack. He answers with his way of working: “We have renounced the shameful things that one hides; we refuse to practice cunning or to falsify God’s word; but by the open statement of the truth we commend ourselves to the conscience of everyone in the sight of God.” A messenger of the Gospel has no secret plan. He does not bend the word to please, to frighten or to gain. He puts the truth in the open and lets every conscience judge it, because God is watching.

Paul is honest also about the sorrow of preaching: “And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.” We read this with sorrow, not with scorn. Paul is not speaking of our neighbours of other faiths, whom the Church respects; he speaks of the blindness that can fall on any heart, ours included, when money, comfort or reputation take the place of God. Then comes the sentence that every priest, catechist, parish council member and parent can test their work against: “For we do not proclaim ourselves; we proclaim Jesus Christ as Lord and ourselves as your slaves for Jesus’ sake.” Am I proclaiming Christ, or myself? The reading ends in light: “For it is the God who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” Paul has the first day of creation in mind (“Then God said, ‘Let there be light’; and there was light”) and his own day outside Damascus. The light of God is not only an idea; it has a face, and we see it in Jesus.

The Gospel takes us into the Temple in the last days of Jesus' ministry, where he speaks sharply to the scribes and Pharisees. We must hear these words as the Church hears them. Jesus is a Jew speaking to his own people, in the manner of the prophets, who also scolded priests and teachers out of love for the covenant. The “woes” are not a verdict on a whole people, and the Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in his Passion cannot be charged against all Jews of that time or of ours (Nostra Aetate 4). They are a warning to every religious leader and every believer, and so to us. The first woe: “you lock people out of the kingdom of heaven. For you do not go in yourselves, and when others are going in, you stop them.” Religion can become a gatekeeper instead of a door. The second: a zeal that crosses “sea and land to make a single convert”, but without the truth and love that make a person new. A Church that is busy and loud but has not itself been converted can do harm.

Then Jesus turns to oaths. The teachers had made a system of fine distinctions: an oath by the sanctuary binds nothing, but an oath by the gold of the sanctuary binds; an oath by the altar binds nothing, but an oath by the gift on the altar binds. Jesus answers with plain questions: “which is greater, the gold or the sanctuary that has made the gold sacred?” and “which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred?” Then he closes every loophole: “So whoever swears by the altar, swears by it and by everything on it; and whoever swears by the sanctuary, swears by it and by the one who dwells in it; and whoever swears by heaven, swears by the throne of God and by the one who is seated upon it.” God is present in every word spoken before him, and there is no small oath that he does not hear. In a country where people swear by temples, by their children and by God in courts and markets, this is very practical. The Catechism teaches that the holiness of God's name forbids false and careless oaths (CCC 2153–2155). Let our word be so true that no oath is needed: “Let your word be ‘Yes, Yes’ or ‘No, No’.” The apostle who does not falsify God's word and the believer whose Yes is Yes are the people through whom the light of Christ's face reaches others.
conn: Light out of darkness.
“Then God said, ‘Let there be light’; and there was light” (Genesis 1:3); “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it” (John 1:5).
The image of God.
“He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15).
Treasure in clay jars.

“But we have this treasure in clay jars, so that it may be made clear that this extraordinary power belongs to God and does not come from us” (2 Corinthians 4:7): the calendar's heading for today's Epistle.
Yes and No.
“Let your word be ‘Yes, Yes’ or ‘No, No’; anything more than this comes from the evil one” (Matthew 5:37).
Lips and hearts.
“Because these people draw near with their mouths and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me” (Isaiah 29:13).
The gift and the altar.

“So when you are offering your gift at the altar, if you remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23–24).
outline: Opening
Two kinds of speaking: the open statement of the truth, and clever words that hide the heart.
Point 1 · We do not lose heart
Paul's ministry: no cunning, no falsifying of God's word, no proclaiming of ourselves.
Point 2 · The light in the face of Christ
Let light shine out of darkness: the Gospel has a face.
Point 3 · Woe to the gatekeepers
Religion that locks the door, and zeal without conversion.
Point 4 · The sacred and the oath
The altar and the sanctuary make holy; every word is spoken before God.
Take-home line
“Let your word be ‘Yes, Yes’ or ‘No, No’.”
live: One honest word (Matthew 5:37)
Choose one promise you made and put off, a debt, a visit, a call, and keep it this week. Let your Yes be Yes.
Test your message (2 Corinthians 4:5)
Before you speak in the parish, at home or online, ask: does this point people to Christ, or to me? Delete what points only to you.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The person who understands that an oath is not among the good things but among the necessary ones restrains himself as much as he can from using it, and swears only when there is a necessity. Truthful people do not need many words.
St Gregory the Great (in substance)

Whoever is compelled by his rank to speak of the highest things is compelled by the same rank to show the highest things in his life. Words that the preacher's own life does not support do not reach the heart.
magis: Catechism 2153–2155 (in substance)

The second commandment forbids false and careless oaths. The Lord teaches his disciples to say simply Yes or No, and the Church allows an oath only for a grave and just reason, in truth, in judgement and in justice.
Catechism 2468 (in substance)
Truthfulness, or sincerity, is the virtue of showing oneself true in deeds and truthful in words, guarding against duplicity, dissimulation and hypocrisy.
saints: Seventh Thursday of the Apostles. In popular devotion July is the month of the Precious Blood of Jesus; many families pray the litany of the Precious Blood this month. July also brings the heart of the monsoon in Kerala.

1–6 July: the last three days of the Season of the Apostles, then the opening of the Season of Kaitha. Thu 1: Seventh Thursday of the Apostles. Fri 2: the Seventy Disciples of Jesus, and the First Friday. Sat 3: the Dukhrana of St Thomas, an important feast and a day of obligation. Sun 4: First Sunday of Kaitha, the Feast of the Twelve Apostles. Mon 5 and Tue 6: the first Monday and Tuesday of Kaitha; on Tuesday also St Maria Goretti. Looking ahead: Fri 9 July, the First Friday of Kaitha, St James of Nisibis.
2027-07-01.prayer: Lord God, you said, “Let light shine out of darkness”, and you have shone in our hearts in the face of Jesus Christ. Keep us from every cunning and every double heart. Make us preachers who proclaim your Son and not ourselves, believers whose Yes is Yes, and a Church that is a door and not a gatekeeper. Teach us to speak every word as in your sight, and let the light of Christ's face shine in our homes and parishes. Through Christ our Lord, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, for ever. Amen.
altar: The altar makes the gift holy, Jesus says, and the gift on the altar is not a thing to swear by but a sacrifice to offer. At the Holy Qurbana the bread and wine are placed on the altar, and with them our word, our work and our reconciliations: “first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.” The Lord who dwells in the sanctuary and sits on the throne of God gives himself to us there, so that we may carry his light, in clay jars, into every word we speak.

2027-07-02.title: Seventh Friday of the Apostles · The Seventy Disciples of Jesus · First Friday
2027-07-02.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: I will open rivers on the bare heights
Paul proclaims the promised Saviour at Antioch
Who will separate us from the love of Christ?
The cost of discipleship, and its reward
2027-07-02.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. This is the last weekend of the season: the Season of Kaitha begins on Sunday 4 July. The calendar keeps today as the day of the Seventy Disciples of Jesus, with four readings, and marks it as the First Friday. Its own headings: “Protecting love of God”; “Proclaiming the Messiah, the promised one”; “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?”; “The cost of discipleship and reward”. The calendar's longer forms are Isaiah 41:8–20; Acts 13:13–23; Romans 8:28–9:5; Matthew 10:37–11:15. Verify locally how the parish keeps the First Friday. Some ancient manuscripts of Luke 10:1 read seventy-two, and the Malayalam Bible (POC) has seventy-two; the calendar and our tradition say seventy.
2027-07-02.verse: Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.
theo: Today the Church remembers a large and nameless band: the Seventy Disciples of Jesus. “After this the Lord appointed seventy others and sent them on ahead of him in pairs to every town and place where he himself intended to go. He said to them, ‘The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.’” Notice the word “others”. Jesus had already sent the Twelve; now he sends seventy more, ordinary disciples whose names the Gospel does not give. The mission of the Church does not belong only to bishops and priests; it belongs to every baptised person (CCC 863). The number echoes the seventy elders on whom God put the spirit of Moses, when Moses said, “Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets, and that the Lord would put his spirit on them!” Our East Syriac tradition counts Mar Addai among the Seventy and tells that he was sent to Edessa, and Mar Mari after him; their names are on the Anaphora of Addai and Mari with which we celebrate the Holy Qurbana. So the Seventy are not far away from us: every Sunday we pray with words that come from their mission.

The first reading is for the thirsty. The exiles of Israel were far from home, poor and parched, and God speaks to them: “When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I the Lord will answer them, I the God of Israel will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the bare heights, and fountains in the midst of the valleys; I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water.” Before this, God had said, “do not fear, for I am with you.” The Seventy go out into a dry world with only that promise. In Kerala this week the rain is falling on dry wells and paddy fields, and the image is easy to see: where the Gospel arrives, springs open. Jesus himself stood on the last day of the festival and cried, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink.” The Seventy carry that cry from house to house.

In the second reading Paul stands up in the synagogue at Antioch in Pisidia, having been sent off by the Church with fasting and prayer and the laying on of hands, and he begins not with himself but with the history of God's faithfulness: “The God of this people Israel chose our ancestors and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it.” Forty years in the wilderness, the judges, Samuel, Saul, and then David, “a man after my heart, who will carry out all my wishes.” And at the end: “Of this man’s posterity God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised.” Paul speaks as a son of Israel to his own people, and the Church remembers that she draws her life from that holy root. A good missionary tells first what God has done, and only then what we must do.

The Epistle is for those who are afraid, and every missionary is afraid at times. “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose.” Then Paul asks the questions that make a coward brave: “If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not withhold his own Son, but gave him up for all of us, will he not with him also give us everything else?” And the great question: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will hardship, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” Jesus had said that he was sending the Seventy “like lambs into the midst of wolves”; Paul's answer is the answer of those who have come back with joy: “No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” Today is also the First Friday, when the Church thinks of the open heart of the Lord, from which “at once blood and water came out”. That heart is the love from which, as Paul says, “neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor rulers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor anything else in all creation” can separate us (CCC 478).

The Gospel tells the price and the pay of discipleship. The price: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” Jesus does not ask us to love our families less; the Catechism reminds us that he asks us to put him first, and then we love them rightly (CCC 2232). “Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.” The pay: not great wages but small welcomes. “Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.” The Seventy needed hosts, people who would say “Peace to this house!” and open a door, and the Lord counts the host as a partner in the mission. “And whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, none of these will lose their reward.” In Kerala the first thing a guest receives is a glass of water; Jesus says that this ordinary kindness is seen in heaven. The whole world is evangelised, in the end, by a thousand glasses of water and a few brave people who walk to the next village.
conn: Seventy elders.
“Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets, and that the Lord would put his spirit on them!” (Numbers 11:29).
Like lambs.
“Go on your way. See, I am sending you out like lambs into the midst of wolves” (Luke 10:3); “The seventy returned with joy” (Luke 10:17).
Rivers in the desert.
“Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink” (John 7:37).
Sent by the Spirit.
“Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2).
The least of these.
“Just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).
Beautiful feet.
“How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” (Romans 10:15).
outline: Opening
Seventy others: the nameless disciples, and the glass of water.
Point 1 · Sent in pairs
The harvest is plentiful; the mission belongs to every baptised person; Addai and Mari among the Seventy.
Point 2 · Rivers in the desert
God answers the thirsty; the Gospel opens springs.
Point 3 · If God is for us
Paul's story of God's faithfulness; nothing separates us from the love of Christ; the First Friday and the open heart.
Point 4 · The price and the pay
Christ first; the cross; welcome and the cup of cold water.
Take-home line
“Whoever welcomes you welcomes me.”
live: Pray for labourers (Luke 10:2)
Pray each day this week, by name, for one priest, one sister or brother, and one lay missionary, and ask the Lord of the harvest for more.
Offer a cup of water (Matthew 10:42)
Welcome someone this week in the name of Christ: a new neighbour, a visitor to the parish, a person who is lonely. Begin with a glass of water and a few minutes of your time.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

The harvest is indeed great, but the labourers are few. We cannot say this without sorrow: there are people ready to hear good things, and there are too few to speak them. Let us ask the Lord of the harvest to send labourers, and let those who hear be ready to be sent.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
Paul counted the love of Christ as greater than everything else the Lord could give. He said that to be loved by Christ is more than any kingdom, and that it was worth any suffering.
magis: Catechism 863 (in substance)
The whole Church is apostolic, and all her members, each in his own way, share in her mission. The vocation of the Christian is also a vocation to the apostolate.
Catechism 478 (in substance)
The Son of God loved us with a human heart; the pierced heart of Jesus, wounded for our sins and for our salvation, is the sign of the love with which he loves us.
saints: Seventh Friday of the Apostles: the Seventy Disciples of Jesus. The First Friday: many parishes keep it with Holy Qurbana, adoration and the devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus (verify locally).

1–6 July: the last three days of the Season of the Apostles, then the opening of the Season of Kaitha. Thu 1: Seventh Thursday of the Apostles. Fri 2: the Seventy Disciples of Jesus, and the First Friday. Sat 3: the Dukhrana of St Thomas, an important feast and a day of obligation. Sun 4: First Sunday of Kaitha, the Feast of the Twelve Apostles. Mon 5 and Tue 6: the first Monday and Tuesday of Kaitha; on Tuesday also St Maria Goretti. Looking ahead: Fri 9 July, the First Friday of Kaitha, St James of Nisibis.
2027-07-02.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you sent seventy disciples ahead of you, two by two, to every place where you meant to go. Send labourers into your harvest, and give us hearts open to be sent and doors open to welcome. Open rivers in the dry places of our time; keep us in your love, from which nothing can separate us; and teach us to love you above all and to give a cup of cold water in your name. By the open heart that you showed us on the cross, make us missionaries of your mercy, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Church uses the words handed down from Mar Addai and Mar Mari, two of the disciples whom tradition counts among the Seventy. The Lord who sent them sends us from every Qurbana with the words “Go in peace”; and the Heart that gave blood and water gives us in the Eucharist the love from which nothing can separate us. “Whoever welcomes you welcomes me”: he welcomes us at his table so that we may welcome others.

2027-07-05.title: First Monday of Kaitha
2027-07-05.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: When you come together, is it really the Lord's supper?
Do the will of the Father
2027-07-05.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which opens on the Sunday after the Dukhrana of St Thomas: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church contemplates its growth and harvest, in the apostles, martyrs and saints who watered the Church with their blood. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “There should not be divisions among you”; “Do the will of the Father”. The Gospel is the parable of the two sons; in the Malayalam Bible (POC) the order of the two sons is reversed, with the first saying “I will go” and not going, and the second saying “I will not” and later going: the lesson is the same.
2027-07-05.verse: For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
theo: On the first Monday of Kaitha the Church begins the season of summer and harvest with an uncomfortable passage, and that is a mercy. Paul writes to the Corinthians about what happened when they came together for the Lord's Supper. “Now in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. For, to begin with, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you; and to some extent I believe it.” In the first century the Eucharist was celebrated within a shared meal. At Corinth the rich arrived early and ate and drank their own food, and the poor, who had to work until evening, arrived to find nothing left. “When you come together, it is not really to eat the Lord’s supper. For when the time comes to eat, each of you goes ahead with your own supper, and one goes hungry and another becomes drunk.” Paul is angry, and his anger is love for the poor: “What! Do you not have homes to eat and drink in? Or do you show contempt for the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What should I say to you? Should I commend you? In this matter I do not commend you!” Yesterday's Epistle asked, “Has Christ been divided?”; today's shows how a community can divide the very table of unity. The verse in between, “there have to be factions among you, for only so will it become clear who among you are genuine”, does not praise division. It says that when divisions appear, the way people act shows who really lives by Christ.

Paul does not stop at rebuke. The very next verses, which the Church has always kept beside today's passage, give the oldest written account of the Eucharist, set down about the year 55, before any of the Gospels: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, ‘This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ In the same way he took the cup also, after supper, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.’ For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.” This is the Qurbana in its first form. The bread is his body given for us, the cup his blood; the Qurbana is the memorial of his death and the pledge of his coming. And the Church holds, in her faith in the Real Presence, that what is on the altar after the consecration is truly the Body and Blood of Christ (CCC 1374). That is why Paul says elsewhere, “The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.” To eat the one bread and to despise the hungry brother is a contradiction. “For all who eat and drink without discerning the body, eat and drink judgment against themselves.” To discern the body means to recognise Christ in the bread, and also in the community gathered round it, and above all in its poorest member (CCC 1385, 1397).

The Gospel is a short parable which asks us a question: “What do you think?” Jesus has been teaching in the Temple, where the chief priests and the elders of the people have come to him to ask, “By what authority are you doing these things?” He answers with a story. “A man had two sons; he went to the first and said, ‘Son, go and work in the vineyard today.’ He answered, ‘I will not’; but later he changed his mind and went. The father went to the second and said the same; and he answered, ‘I go, sir’; but he did not go. Which of the two did the will of his father?” They give the plain answer: the one who went, whatever he first said. Jesus then says, “Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes are going into the kingdom of God ahead of you. For John came to you in the way of righteousness and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him; and even after you saw it, you did not change your minds and believe him.” The parable is told to the leaders who were questioning him, and it is not a verdict on a people. It is a call to every one of us to change our minds: the tax collectors, who had said No to God by their way of life, heard John and turned back; those who said Yes in their words did not follow through in their lives. The word of the Gospel here is the same word the Church uses for repentance: a change of mind and heart.

The parable fits Paul's rebuke exactly. The Corinthians were saying “I go, sir” every Sunday, with the Lord's Supper on their lips, and they were not doing the Father's will, which is love for the poor brother and sister at the same table. “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven.” The Catechism teaches that we enter the kingdom not by speaking but by doing the Father's will, and that prayer is where we learn it (CCC 2826). Jesus himself is the Son who always says Yes: “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me”; and Mary, the first disciple, said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.” And the first son gives us hope: a No said in anger or fear or pride is not final. “Bear fruit worthy of repentance.” Kaitha is the season of fruit. In these monsoon weeks, when the fields must be sown and tended in the rain, the father's word is very concrete: “go and work in the vineyard today.” Not tomorrow, and not only when it is convenient. Today, this Monday, with our hands, at the table of the Lord and the table of the poor, we say Yes.
conn: One bread, one body.
“Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17).
Reconciled first.
“Leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24).
Sharing everything.
“All who believed were together and had all things in common; they would sell their possessions and goods and distribute the proceeds to all, as any had need” (Acts 2:44–45).
Share your bread.
“Is it not to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house?” (Isaiah 58:7).
Not everyone who says Lord, Lord.
“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven” (Matthew 7:21).
Rend your hearts.
“Rend your hearts and not your clothing. Return to the Lord, your God, for he is gracious and merciful” (Joel 2:13).
The Yes of the Son and of Mary.
“I delight to do your will, O my God” (Psalm 40:8); “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).
outline: Opening
A table that divides: Corinth, the rich and the hungry, and the question, “Do you not have homes to eat in?”
Point 1 · Not really the Lord's supper
The divisions at Corinth; Paul's anger as love for the poor.
Point 2 · This is my body for you
The oldest account of the Eucharist; one bread, one body; discerning the body.
Point 3 · Which of the two did the will of the father?
The two sons; a No that becomes a Yes; a Yes that is only words.
Point 4 · Go and work today
The vineyard in the monsoon; Kaitha as the season of fruit.
Take-home line
“Son, go and work in the vineyard today.”
live: Discern the body (1 Corinthians 11:29)
Before the Holy Qurbana this Sunday, make peace with anyone you are at odds with, and greet the person in the next pew, especially one you usually avoid.
Say Yes today (Matthew 21:28)
Think of one task that you have said No or Later to: a visit, an apology, a donation, a duty at home. Do it today.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Do you wish to honour the body of Christ? Do not ignore him when he is naked, and do not honour him here in church with silk and then neglect him outside, perishing from cold and nakedness. What use is a table overloaded with golden cups if Christ himself is dying of hunger? First feed the hungry, and then adorn the altar.
St Basil the Great (in substance)
The bread you keep belongs to the hungry; the coat that hangs unused in your wardrobe belongs to the one who has none. You do wrong to as many people as you could have helped.
magis: Catechism 1397 (in substance)
The Eucharist commits us to the poor. To receive in truth the Body and Blood of Christ given up for us, we must recognise Christ in the poorest, his brothers and sisters.
Catechism 2826 (in substance)
Jesus teaches that one enters the kingdom of heaven not by speaking but by doing the will of the Father; in prayer we learn to discern that will and to receive the strength to do it.
saints: First Monday of Kaitha. The Season of Kaitha began yesterday.

1–6 July: the last three days of the Season of the Apostles, then the opening of the Season of Kaitha. Thu 1: Seventh Thursday of the Apostles. Fri 2: the Seventy Disciples of Jesus, and the First Friday. Sat 3: the Dukhrana of St Thomas, an important feast and a day of obligation. Sun 4: First Sunday of Kaitha, the Feast of the Twelve Apostles. Mon 5 and Tue 6: the first Monday and Tuesday of Kaitha; on Tuesday also St Maria Goretti. Looking ahead: Fri 9 July, the First Friday of Kaitha, St James of Nisibis.
2027-07-05.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, on the night when you were betrayed you took bread and a cup and gave us your Body and your Blood. Forgive us the divisions at your table and the contempt we show to those who have nothing. Teach us to discern your body in the bread and in the poor, and to share what we have with a glad heart. When we say No, turn our hearts; when we say Yes, make our Yes true. Send us today into the Father's vineyard, to work with you for a harvest of mercy. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.
altar: Paul tells the Corinthians what the Lord did at the Last Supper, and the Church does it at every Qurbana: “Take... this is my body that is for you.” We come to one altar, one bread, one cup. The prayer of the peace before the Qurbana, when the sign of peace is passed, is not a courtesy: it is the sign that we are reconciled before we offer, and that we have made room at the table for every sister and brother. We leave the altar to go and work in the vineyard today.

2027-07-06.title: First Tuesday of Kaitha · Saint Maria Goretti
2027-07-06.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Be faithful with what the Lord has entrusted
2027-07-06.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which opens on the Sunday after the Dukhrana of St Thomas: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church contemplates its growth and harvest, in the apostles, martyrs and saints who watered the Church with their blood. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “Be infants in evil, but in thinking be mature”; “Be faithful in a very little”. The calendar also lists Saint Maria Goretti today but prints no readings for her, so none are given here; she is remembered below. In Luke 19 the English Bible speaks of ten pounds; the Malayalam Bible speaks of ten coins.
2027-07-06.verse: Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much; and whoever is dishonest in a very little is dishonest also in much.
theo: Paul's reading is about the Church at worship, and about what an outsider sees when he walks in. The Corinthians loved the spectacular gifts of the Spirit, above all speaking in tongues, and some of their meetings had become a contest of display. Paul begins with a sentence that is full of tenderness and good sense: “Brothers and sisters, do not be children in your thinking; rather, be infants in evil, but in thinking be adults.” Be as innocent as a baby about evil, and as grown up as an adult in your judgement. Then he thinks of a visitor, a neighbour or a stranger, who comes in on the day of worship. “If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your mind? But if all prophesy, an unbeliever or outsider who enters is reproved by all and called to account by all. After the secrets of the unbeliever’s heart are disclosed, that person will bow down before God and worship him, declaring, ‘God is really among you.’” By prophecy Paul means the word of God spoken so that it can be understood and can touch the heart. The test of a gathering is whether a stranger who comes in can say that God is really there. Gifts are given “for building up the church”; the Church teaches that every charism, simple or striking, is a grace of the Holy Spirit for the good of all (CCC 799). The Second Vatican Council asked in the same spirit that the rites should be “within the people's powers of comprehension” (Sacrosanctum Concilium 34). In Kerala, neighbours of all faiths come to our weddings, funerals and feasts. What do they see and hear? Do they see reverence, a word they can understand, and people who love each other?

Why does the Church put “infants in evil” beside a parable about business? Because both are about what we do with what God has given. In the Gospel Jesus is near Jerusalem, and his hearers “supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately”, so he tells them a parable about the time between. “A nobleman went to a distant country to get royal power for himself and then return. He summoned ten of his slaves, and gave them ten pounds, and said to them, ‘Do business with these until I come back.’ But the citizens of his country hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to rule over us.’” Scholars often hear in this an echo of the journey of Archelaus, a son of King Herod, to Rome to have his kingship confirmed, while a delegation of Jews and others opposed him; Jesus' hearers knew such stories. When the nobleman returns, the first says, “Lord, your pound has made ten more pounds”, and is told, “Well done, good slave! Because you have been trustworthy in a very small thing, take charge of ten cities.” The second has made five and receives five cities. “Then the other came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your pound. I wrapped it up in a piece of cloth, for I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man; you take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’” The master answers, “I will judge you by your own words”: if he really thought him so demanding, he should at least have put the money in the bank. And the principle: “I tell you, to all those who have, more will be given; but from those who have nothing, even what they have will be taken away.”

The heart of the parable is the third servant's picture of God. He did nothing wrong, he stole nothing and spent nothing; he buried the gift. But he thought the master was harsh, and fear made him idle. Many people live their faith in this way: keeping everything safe and clean, wrapped in a cloth, and giving nothing to anyone. The Lord is not a harsh man reaping where he did not sow; he is the generous giver of every gift, and he wants it to be used. “Like good stewards of the manifold grace of God, serve one another with whatever gift each of you has received.” The Catechism teaches that God gives different gifts to people so that each may receive what he needs from others, and that those endowed with talents share their benefits with those who need them (CCC 1937). The first servants are praised not for the amount, because one made ten and the other five, but for being “trustworthy in a very small thing”: “Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” The ending of the parable is hard: the nobleman says of the citizens who rejected him, “bring them here and slaughter them in my presence.” This is the king of the story speaking; Jesus himself, as he goes up to Jerusalem, will not strike anyone but will give his own life. The verse is a picture of the seriousness of rejecting the king, and the judgement belongs to God alone, never to us. It does not speak of any one people; it speaks of every heart that says, “We do not want this man to rule over us.” In Kaitha, the season of fruit, the Lord asks each of us: what have you done with my gift? Trade with it until I come back.

Today's calendar also lists Saint Maria Goretti, and she belongs naturally beside Paul's first sentence, “be infants in evil, but in thinking be adults.” Maria was born in 1890 into a poor farming family in Italy and grew up in the marshlands south of Rome, where her father died of malaria when she was nine. She worked from morning to night, looking after her small brothers and sisters while her mother worked in the fields, and she prepared with great care for her First Communion. On 5 July 1902, when she was eleven, a young man from the neighbouring family tried to assault her, and she refused him: she knew that what he asked was a sin against God. He stabbed her many times. She died the next day, 6 July, in hospital, and before she died she forgave him and said that she wanted him to be with her in paradise. Years later the man, Alessandro, who had been in prison, repented, asked her mother's forgiveness and was received by her, and he lived a quiet life of penance. Maria was canonised by Pope Pius XII in 1950. In her we see what it means to be “an infant in evil” and an adult in judgement: she was a child in age, but she was clear and strong in her choice. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God”, and “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good”: she overcame it with a forgiveness that echoes the words of Jesus from the cross, “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing” (CCC 2844). The Church holds her up to young people today as a friend and companion in the struggle for purity, and to everyone who has suffered violence as a protector.
conn: Children in malice.

“Truly I tell you, unless you change and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3); “See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16).
Wise in good.
“I want you to be wise in what is good and guileless in what is evil” (Romans 16:19).
For building up the church.
“Since you are eager for spiritual gifts, strive to excel in them for building up the church” (1 Corinthians 14:12).
Well done, good and trustworthy slave.
“Well done, good and trustworthy slave; you have been trustworthy in a few things, I will put you in charge of many things; enter into the joy of your master” (Matthew 25:21).
Much will be required.
“From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and from the one to whom much has been entrusted, even more will be demanded” (Luke 12:48).
The work of our hands.
“Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and prosper for us the work of our hands” (Psalm 90:17).
Forgiveness.
“Then Jesus said, ‘Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing’” (Luke 23:34); “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).
outline: Opening
What does the stranger see when he comes in? And what has the Lord given me to trade with?
Point 1 · Infants in evil, adults in thinking
Paul's advice to the Corinthians; the gifts of the Spirit for building up; an assembly where God is really present.
Point 2 · Trade until I come back
The parable of the pounds: the faithful servants and the one who buried his.
Point 3 · The picture of God
The harsh master in the servant's mind; fear that buries gifts; trust that trades.
Point 4 · Saint Maria Goretti
A child in age, clear in choice, who forgave.
Take-home line
“Be infants in evil, but in thinking be adults.”
live: Look as a stranger (1 Corinthians 14:24–25)
At the next Qurbana, notice what a visitor would see and hear: the welcome, the reading, the singing. Do one thing to make it easier for someone to say, “God is really among you.”
Use your pound (Luke 19:13)
Write down one gift you have (a skill, time, money, a voice, patience) and one concrete way to use it this month for your parish or a neighbour.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

Let the one who has understanding take care not to be silent; let the one who has abundance of goods not be idle in mercy; let the one who has a skill in daily affairs share its use and profit with his neighbour; let the one who has influence with the rich speak up for the poor.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Paul asks us to be children in evil, and children are the best teachers of this. A child bears no grudge, does not envy, and does not remember an injury for long; but in thinking he wants us to be adults, firm and wise.
magis: Catechism 799 (in substance)

Whether extraordinary or simple and humble, charisms are graces of the Holy Spirit that directly or indirectly benefit the Church, ordered to her building up, to the good of men and to the needs of the world.
Catechism 1937 (in substance)
The differences among people belong to God's plan, who wills that each receive what he needs from others, and that those endowed with talents share the benefits with those who need them.
saints: First Tuesday of Kaitha. Saint Maria Goretti (1890–1902), virgin and martyr, is remembered today; the calendar lists her without readings. The Latin Church keeps her as an optional memorial.

1–6 July: the last three days of the Season of the Apostles, then the opening of the Season of Kaitha. Thu 1: Seventh Thursday of the Apostles. Fri 2: the Seventy Disciples of Jesus, and the First Friday. Sat 3: the Dukhrana of St Thomas, an important feast and a day of obligation. Sun 4: First Sunday of Kaitha, the Feast of the Twelve Apostles. Mon 5 and Tue 6: the first Monday and Tuesday of Kaitha; on Tuesday also St Maria Goretti. Looking ahead: Fri 9 July, the First Friday of Kaitha, St James of Nisibis.
2027-07-06.prayer: Lord God, you give to each of us different gifts and ask that we trade with them until your Son comes again. Keep us from burying them in fear. Make us childlike in evil and mature in judgement; and make our worship so true that the stranger who enters may say, “God is really among you.” Through the prayers of Saint Maria Goretti, who chose purity and forgave her attacker, give young people strength to say Yes to you, and give us all the grace to forgive and to overcome evil with good. Through Christ our Lord, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the whole Church comes together, the stranger enters, and the word is read and explained so that all can understand. When the bread and wine are offered, we offer also our gifts: our time, our skills and our money, in trust that the Lord will multiply them. And in the Body of Christ we receive the one who calls himself the Master and acts as the servant, who gives us the strength to trade faithfully until he comes again.

2027-07-07.title: First Wednesday of Kaitha
2027-07-07.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: My deeds give witness to me
2027-07-07.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church looks at its growth and fruit. This is the season of the apostles and martyrs who watered the Church with their blood, and of watchfulness for the coming of the Lord. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints of the East Syriac tradition. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “Fight of the faithful”; “My deeds give witness to me”.
2027-07-07.verse: My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me.
theo: Paul's letter to Timothy reaches its climax in a charge, and the charge begins with a title: “But as for you, man of God.” In the Old Testament this is the name of Moses, Samuel, Elijah and the prophets, people who belonged wholly to God. Timothy is a young bishop, and the title reminds him who he is. What follows is a list of what to run from and what to run after: “shun all this”, that is, the love of money which Paul has just called the root of all kinds of evil, and “pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness”. Six words, and not one of them is loud. Then the athlete's picture: “Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of the eternal life, to which you were called and for which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.” The fight is not against people. It is the long struggle to stay faithful, and the prize is already in the hand, because eternal life is something to be taken hold of today.

Paul sets Timothy's confession beside the confession of Christ himself, “who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession”. Before the Roman governor Jesus said that he was a King, and that his kingdom was not of this world, and he said it knowing the cost. The charge ends in a hymn that Paul may have taken from the liturgy of his Church: Christ will be manifested “at the right time”; God is “the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords. It is he alone who has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see.” We stand at the beginning of Kaitha, the season in which the Church looks at her growth and waits for her Lord. The reading reminds us that the harvest belongs to the One who dwells in unapproachable light, and that our task is to keep the commandment “without spot or blame” until he appears.

In the Gospel Jesus walks in the portico of Solomon at the feast of the Dedication, the winter feast in which the Jewish people remember the cleansing and re-dedication of the Temple. Some of the leaders gather round him: “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.” Jesus has already told them, and he points them to his works: “The works that I do in my Father’s name testify to me.” Then he says something hard: “you do not believe, because you do not belong to my sheep.” This is not a rejection of the Jewish people, from whom Jesus, Mary and the apostles came; John's Gospel, in speaking of “the Jews”, usually means these particular leaders in Jerusalem, and the Church teaches that what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews of that time, still less against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4). The sentence names a danger for every listener, including us: one can stand beside Jesus, ask him questions, and never listen.

Then comes the shepherd's voice. “My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one will snatch them out of my hand.” Hearing, being known, following: three steps, and the whole of Christian life is in them. In the villages of Kerala a shepherd's call is not common now, but every mother knows how a child in a crowded market can pick out one voice from a hundred. Our phones fill every hour with voices, and many of them sound confident. The sheep of Christ learn his voice in the Gospel read at the Holy Qurbana, in daily prayer and in the family Rosary, and then they can tell it from the others. St Gregory the Great taught that when the Lord says “I know my sheep” he means “I love them”. We are not held by our own grip, which grows tired, but by the hand that no one can pry open.
outline: Opening
Which voice do I follow today, out of the hundred that call me?
Point 1 · Man of God
Shun the love of money; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness.
Point 2 · The good confession
Timothy's confession and Christ's before Pilate; the King of kings in unapproachable light.
Point 3 · The shepherd's voice
Hear, be known, follow; no one will snatch them out of his hand.
Take-home line
“My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me.”
live: Pursue one virtue (1 Timothy 6:11)
Choose one of the six, for example gentleness, and practise it with one particular person at home this week.
Know the voice (John 10:27)
Read the Gospel of the day slowly each morning before you look at your phone, and ask: Lord, what are you saying to me?
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

When the Lord says, I know my sheep, he means: I love my sheep. Whoever does not love the truth has not yet been known by it. Let us then see whether we are his sheep: let us ask whether we believe, whether we love, and whether we follow.
St Ignatius of Antioch (in substance)
It is better for me to die for Jesus Christ than to rule over the ends of the earth. Him I seek, who died for us; him I desire, who rose for us.
magis: Catechism 754
The Church is a sheepfold, the sole and necessary gate of which is Christ; she is guided by the Good Shepherd, who gave his life for his sheep.
Catechism 1816
The disciple of Christ must not only keep the faith and live on it, but also profess it, bear witness to it with confidence, and spread it.
Nostra Aetate 4
What happened in Christ's Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, without distinction, nor against the Jews of today.
saints: First Wednesday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar it is the Wednesday of the fourteenth week in Ordinary Time.

7–12 July: first week and second Sunday of the Season of Kaitha. Fri 9: First Friday of Kaitha, Saint James of Nisibis (Mar Yakob). Sun 11: Second Sunday of Kaitha (in the Latin calendar the Fifteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time; St Benedict gives way to the Sunday). Looking ahead: Thu 15, Sts Kuriakose and Julitta; Fri 16, Our Lady of Mount Carmel and Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai.
2027-07-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Good Shepherd, you spoke plainly to those who asked, and you still speak to us in your word. Open our ears to your voice among the many voices of the world; let us hear you, be known by you, and follow you. Make us men and women of God, pursuing righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness. Teach us to fight the good fight of the faith and to make the good confession by the way we live. Hold us in your hand, from which no one can snatch us, until the day when you are revealed, King of kings and Lord of lords, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Shepherd speaks in the readings and then feeds his sheep with his own Body and Blood. We hear his voice, we are known by name, and we follow him from the altar into the week. The hand that no one can open is the hand that gives us the Bread of eternal life.

2027-07-08.title: First Thursday of Kaitha
2027-07-08.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The gift of the Spirit for the growth of the Church
2027-07-08.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church looks at its growth and fruit. This is the season of the apostles and martyrs who watered the Church with their blood, and of watchfulness for the coming of the Lord. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints of the East Syriac tradition. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “The gift of the Spirit for the growth of the Church”; “Before Abraham was, I am”.
2027-07-08.verse: Jesus said to them, “Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.”
theo: The Corinthian church was rich in gifts, and the gift they prized most was speaking in tongues, ecstatic prayer in sounds no one could understand. Paul does not despise it; he thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than all of them. But in chapter 14 he asks a pastor's question: what does the gift do for the whole assembly? “One who speaks in a tongue should pray for the power to interpret.” Then he gives one of the clearest sentences in the New Testament on how a Christian prays: “I will pray with the spirit, but I will pray with the mind also; I will sing praise with the spirit, but I will sing praise with the mind also.” Heart and head are not rivals. Prayer that is only feeling, without understanding, leaves the mind “unproductive”, and prayer that is only thought, without the Spirit, is dry. The Church prays with both.

The second half of the reading takes us into the Church's worship. If you give thanks only in the spirit, “how can anyone in the position of an outsider say the ‘Amen’ to your thanksgiving, since the outsider does not know what you are saying?” The Greek word for thanksgiving here is the word from which we have Eucharist, and the Amen is the people's answer. In the Qurbana the people do not watch; they answer, and the Amen is their signature on the prayer, as if each one said: this is mine as well. For that Amen to be true it must be understood, which is why our Church celebrates the Qurbana in the mother tongue of the people, and why Paul would rather speak “five words with my mind, in order to instruct others also, than ten thousand words in a tongue”. The measure of the gift is how it builds up the Church. This is a good word at the opening of Kaitha, the season of the Church's growth.

In the Gospel the argument in the Temple court has become sharp. Jesus has said, “whoever keeps my word will never see death,” and his hearers answer with an insult: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” They are Jews speaking to a Jew, in a family quarrel about who he is, as the prophets had quarrelled with their own people. John's phrase “the Jews” names these hostile voices in Jerusalem; it cannot be turned against the Jewish people, and Christians have often sinned by doing so. The Church condemns every hatred and persecution of the Jews (Nostra Aetate 4). Jesus answers calmly: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and he is the judge.” He does not defend himself; he honours the Father.

Then the argument turns to Abraham. “Your ancestor Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.” The Jewish tradition spoke of Abraham seeing the days to come, and the Church has read in Isaac's birth and the sacrifice on Moriah a sign of the One to come. His hearers object: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” And Jesus says the sentence on which the whole Gospel of John rests: “Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.” He does not say “I was”; he says “I am”. It is the name God gave to Moses at the burning bush, “I am who I am”, now spoken by a man standing in the Temple. They pick up stones, for they understood him. Jesus hides himself and goes out. For us the “I am” is not a danger but a promise: the One who is before Abraham, before the world, is with us in every Qurbana, and whoever keeps his word will not see death for ever.
outline: Opening
Do I pray only with feeling, or only with my head, or with both?
Point 1 · Spirit and mind
The gift of tongues and its limit; pray, sing and think with the Spirit and with the mind.
Point 2 · The Amen that builds up
Thanksgiving that all can understand and answer; five words with the mind.
Point 3 · Before Abraham was, I am
The quarrel in the Temple; Abraham's joy; the divine name spoken by Jesus.
Take-home line
“Before Abraham was, I am.”
live: Pray with the mind (1 Corinthians 14:15)
At the next Qurbana follow every prayer in your own language, and say each Amen as a word you mean.
Keep his word (John 8:51)
Choose one saying of Jesus and keep it this week in one concrete action.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Notice what he says: not, before Abraham was, I was, but, before Abraham was made, I am. Abraham was made, but the one who made Abraham was not made. He does not say I was, for he does not pass away; he is.
St Augustine on the Amen (in substance)
You say Amen to what you are. Be what you see on the altar, and receive what you are: when you answer Amen you sign your own name to the Body of Christ.
magis: Catechism 590
Jesus claims the divine name and the divine authority over the Law; only his divine identity can justify such a claim, and so those who heard him found it a scandal.
Catechism 1061–1065
Amen, the word that closes the Creed and the prayers of the Church, means: let it be so, it is true; it is the faithful answer to God's own faithfulness.
Nostra Aetate 4
The Church rejects all hatred, persecution and displays of anti-Semitism directed against Jews at any time and from any source.
saints: First Thursday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar it is the Thursday of the fourteenth week in Ordinary Time.

7–12 July: first week and second Sunday of the Season of Kaitha. Fri 9: First Friday of Kaitha, Saint James of Nisibis (Mar Yakob). Sun 11: Second Sunday of Kaitha (in the Latin calendar the Fifteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time; St Benedict gives way to the Sunday). Looking ahead: Thu 15, Sts Kuriakose and Julitta; Fri 16, Our Lady of Mount Carmel and Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai.
2027-07-08.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are before Abraham and before all ages, and you are with us now. Teach us to pray with the Spirit and with the mind, so that our Amen may be true. Let every word of thanksgiving at the altar be understood and answered by the whole assembly, and let every gift you give us build up your Church. Help us to keep your word, and give us the joy of Abraham, who saw your day and was glad. Keep us from every hatred of our neighbours, and make us your witnesses in a world that does not know you. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: The word “thanksgiving” in the reading is the word Eucharist. At the Holy Qurbana the people answer every prayer with their Amen, and at the moment of communion the Amen says: this is truly the Body of Christ, and I am part of it. The One who is before Abraham comes to us under the sign of bread, and the Church grows by this Amen.

2027-07-09.title: First Friday of Kaitha · Saint James of Nisibis (Mar Yakob)
2027-07-09.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Wonders and signs through the apostles
2027-07-09.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church looks at its growth and fruit. This is the season of the apostles and martyrs who watered the Church with their blood, and of watchfulness for the coming of the Lord. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints of the East Syriac tradition. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar gives the longer forms Acts 19:8–20, 2 Corinthians 10:3–18 and Luke 12:1–12 and lists the day among the Commemorations of Martyrs and Saints; it prints four readings for the day (verify locally). The calendar's own headings: “I have chosen you”; “Wonders and signs through the Apostles”; “Apostles build up the Church”; “Bear witness fearlessly”.
2027-07-09.verse: do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my victorious right hand.
theo: The first Friday of Kaitha belongs to a bishop of the border, Mar Yakob of Nisibis, James of Nisibis, who died about the year 338. Nisibis, today Nusaybin on the Turkish-Syrian frontier, stood at the edge of two empires, the Roman and the Persian, and its Christians lived under the threat of war. According to the Syriac tradition he was a man of prayer and of the Scriptures who became the first bishop of the city and the teacher of the young Ephrem, who later became the great poet and Doctor of the Church; tradition also says he took part in the Council of Nicaea in 325. When the Persian armies came against the city, the people looked to their bishop, and the Church of Nisibis remembered how her prayer, and not only her walls, had kept her. We keep his memory because we belong to the same family: our liturgy, the Qurbana of Addai and Mari, comes from the Church of the East, which had its roots in this Syriac world.

The readings give a fine frame for such a life. In Isaiah, God speaks to a small and frightened people: “But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen.” The name Jacob is the name of our saint, Yakob in Syriac, and it is easy to hear the promise spoken over him: “do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my victorious right hand.” Isaiah dares to call the nation “you worm Jacob”, so small and weak, and then tells it that the Holy One of Israel is its Redeemer. The Church of Nisibis was small and exposed, and she was held by the same hand. So are we, whenever we are tired and alone: God does not choose the strong first.

In Acts the word of the Lord grows “mightily” at Ephesus, a city of magic and of the great temple of Artemis. God does “extraordinary miracles” through Paul; the sons of Sceva, who try to use the name of Jesus like a charm without belonging to him, are overpowered, and many believers confess and burn their books of magic, worth fifty thousand silver coins, before everyone. The lesson is two-sided: the name of Jesus is not a spell, and a Christian leaves the old powers openly. In Kerala some still go to astrologers, amulets and charms in time of fear; the Church asks us to put our trust in Christ alone (Catechism 2116–2117). In the Epistle Paul says that his weapons are not human: “we destroy arguments and every proud obstacle raised up against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive to obey Christ.” The weapon of a bishop is prayer, the word and the sacraments, and also patient teaching, as James taught young Ephrem. Paul adds that the authority was given “for building you up and not for tearing you down”.

The Gospel is the great word to those who bear witness. “Do not fear those who kill the body, and after that can do nothing more.” Jesus says it to his friends, and in the same breath tells them of a Father who forgets not one of five sparrows sold for two pennies and who has counted the hairs of their head. The call to confess him is clear: “everyone who acknowledges me before others, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God.” And when they are brought before rulers, they should not worry, “for the Holy Spirit will teach you at that very hour what you ought to say.” The Church of the East knew this hour well; in the Persian Empire thousands of her sons and daughters were martyred in the century after Nisibis, and the Thomas Christians of India honour them in their calendar to this day. On this first Friday of Kaitha, the Friday of martyrs and saints, we ask for the same fearlessness: not the boldness of the proud, but the quiet courage of those who know that they are counted and held.
outline: Opening
A small frontier city, a praying bishop, and a God who says: do not fear.
Point 1 · Do not fear, I am with you
Isaiah's promise to Jacob the worm; the Church at the edge of two empires.
Point 2 · Not a charm, but the name
Ephesus, Sceva's sons, the burning of the books; trust in Christ alone.
Point 3 · Weapons not of this world
Paul's divine weapons; build up and do not tear down; teaching as Mar Yakob taught Ephrem.
Point 4 · Bear witness
Not one sparrow forgotten; acknowledge him; the Spirit teaches in the hour.
Take-home line
“Do not fear, for I am with you.”
live: Put away a charm (Acts 19:19)
If there is any amulet, horoscope or charm in your house or phone that you trust, put it away, and entrust yourself to Christ in prayer.
Confess him (Luke 12:8)
This week acknowledge your faith once in a quiet and respectful way in a place where it usually goes unmentioned.
Teach one person (2 Corinthians 10:8)
Teach a child or a younger person one prayer, and pray it with them.
fathers: Tertullian (in substance)
We multiply whenever you mow us down; the blood of Christians is seed.
St Augustine (in substance)
It is not the punishment but the cause that makes a martyr.
magis: Catechism 2473
Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith; the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity.
Catechism 2116–2117
All forms of divination, magic and sorcery are to be rejected; they contradict the honour, respect and loving fear that we owe to God alone.
Catechism 1816
The disciple of Christ must not only keep the faith but profess it, bear witness to it with confidence, and spread it.
saints: First Friday of Kaitha: Saint James of Nisibis (Mar Yakob), a bishop of the Syriac Church whose memory the calendar keeps among the saints. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints of the Church of the East. In the Latin calendar it is the Friday of the fourteenth week in Ordinary Time, with the optional memorial of St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, martyrs of China.

7–12 July: first week and second Sunday of the Season of Kaitha. Fri 9: First Friday of Kaitha, Saint James of Nisibis (Mar Yakob). Sun 11: Second Sunday of Kaitha (in the Latin calendar the Fifteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time; St Benedict gives way to the Sunday). Looking ahead: Thu 15, Sts Kuriakose and Julitta; Fri 16, Our Lady of Mount Carmel and Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai.
2027-07-09.prayer: God our Father, you chose Jacob and told him not to fear, for you were with him. We thank you for your servant Mar Yakob, bishop of Nisibis, who taught your word, led his people in prayer and was a father in the faith to the young Ephrem. Through his intercession keep your Church safe from fear and from every false trust. Teach us to put away the charms and idols that we hold, and to place our whole trust in the name of Jesus. Give us weapons that are not of this world, the word, the sacraments and love, and strengthen all who suffer for the faith, as you strengthened the martyrs of the Church of the East. Teach us by your Holy Spirit what to say, and when we are afraid, uphold us with your right hand. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana of Addai and Mari we pray in the tradition that the Church of the East handed down, the tradition of Mar Yakob and Ephrem. The altar is where the weak are held by the right hand of God: in the Body and Blood of Christ we are given the courage not to be afraid, and in the bread and the cup we are counted and remembered, as the sparrows are counted by the Father.

2027-07-10.title: First Saturday of Kaitha
2027-07-10.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-07-10.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church looks at its growth and fruit. This is the season of the apostles and martyrs who watered the Church with their blood, and of watchfulness for the coming of the Lord. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints of the East Syriac tradition. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “The Temple of God”; “Jesus heals the paralytic”. Saturday is kept in many homes as Mary's day.
2027-07-10.verse: When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.”
theo: Paul's picture in the Epistle is taken from the Law of Moses: “Do not be mismatched with unbelievers.” The Greek word means to be yoked unequally, like an ox and a donkey under one yoke, which the Law of Moses forbids (Deuteronomy 22:10). Then follows a series of questions, each with the answer no: “what partnership is there between righteousness and lawlessness? Or what fellowship is there between light and darkness? What agreement does Christ have with Beliar? Or what does a believer share with an unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols?” In Corinth the practical question was sharing in the feasts held in pagan temples, with their sacrifices to idols and their immorality. Paul is not telling Christians to cut off their neighbours; in the first letter he says that then they would have to go out of the world (1 Corinthians 5:10). He asks them to refuse partnership in idolatry and sin.

In India, where Christians live among neighbours of many faiths, this needs care. The Church “rejects nothing that is true and holy” in other religions and urges respect, friendship and dialogue with them (Nostra Aetate 2). What we refuse is not a neighbour but a yoke: the bribe, the cruelty, the lie, the unclean practice, anything that would put another master in the place of Christ. Paul's reason is a gift before it is a command: “For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, ‘I will live in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.’” God walked among Israel in the tent and the Temple, as he walked with Adam in the garden. Now he lives in us, in the Church and in each baptised person. A temple is not a place where everything is permitted; it is a place that belongs to God. The reading ends in a promise of tenderness: “I will welcome you, and I will be your father, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.”

The Gospel is one of the most vivid scenes in Mark. Jesus is “at home” in Capernaum, and the house is so full that there is no room even at the door. Four men arrive carrying a paralysed friend. They cannot get through the crowd, so they climb the outside stairs, dig through the roof, made of beams, branches and clay, and lower the man on his mat to the feet of Jesus. We do not know their names, only that they would not give up. Mark says: “When Jesus saw their faith.” It is their faith, and the paralytic's, that Jesus sees. Here is a mystery that every parish knows: someone is carried to Jesus by the faith of others, by a mother's prayer, a friend's visit, a catechist, a neighbour who sits by a sickbed.

Jesus does not begin with the healing of the legs. “Son, your sins are forgiven.” The man had come for his body; Jesus first gives him what he needs most, and calls him “Son”. Some scribes, sitting there, think: “It is blasphemy! Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Their premise is correct, and they ask honestly; only God can forgive sins. Jesus answers by doing the visible thing to prove the invisible: “But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins… I say to you, stand up, take your mat and go to your home.” The man stands, takes his mat and walks out before all of them, and all are amazed: “We have never seen anything like this!” Jesus forgives as God forgives, and this authority has been given to his Church in the sacrament of Reconciliation (John 20:23). On this Saturday, when many families remember the Mother of the Lord, we remember that she is the one who, at Cana, brought the need of others to her Son; she is the best of all those who carry friends to Jesus.
outline: Opening
A man on a mat, four friends and a hole in the roof.
Point 1 · The temple of the living God
Not mismatched: God lives in us and walks among us.
Point 2 · Come out, not from people, but from sin
Refuse idols and impurity, and respect our neighbours.
Point 3 · When Jesus saw their faith
The carried man; the friends who would not give up.
Point 4 · Son, your sins are forgiven
Only God forgives; the Son of Man has the authority; the sacrament of mercy.
Take-home line
“Son, your sins are forgiven.”
live: Be one of the four (Mark 2:3)
Name one person who is paralysed by illness, sin or discouragement, and carry them to Jesus: pray, visit, and offer a Qurbana for them.
Go to confession (Mark 2:10)
If you have not been for a long time, plan this week to receive the sacrament of Reconciliation.
Refuse one yoke (2 Corinthians 6:14)
Name one partnership in a dishonest practice and step out of it.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)
The paralytic came for the healing of his body, and Christ healed his soul first, since this was the greater need. Then, to prove what no one could see, he did what everyone could see.
St Augustine (in substance)
God's house is built of living stones. You are what is being built; do not let the idols of your heart stand in the temple. Let it be clean, so that the Lord may come and dwell there.
magis: Catechism 1441
Only God forgives sins. Since Jesus is the Son of God, he says of himself, “The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”, and he exercises this divine power.
Catechism 1421

The Lord Jesus Christ, physician of our souls and bodies, who forgave the sins of the paralytic and restored him to bodily health, has willed that his Church continue his work of healing and salvation.
Nostra Aetate 2
The Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions, and urges her sons and daughters to enter with prudence and charity into dialogue and collaboration.
saints: First Saturday of Kaitha. Saturday is kept in many Kerala homes as Mary's day, with a litany of the Mother of God. In the Latin calendar it is the Saturday of the fourteenth week in Ordinary Time.

7–12 July: first week and second Sunday of the Season of Kaitha. Fri 9: First Friday of Kaitha, Saint James of Nisibis (Mar Yakob). Sun 11: Second Sunday of Kaitha (in the Latin calendar the Fifteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time; St Benedict gives way to the Sunday). Looking ahead: Thu 15, Sts Kuriakose and Julitta; Fri 16, Our Lady of Mount Carmel and Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai.
2027-07-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you see the faith of those who carry others to you, and you say to the weak: Son, your sins are forgiven. Make us temples of the living God, clean from every idol, and give us the grace to refuse every partnership with sin. Teach us to carry our friends, our families and our parish to you, and never to give up when the crowd is in the way. Heal us in body and soul, and give us the courage to come to the sacrament of your mercy. Through the prayer of your Mother, who brings the needs of her children to you, make us your dwelling place, for you are God for ever and ever. Amen.
altar: The Body of Christ in the Holy Qurbana is the place where heaven opens over the paralysed. At the altar, the Church lowers us, like the man on the mat, to the feet of Jesus, and we hear: your sins are forgiven. Those who receive him become his temple, and the Lord who lives in us walks with us into the week.

2027-07-12.title: Second Monday of Kaitha
2027-07-12.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The crown of life for those who endure the trial
Those who do the will of God enter the Kingdom
2027-07-12.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church looks at its growth and fruit. This is the season of the apostles and martyrs who watered the Church with their blood, and of watchfulness for the coming of the Lord. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints of the East Syriac tradition. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “The crown of life for those who endure the trial”; “Those who do the will of God enter the Kingdom”. In the Latin calendar today is the Monday of the fifteenth week in Ordinary Time (the readings there begin the book of Exodus); St Benedict was remembered yesterday.
2027-07-12.verse: Blessed is anyone who endures temptation. Such a one has stood the test and will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love him.
theo: The letter of James opens its first chapter with a blessing for those who hold on: “Blessed is anyone who endures temptation. Such a one has stood the test and will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love him.” The Greek word means both a trial and a temptation; it is the same test seen from two sides, depending on what the person does with it. The crown of life is the wreath that is given to the athlete who has finished the race, here the life of God himself, promised to those who love him. Then James has to be careful, because people in trouble are quick to blame God. “No one, when tempted, should say, ‘I am being tempted by God’; for God cannot be tempted by evil and he himself tempts no one.” God may test, as he tested Abraham, in order to strengthen; he never draws anyone towards sin. The Lord's Prayer asks the Father, “Lead us not into temptation”, and the Catechism explains that this is a prayer that the Spirit may help us tell a trial that makes us grow from a temptation that leads to sin and death (Catechism 2846–2847).

Then James gives the anatomy of a fall, as in a pregnancy: “But one is tempted by one's own desire, being lured and enticed by it; then, when that desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin, and that sin, when it is fully grown, gives birth to death.” Desire is the bait, and the fish is hooked by what it wants. Nothing happens suddenly: the thought, the consent, the act, the habit, and finally death. The sentence is a mirror held up to a Kerala household. The glance at the phone that becomes a hidden habit, the first drink, the first small lie about money, the first bitter word that becomes silence at the table: each grows. And against this birth that ends in death, the apostle places another birth. “In fulfillment of his own purpose he gave us birth by the word of truth, so that we would become a kind of first fruits of his creatures.” Desire gives birth to death; God gives birth to us by his word, which is truth. The second birth is baptism and the faith that comes by hearing the Gospel.
