Between the two births stands the great sentence on God's character: “Every generous act of giving, with every perfect gift, is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change.” The sun, the moon and the stars change, and the monsoon sky is never the same for two hours together, with its light and shadows. The Father of lights does not change. Everything good that reaches us, a child's birth, a harvest, a healing, the forgiveness of sins, comes from him, and he never takes back what he gave. And we are “first fruits”. In Israel the first sheaf of the harvest was brought to the priest and offered to God (Leviticus 23:10) as the sign that the whole harvest belongs to him. In this season of Kaitha, when the Church looks at her growth and fruit, James tells us that the baptised are that offering: the first of a harvest that will include the whole creation.

The Gospel is the end of the Sermon on the Mount, and it is a test of everything we have heard so far. “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven.” Even prophesying, casting out demons and deeds of power in his name are not a passport if there is no obedience. The words “I never knew you” are terrible, and they should be read alongside the Father's own way of knowing, which is loving. Then comes the parable known to every child in Kerala. Two houses stand through the same weather: “The rain fell, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house.” We have lived this: the great floods of 2018 showed us what is carried away and what stands. The house on rock stands, and the house on sand falls “and great was its fall!” The only difference is that one builder “hears these words of mine and acts on them”. The rock is Christ and his word, and building on the rock means acting on it, in small things on an ordinary Monday: the honest day's work, the forgiveness offered, the prayer kept. “Now when Jesus had finished saying these things, the crowds were astounded at his teaching.” The crowd was astonished, but the wise man built.
outline: Opening
Two houses, one storm: what is under the floor?
Point 1 · Trial and temptation
Blessed are those who endure; God tests but never tempts.
Point 2 · Two births
Desire gives birth to sin and death; God gives birth to us by the word of truth.
Point 3 · The Father of lights
Every good gift from above; no shadow of change; first fruits.
Point 4 · Rock and sand
Not those who say Lord, Lord, but those who do the Father's will; hearing and acting.
Take-home line
“Everyone then who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock.”
live: Cut the chain early (James 1:14–15)
Name one desire that is beginning to lead you into sin and stop it at the first thought, with a short prayer: ‘Lord, help me.’
Count the gifts (James 1:17)
Each evening this week write down three good gifts from the Father of lights and thank him.
Act on one word (Matthew 7:24)
Choose one saying of Jesus, such as ‘forgive’, and do it this week in a concrete way.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Whoever hears the words of the Lord and does them builds on rock; whoever hears them and does not do them builds on sand. It is not enough to hear. The rock is the firmness of doing what the Lord has commanded.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Do not think that it is enough to say Lord, Lord, or to have done great things in his name. What matters is the life that follows the word. For faith without works is dead, and works are the proof that the faith is alive.
magis: Catechism 2846–2847

God tempts no one to evil; in the Lord's Prayer we ask not to be led into temptation, and the Holy Spirit helps us to tell the trial that makes us grow from the temptation that leads to sin and death.
Catechism 2822–2827
The will of the Father is that all be saved; we ask in the Our Father that his will be done on earth as it is in heaven, and we do it by joining ourselves to the obedience of Jesus.
Catechism 2013
All Christians, in any state or walk of life, are called to the fullness of Christian life and to the perfection of charity.
saints: Second Monday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar, the Monday of the fifteenth week in Ordinary Time. St Benedict, patron of Europe, was remembered yesterday, and the Benedictine motto “Ora et labora”, prayer and work, is a good commentary on today's Gospel.

7–12 July: first week and second Sunday of the Season of Kaitha. Fri 9: First Friday of Kaitha, Saint James of Nisibis (Mar Yakob). Sun 11: Second Sunday of Kaitha (in the Latin calendar the Fifteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time; St Benedict gives way to the Sunday). Looking ahead: Thu 15, Sts Kuriakose and Julitta; Fri 16, Our Lady of Mount Carmel and Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai.
2027-07-12.prayer: Father of lights, from whom every good gift comes down and with whom there is no change, we thank you for the gift of life, of faith and of every blessing of this day. Keep us in time of trial, and let us never say that you tempt us. When desire lures us, give us the grace to turn from it at the first thought. You have given us birth by the word of truth: make us the first fruits of your creation, a harvest that is pleasing to you. Teach us not only to say, ‘Lord, Lord’, but to do your will, and set the house of our family, our parish and our heart upon the rock of your Son, so that in the rain and the flood and the wind we may stand. We ask this through Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever and ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we hear the word, which is the first work, and then we stand at the altar, where Christ himself, the rock, gathers his Church. The Body and Blood of the Lord are the gift from above, the Father's generous gift that never changes. We receive him so that we may carry what we have heard into the ordinary week and build upon it.

2027-07-13.title: Second Tuesday of Kaitha
2027-07-13.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: A friend of the world becomes an enemy of God
2027-07-13.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which follows the Season of the Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when we remember the apostles, martyrs and saints who sowed the Gospel and watered it with their blood, and keep ourselves ready for the coming of the Lord. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “A friend of the world becomes an enemy of God”; “Beatitudes”.
2027-07-13.verse: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
theo: On the second Tuesday of Kaitha the readings begin with a question that every family, parish and village has asked at some time: “Those conflicts and disputes among you, where do they come from?” James does not blame the weather, the neighbours or the committee. He points inward: “Do they not come from your cravings that are at war within you?” The word he uses for cravings is the one from which we get our word hedonism, the pull toward pleasure. The war outside begins with a war inside: “You want something and do not have it; so you commit murder. And you covet something and cannot obtain it; so you engage in disputes and conflicts.” James uses the strongest words on purpose, because envy, left to grow, walks the road of Cain. Even prayer can be infected by it: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, in order to spend what you get on your pleasures.” A prayer that only wants to add to our pile has not yet become a prayer.

Then the language grows sharper: “Adulterers! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God?” The prophets called Israel an unfaithful wife when she ran after other lovers, and James uses the same voice for a Church that wants Christ and also every prize the world hands out. “The world” here is not creation, which God made good and loved so much that he gave his Son (John 3:16). It is the order of life that organises itself without God and measures a person by what he owns and what others say of him. Against it James sets the jealous love of God: “God yearns jealously for the spirit that he has made to dwell in us.” God is not the rival of our happiness; he is a lover who wants us whole. And his answer to our cravings is a gift, not a rule: “But he gives all the more grace; therefore it says, ‘God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” Then comes the short road home: “Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”

The Gospel shows what the grace given to the humble looks like. In Luke's Sermon on the Plain, Jesus “looked up at his disciples” and speaks four blessings and four woes. “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.” The verb is in the present: the kingdom is theirs now. “Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.” Jesus is not praising misery, and he is not saying that hunger is good. He is saying that God has taken the side of the one whose only possession is God, and that the reversal is certain. The fourth blessing is the one the martyrs of the Church lived: “Blessed are you when people hate you, and when they exclude you, revile you, and defame you on account of the Son of Man. Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, for surely your reward is great in heaven.” The Church in Kaitha looks at her martyrs and sees this joy in a human face.

Then come the four woes: “But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation.” A woe is a lament, like the cry over a house about to fall, and not a curse. Jesus grieves for those whose comfort is already complete, who have nothing left to hope for. The last woe stings the preacher and the politician most: “Woe to you when all speak well of you, for that is what their ancestors did to the false prophets.” Put James and Luke side by side. The one who owns the kingdom does not need to go to war for a plot of land, a seat on a committee or a good name; the one who is ruled by cravings is never full. In Kerala, where a quarrel over a boundary or an inheritance can run for years in the courts and can even divide a family at the church door, the reading puts a gentle and hard question: what are we really fighting for, and did we first ask God for it in the right way?
outline: Opening
A war outside begins with a war inside: where do our quarrels come from?
Point 1 · Cravings at war within
Envy and the road of Cain; the prayer that only wants to add to our pile.
Point 2 · Friend of the world, friend of God
The jealous love of God; grace for the humble; submit and resist.
Point 3 · Blessed and woe
The kingdom is already theirs; the reversal Jesus promises; the consolation we must not settle for.
Take-home line
“Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.”
live: Ask rightly (James 4:2–3)
Before your next prayer for something you want, ask: would I still want it if no one ever knew I had it? Offer the wish to God and ask for what you truly need.
End one quarrel (James 4:1)
Think of one family or parish quarrel that has run too long. Make the first move this week: a call, a visit, a cup of tea.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Do you want to be great? Begin with the least. You are planning a great building that will rise to the sky? Think first of the foundation of humility. The higher the building, the deeper the foundation must be dug.
St Basil the Great (in substance)

The bread in your cupboard belongs to the hungry; the coat hanging in your wardrobe belongs to the one who has none; the shoes you do not wear belong to the barefoot; the money in your vault belongs to the needy.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
Not to let the poor share in our goods is to steal from them and to take away their life; what we hold is not our own, but theirs.
magis: Catechism 2538–2539
The tenth commandment requires that envy be banished from the human heart. Envy is a capital sin: sadness at the sight of another's goods and the immoderate desire to get them for oneself.
Catechism 2547
The Lord grieves over the rich, because they find their consolation in the abundance of goods. The poor in spirit are those to whom the kingdom already belongs.
Catechism 2446
Giving to the poor is not an act of charity only; it is a payment of what is owed, a work of justice pleasing to God.
saints: Second Tuesday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar, St Henry (an optional memorial).

13–18 July: the second week of Kaitha. Tue 13 and Wed 14: Second Tuesday and Wednesday of Kaitha. Thu 15: Sts Kuriakose and Julitta, an Ordinary Feast of the Oriental tradition (in the Latin calendar, St Bonaventure). Fri 16: the Second Friday of Kaitha, Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai, and Our Lady of Mount Carmel, an Important Marian Feast. Sat 17: Second Saturday of Kaitha. Sun 18: Third Sunday of Kaitha. Looking ahead: St Mary Magdalene on Thursday 22 July, and St Alphonsa, the first woman of India to be raised to the altars, on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-13.prayer: Lord God, you love us with a jealous love and give grace to the humble. Quiet the cravings that make war within us and in our homes. Teach us to ask for what is good, to share what we have, and to count ourselves blessed when we have you alone. Turn our quarrels into peace, our envy into thanksgiving, and our fear of what others say into joy in your kingdom. Through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the poor man's bread and the rich man's wine are placed on the same altar, and the same Lord gives himself to both. Whoever receives him cannot go on counting what the neighbour has: in the Body of Christ the hungry are filled, and the one who comes to the table with empty hands is already an heir of the kingdom.

2027-07-14.title: Second Wednesday of Kaitha
2027-07-14.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Our inner nature is renewed day by day; a building from God
The grain of wheat that falls into the earth and dies
2027-07-14.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which follows the Season of the Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when we remember the apostles, martyrs and saints who sowed the Gospel and watered it with their blood, and keep ourselves ready for the coming of the Lord. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “Eternal building from God”; “Grain of wheat should fall into the earth and die”. In the Latin calendar, St Camillus de Lellis (an optional memorial).
2027-07-14.verse: Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
theo: Kaitha is the season of harvest, and today the readings tell us how a harvest begins: with a seed that goes under the ground. Paul writes to the Corinthians from a life of daily pressure, and the verse that opens our reading is the root of his courage: “because we know that the one who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus, and will bring us with you into his presence.” Just before, he had described himself and his companions as treasure carried in clay jars: “We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed.” What keeps the jar from breaking is not its own strength but the faith that the One who raised Jesus will raise us. And Paul adds that none of this is for himself: “Yes, everything is for your sake, so that grace, as it extends to more and more people, may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.” A suffering that is offered for others is already becoming thanksgiving.

Then comes one of the most consoling sentences in Scripture: “So we do not lose heart. Even though our outer nature is wasting away, our inner nature is being renewed day by day.” Anyone who has watched a parent grow old, or who feels the years in his own knees at the Sunday Qurbana, knows the first half of that sentence. Paul wants us to believe the second half just as firmly: the person who prays, forgives and gives is growing younger in what matters. He does not make light of pain; he himself had been beaten, shipwrecked and stoned. But he weighs it against glory: “For this slight momentary affliction is preparing us for an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, because we look not at what can be seen but at what cannot be seen; for what can be seen is temporary, but what cannot be seen is eternal.” The word “preparing” matters: suffering joined to Christ is not wasted; it is work being done in us.

The reading ends with an image from Paul's own trade, for he was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3): “For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.” A tent is a home for a journey, folded away when the journey ends. Paul does not despise the body, for the Church believes in the resurrection of the body, the very flesh we now carry; but he knows that our present life is a tent, and that God is preparing a house which no monsoon, no fire and no death can bring down. For the families of Kerala who have laid parents and children in the churchyard, this is no poetry. It is the ground on which they stand when they say at the grave: we believe in the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.

The Gospel puts this hope in the hands of Jesus. Some Greeks had come to Philip saying, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus”, and Jesus answers by saying that the hour has come: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” Then he shows what glory looks like: “Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” Every farmer who sows in the monsoon soil knows this. A seed kept in a tin is safe and useless; a seed buried in wet earth seems lost and becomes a field. Jesus is speaking first of himself, for the Cross is the grain falling, and the Church is the harvest. Then he opens the saying to all who follow: “Those who love their life lose it, and those who hate their life in this world will keep it for eternal life.” To “hate” one's life is a way of speaking in Semitic idiom, meaning to love it less than him. “Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.” The martyrs of the Church are the grain that fell: the blood of the martyrs, the early Christians said, is the seed of the Church. Even Jesus is not spared the trembling: “Now my soul is troubled.” He does not pretend. He asks the question that every one of us has asked and then gives himself to the Father: “No, it is for this reason that I have come to this hour. Father, glorify your name.” And the voice from heaven answers: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”
outline: Opening
A seed in a tin or a seed in the soil: which will become a harvest?
Point 1 · We do not lose heart
The One who raised Jesus will raise us; the treasure in clay jars; suffering offered for others becomes thanksgiving.
Point 2 · Inner nature renewed
The slight momentary affliction; what cannot be seen; the earthly tent and the house from God.
Point 3 · The grain of wheat
The hour of glory is the Cross; whoever serves must follow; the troubled soul that gives itself to the Father.
Take-home line
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
live: Look at what cannot be seen (2 Corinthians 4:18)
Choose one heavy trouble of this week. Say a short prayer over it each morning: “Lord, let this prepare something good in me.”
Let a seed fall (John 12:24)
Choose one small dying to self this week: a favourite seat given up, a sharp answer swallowed, an hour given to a sick or elderly person.
fathers: St Ignatius of Antioch (in substance)
I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts so that I may be found pure bread of Christ. Let me be the food of the beasts; through them I shall come to God.
Tertullian (in substance)
Cut us down as often as you like: the more we are mown by you, the more we grow. The blood of Christians is seed.
St Augustine (in substance)
The Lord speaks of himself: he is the grain that had to die to be multiplied. He was sown in the humility of the flesh, and he rose in glory; and all who believe in him are the harvest of his death.
magis: Catechism 1010
Because of Christ, Christian death has a positive meaning: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” The Christian who dies in Christ goes to be with him.
Catechism 1017
We believe in the true resurrection of the flesh that we now possess.
Catechism 2473
Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: it means bearing witness even unto death. The martyr bears witness to Christ, who died and rose.
saints: Second Wednesday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar, St Camillus de Lellis, priest, patron of the sick and of nurses (an optional memorial).

13–18 July: the second week of Kaitha. Tue 13 and Wed 14: Second Tuesday and Wednesday of Kaitha. Thu 15: Sts Kuriakose and Julitta, an Ordinary Feast of the Oriental tradition (in the Latin calendar, St Bonaventure). Fri 16: the Second Friday of Kaitha, Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai, and Our Lady of Mount Carmel, an Important Marian Feast. Sat 17: Second Saturday of Kaitha. Sun 18: Third Sunday of Kaitha. Looking ahead: St Mary Magdalene on Thursday 22 July, and St Alphonsa, the first woman of India to be raised to the altars, on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, grain of wheat fallen into the earth, you died to bring forth a great harvest. Give us the courage not to lose heart when our bodies grow weak or our hopes seem buried. Renew our inner life day by day; teach us to look at what cannot be seen; and make us willing to fall into the earth and die to ourselves, so that the grace we receive may grow into thanksgiving for many. Prepare for us, and for all our beloved dead, the house not made with hands. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.
altar: On the altar bread, made of many grains of wheat crushed and baked, becomes the Body of the Lord who fell into the earth and rose. Whoever receives him receives the seed of resurrection: the same Christ who was buried and raised will raise our mortal bodies, and the tent in which we now live will be exchanged for the house of God.

2027-07-16.title: Our Lady of Mount Carmel · Second Friday of Kaitha · Mar Mari, Disciple of Mar Addai
2027-07-16.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Our Lady of Mount Carmel · First Reading
Our Lady of Mount Carmel · Second Reading
Our Lady of Mount Carmel · Epistle
Participation in the sufferings and the consolation of Christ
Our Lady of Mount Carmel · Gospel
I made him a witness to the peoples (the calendar gives 55:4–13)
Those who believed were of one heart and soul (the calendar gives 4:32–5:11)
The apostle proclaims the risen Christ (the calendar gives 15:1–19)
The risen Christ appears to the apostles (the calendar gives 20:19–31)
2027-07-16.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which follows the Season of the Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when we remember the apostles, martyrs and saints who sowed the Gospel and watered it with their blood, and keep ourselves ready for the coming of the Lord. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. Today the calendar gives two commemorations, each with four readings of its own: Our Lady of Mount Carmel, an Important Marian Feast (fixed on 16 July), and the Second Friday of Kaitha, Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai, one of the Commemorations of Martyrs and Saints; both sets are shown here (verify locally which are read). The day is built on Our Lady of Mount Carmel, with a full paragraph on Mar Mari. The calendar's own headings: “Elijah brings rain through prayer”; “The splendour of Carmel”; “The blessedness of Mary”; “I made him a witness to the peoples”; “Apostle proclaims the Risen Christ”. In the Latin calendar, Our Lady of Mount Carmel is an optional memorial.
2027-07-16.verse: But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!”
theo: On the second Friday of Kaitha the Church looks at a mountain. Carmel rises from the Mediterranean coast of the Holy Land, a green ridge in a dry country, and its name means something like garden or orchard. On this mountain the prophet Elijah, after a drought of three years, prayed for rain. The Book of Kings sets the scene: “Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; there he bowed himself down upon the earth and put his face between his knees.” He sends his servant to look toward the sea. “There is nothing.” “Go again seven times.” Seven times the prophet prays and seven times the servant looks, until at the seventh time he says, “Look, a little cloud no bigger than a person’s hand is rising out of the sea.” That was enough. “In a little while the heavens grew black with clouds and wind; there was a heavy rain.” James tells us why this matters to us: “Elijah was a human being like us, and he prayed fervently” (James 5:17). Prayer that persists, that goes up again when the sky is empty, is not a magic trick; it is a human being's faith holding on until God's promise arrives. The monsoon rains of Kerala have taught us to understand a drought and the sound of rain on the roof; Elijah teaches us to wait for it with our face to the ground.

Isaiah sings of the same land restored. “The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad, the desert shall rejoice and blossom; like the crocus it shall blossom abundantly, and rejoice with joy and singing.” Then comes the name: “The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the majesty of Carmel and Sharon.” The prophet chooses Carmel as the picture of the whole world made green again by God. And he turns to the weary: “Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to those who are of a fearful heart, ‘Be strong, do not fear! Here is your God… He will come and save you.’” Christian tradition, and above all the Carmelite tradition, has read the little cloud that rose from the sea as a sign of Mary: small, humble, from the lowly, and bringing in her womb the rain of grace, the Saviour who makes the dry earth bloom. It is a loving reading that the Church allows and cherishes, not a doctrine.

Our Lady of Mount Carmel is the title under which Mary is honoured by the Order of Carmelites. In the twelfth century some pilgrims and Crusaders settled as hermits on Mount Carmel, near the spring that tradition calls Elijah's, and built there a chapel in honour of Mary; they were called the Brothers of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel. When they were forced to leave the Holy Land they spread across Europe, and Carmelite saints such as Teresa of Avila and John of the Cross made them known. The feast is kept on 16 July. An old tradition says that on that day in 1251 Our Lady gave the scapular to Simon Stock, an English Carmelite, as a sign of her protection; the historical details are uncertain, but the devotion is dear to the Church. The brown scapular is a small garment of two pieces of cloth worn over the shoulders, and the Church asks us to understand it not as a charm but as a sign of belonging to Mary: to live as she lived, listening to the word and doing it. Kerala has a rich Carmelite heritage. Saint Kuriakose Elias Chavara founded the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate (CMI) at Mannanam in 1831, the first indigenous religious congregation of men in India, and with Father Leopold he began the Congregation of the Mother of Carmel (CMC) for women, to which Saint Euphrasia belonged. Many families in our parishes wear the scapular, and the Syro-Malabar Church keeps this day as an Important Marian Feast.

The Gospel shows us the Mary of Carmel. Jesus has just said that an empty house, swept and put in order, may be taken over by worse spirits: it is not enough to be cleaned; the house must be filled. And a woman in the crowd cries out, “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you!” We might expect Jesus to agree at once; instead he lifts her words higher: “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!” He is not turning away from his mother, for Mary is first among those who hear the word and obey it. “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). “Blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfilment of what was spoken to her by the Lord” (Luke 1:45). “Mary treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). Saint Augustine said that Mary was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ. The house of Mary was swept and put in order, and it was filled with the Word; so she is the pattern of every disciple who wants to be blessed.

Paul adds the note of consolation. “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction with the consolation with which we ourselves are consoled by God.” Consolation received is consolation to be passed on. Mary stood at the Cross, and the Church has learned to call her Comforter of the Afflicted. Anyone who has sat beside a grieving mother in Kerala, with the rice-water and the silence, knows that the best comfort often comes from those who have wept themselves. “For just as the sufferings of Christ are abundant for us, so also our consolation is abundant through Christ.”

The second commemoration of the day is Mar Mari, and our own Church cannot pass him by. According to the tradition of the East Syriac Church, Mari was a disciple of Mar Addai, Thaddaeus, one of the seventy-two disciples of the Lord. Eusebius, the historian of the early Church, tells that after the Ascension the apostle Thomas sent Thaddaeus to Edessa; and Addai's disciple Mari carried the Gospel further east, into Mesopotamia and the regions along the Tigris, in the area of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, where the Church of the East began to grow. Mar Addai and Mar Mari are honoured as the founders of that Church, and the great Anaphora, the prayer of consecration, that bears their names is one of the three that our Syro-Malabar Church uses at the Holy Qurbana, among the oldest eucharistic prayers still in use. That means on most Sundays we pray with words that have come down from the first apostolic missions of the East. The details of the lives of Mar Addai and Mar Mari come to us through tradition and cannot all be confirmed historically; but the Church's gratitude is real.

The readings given for Mar Mari are like his life. Isaiah gives the promise: “See, I made him a witness to the peoples… See, you shall call nations that you do not know, and nations that do not know you shall run to you.” And God's word is like Carmel's rain: “For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and do not return there until they have watered the earth, making it bring forth and sprout, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty.” The Acts of the Apostles shows the community that was born: “the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul”, and Joseph, called Barnabas, “son of encouragement”, who sold his field and laid the money at the apostles' feet; encouragement and consolation are words of the same family, so the Church's gift of comfort in Paul and her gift of encouragement in Barnabas are one. Paul's reading to the Corinthians is the creed of every missionary: “I handed on to you as of first importance what I in turn had received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day.” Mari, too, handed on what he had received. Finally John's Gospel gives the Risen Christ in the upper room: “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so I send you.” Then Thomas: “My Lord and my God!” The same Thomas whose faith reached the shores of Kerala, and whose sending of Addai, according to tradition, gave the East its first teachers. Carmel and Edessa, the cloud and the word, the Mother and the missionary: today the Church gives thanks that the rain of the Gospel has watered the whole world.
outline: Opening
A mountain, a drought and a little cloud no bigger than a hand.
Point 1 · Elijah's persistent prayer
Seven times he prays, seven times the servant looks; the human prayer that holds on.
Point 2 · Mary, the cloud and the word
The Carmelite tradition, the scapular as a sign of belonging, and the house filled with the Word: “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it.”
Point 3 · God of all consolation
Consolation received is consolation passed on; Mary Comforter of the Afflicted.
Point 4 · Mar Mari and the word that does not return empty
The disciple of Mar Addai, the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Gospel that came from Edessa to the East.
Take-home line
“Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!”
live: Pray seven times (1 Kings 18:43–44)
Choose one prayer you have given up. Bring it to God again each day this week, and look for the small cloud.
Hear the word and keep it (Luke 11:28)
Read the Gospel of the coming Sunday today, and choose one line of it to keep and to do through the week.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Mary was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ. Her nearness as a mother would have done her no good if she had not borne Christ more happily in her heart than in her body.
St Bernard of Clairvaux (in substance)

If the winds of temptation arise, if you run upon the rocks of tribulation, look to the star, call upon Mary. In danger, in distress, in doubt, think of Mary, call upon Mary. Following her, you will not go astray.
Eusebius of Caesarea (in substance)
After the Ascension, Judas who is also called Thomas sent Thaddaeus, one of the seventy, to Edessa, to preach the Gospel and to heal in the name of Jesus.
magis: Lumen Gentium 58

In the course of her Son's preaching she received the words whereby, in extolling a kingdom beyond the calculations and bonds of flesh and blood, he declared blessed those who heard and kept the word of God, as she was faithfully doing.
Catechism 148
The Virgin Mary most perfectly embodies the obedience of faith.
Catechism 971
“All generations will call me blessed”: the Church's devotion to the Blessed Virgin is intrinsic to Christian worship.
saints: Our Lady of Mount Carmel, an Important Marian Feast of the Syro-Malabar Church; the Second Friday of Kaitha, with the commemoration of Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai. In the Latin calendar, Our Lady of Mount Carmel, an optional memorial.

13–18 July: the second week of Kaitha. Tue 13 and Wed 14: Second Tuesday and Wednesday of Kaitha. Thu 15: Sts Kuriakose and Julitta, an Ordinary Feast of the Oriental tradition (in the Latin calendar, St Bonaventure). Fri 16: the Second Friday of Kaitha, Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai, and Our Lady of Mount Carmel, an Important Marian Feast. Sat 17: Second Saturday of Kaitha. Sun 18: Third Sunday of Kaitha. Looking ahead: St Mary Magdalene on Thursday 22 July, and St Alphonsa, the first woman of India to be raised to the altars, on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-16.prayer: Holy Mother of Carmel, Mary, who heard the word of God and kept it, pray for us. Lord God, you sent your prophet Elijah to the mountain and gave rain when the sky was empty; give us the faith that prays seven times and looks for the little cloud. Fill the house of our hearts with your word, so that no emptiness may return to us worse than before. Console the afflicted through us, as you have consoled us. We thank you for Mar Addai and Mar Mari and for all who carried the Gospel to the East; keep alive in us the apostolic faith we celebrate at your altar. Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana, in the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, we use the very words by which the first missionaries of the East offered the Lord's sacrifice. The Word that was received by Mary's faith and was made flesh in her is the Body and Blood given on the altar, and the same Holy Spirit who made the Virgin's womb fruitful descends on bread and wine. Whoever comes to receive him becomes, with Mary, one who hears the word of God and keeps it.

2027-07-17.title: Second Saturday of Kaitha
2027-07-17.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: God chose the poor to be heirs of the kingdom
Those who eat the bread of heaven are blessed: the great dinner
2027-07-17.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which follows the Season of the Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when we remember the apostles, martyrs and saints who sowed the Gospel and watered it with their blood, and keep ourselves ready for the coming of the Lord. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “God selected the poor as the heirs of heaven”; “Those who eat the bread of heaven are blessed”.
2027-07-17.verse: And the slave said, “Sir, what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.”
theo: Saturday in the second week of Kaitha puts before us two tables: the assembly of the Church in James, and the banquet of the kingdom in Luke. James begins with a question that cuts: “My brothers and sisters, do you with your acts of favoritism really believe in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ?” His picture is simple and true to life. “If a person with gold rings and in fine clothes comes into your assembly, and if a poor person in dirty clothes also comes in, and if you take notice of the one wearing the fine clothes and say, ‘Have a seat here, please,’ while to the one who is poor you say, ‘Stand there,’ or, ‘Sit at my feet,’ have you not made distinctions among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts?” The assembly of the Church, which gathers around the Lord's table, is the one place where no one should be placed by his clothes or his wallet. In our own parishes, at the feast-day lunch and at the Sunday Qurbana, the question is just as real: who is welcomed first, who is asked to speak, who is given the good seat, and who stands at the back?

James then says what God does: “Listen, my beloved brothers and sisters. Has not God chosen the poor in the world to be rich in faith and to be heirs of the kingdom that he has promised to those who love him?” God does not despise the rich; but he has a special tenderness for the poor, and the Church's teaching speaks of a preferential love for them. James reminds a community in trouble that the very people they flatter are often those who drag them into court, and “you have dishonored the poor.” The remedy is what he calls the royal law, the law of the King: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Moses had already forbidden partiality in a court: “you shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great: with justice you shall judge your neighbor” (Leviticus 19:15). Whoever loves in this way does well; whoever flatters the great and scorns the small breaks the law of love, however religious he may seem.

In Luke's Gospel Jesus is a guest at table in the house of a leading Pharisee. One of the guests, hearing him talk of invitations and of the resurrection, says a pious thing: “Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” Jesus answers with a story. “Someone gave a great dinner and invited many. At the time for the dinner he sent his slave to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come; for everything is ready now.’ But they all alike began to make excuses.” The excuses are polite, and the things they name are good things: “I have bought a piece of land, and I must go out and see it”; “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out”; “I have just been married, and therefore I cannot come.” Land, work and family are not evil. But each guest puts a good thing before the invitation, and the host's “everything is ready now” goes unanswered. Saint Gregory the Great read in these three excuses the land of pride and possession, the oxen of busy affairs, and the wife of comfort; whatever the reading, the lesson is that the call of God cannot always wait until our business is finished.

Then the host's anger turns into a welcome. “Go out at once into the streets and lanes of the town and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.” The slave goes, and comes back: “Sir, what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.” There is still room: it is the sentence that has driven the Church's mission since the first apostles. The master sends him again to the roads and lanes, “and compel people to come in, so that my house may be filled.” The word “compel” is not an order to force anyone, for the faith can never be forced; it is the host's insistent, urgent love that will not take a polite refusal from those who have never been asked. The parable is not a verdict on any people: it is a mirror held up to each of us who has heard the call, and has found a reason to wait. Put James and Luke together: the poor in the assembly are the guests of the banquet, and the one who prefers the well-dressed to the stranger has already found his excuse. Where is the Qurbana's table set? In the middle of the street, with room for one more. In the Season of Kaitha, the season of harvest, the Church prays that the house will be filled.
outline: Opening
Two tables: the assembly in James and the great dinner in Luke.
Point 1 · No favouritism
Gold rings and dirty clothes; the royal law of love; the one place where no one is ranked by his wallet.
Point 2 · God chose the poor
Rich in faith, heirs of the kingdom; the preferential love of the Church.
Point 3 · Everything is ready now
The excuses of the invited: good things before the call.
Point 4 · There is still room
The streets and lanes; the host's urgent love; the house that must be filled.
Take-home line
“Sir, what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.”
live: Welcome the stranger (James 2:2–4)
At the next Qurbana or parish gathering, greet first and sit beside someone whom nobody is sitting with: a newcomer, an old person, someone poor.
Answer the call today (Luke 14:17)
Look at the excuse you most often give God: work, property, family business. Set aside one hour this week to answer his invitation: the Qurbana, a prayer, a visit.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)
Do you wish to honour the body of Christ? Do not despise him when he is naked. Do not honour him here in church with silk vestments, and then neglect him outside, where he is cold and naked.
St Gregory the Great (in substance)

The three excuses are three snares of the world: the land stands for the pride of possession, the oxen for the care of earthly business, and the wife for the pleasures of the flesh. Whoever is held by them does not come to the banquet.
Clement of Alexandria (in substance)
The Lord did not forbid the rich to be saved; he asked that wealth be made a servant and not a master, and that it be used to feed, to clothe and to welcome the needy.
magis: Catechism 2443
God blesses those who come to the aid of the poor and rebukes those who turn away from them: “Give to him who begs from you, do not refuse him who would borrow from you”.
Catechism 2444
The love of the Church for the poor is part of her constant tradition, inspired by the Gospel of the Beatitudes and by the poverty of Jesus.
Catechism 1384
The Lord addresses an invitation to us, urging us to receive him in the sacrament of the Eucharist.
saints: 13–18 July: the second week of Kaitha. Tue 13 and Wed 14: Second Tuesday and Wednesday of Kaitha. Thu 15: Sts Kuriakose and Julitta, an Ordinary Feast of the Oriental tradition (in the Latin calendar, St Bonaventure). Fri 16: the Second Friday of Kaitha, Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai, and Our Lady of Mount Carmel, an Important Marian Feast. Sat 17: Second Saturday of Kaitha. Sun 18: Third Sunday of Kaitha. Looking ahead: St Mary Magdalene on Thursday 22 July, and St Alphonsa, the first woman of India to be raised to the altars, on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-17.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, host of the great supper, you invite us and tell us that everything is ready. Forgive us the excuses we have put before your call, and the favouritism we have shown in your house. Teach us to love our neighbour as ourselves; make us glad to see the poor in your Church, and give us a heart that makes room for one more. Fill your house with those who have never been asked, and bring us all to the table of your kingdom, where you live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord sets his table and says, “Come; for everything is ready now.” The bread of heaven is given in the same way to the rich man and the beggar, the old and the child, the stranger and the neighbour. Whoever comes to this altar and then despises his brother has not understood the supper: we come as guests, and the master has room for one more.

2027-07-19.title: Third Monday of Kaitha
2027-07-19.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Faith is brought to completion by works
2027-07-19.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when the Church remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her field with their blood and keeps herself ready for the coming of the Lord. The calendar's own headings: “Faith accomplished through the deeds”; “Jesus mourns over Jerusalem”.
2027-07-19.verse: For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is also dead.
theo: The Season of Kaitha is the season of the harvest, and a harvest is judged by its fruit. Today's Epistle asks what the fruit of faith is. James places two very different people side by side: Abraham, the father of believers, and Rahab, a woman of Jericho whom the Bible calls a prostitute. “Was not our ancestor Abraham justified by works when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was brought to completion by the works.” James is not contradicting Paul. Paul argues against those who thought they could earn God's favour by keeping the Law; James argues against those who thought that a belief held in the head, with a closed hand and a closed door, is enough. Both of them quote the same verse, “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6), and both know that faith is God's gift. But a gift received is a gift used. Abraham believed long before he climbed the mountain of Moriah; the climb was his faith made visible, and in that obedience, says James, faith “was brought to completion”. The Church teaches the same: faith is the beginning of salvation, and a faith that is not alive in hope and love does not unite us fully to Christ.

Then James names Rahab: “Likewise, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works when she welcomed the messengers and sent them out by another road?” Her story is told in the Book of Joshua. Two spies come to Jericho; she hides them on her roof, confesses that “The Lord your God is indeed God in heaven above and on earth below” (Joshua 2:11), and asks that her family be spared. Her faith did not stay in words: she risked her life and her house. The Letter to the Hebrews also names her among the people of faith (11:31), and Matthew places her in the family line of the Messiah (Matthew 1:5). So the patriarch and the foreigner, the greatest and the least, are justified in the same way, by a living faith that opens the door. James closes with the sentence that gathers the whole passage: “For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is also dead.”

The Gospel takes us to the last teaching of Jesus in the Temple, after the seven woes. He speaks as a prophet of Israel who loves his people as only one of them could. “Therefore I send you prophets, sages, and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and pursue from town to town.” He points back over the whole long history of faithful witnesses, “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah”, from the first righteous man killed in Genesis to the last in the order of the Hebrew Scriptures (2 Chronicles 24:20–21). The prophets whom he now sends are the apostles and martyrs whom Kaitha honours. These hard words are to be read as the Church reads them: as a warning to every generation, ours included, and not as a verdict on a people. The Church teaches that the Jewish people as a whole are not to be blamed for the death of the Lord (Catechism 597–598), and that God's call to them is irrevocable (Romans 11:29). Jesus, his mother and his first disciples were all Jews.

Then the tone turns from warning to tenderness: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” Every Kerala household knows the picture: at the first shadow of a kite in the sky the mother hen spreads her wings and the chicks run under them. The psalmist already said of God, “he will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge” (Psalm 91:4). It is not God who is unwilling; “you were not willing”. His love never forces. Yet the lament ends with a promise: “you will not see me again until you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’” The words are from Psalm 118:26, which the crowds sing on Palm Sunday and which the Church repeats in the Sanctus of the Holy Qurbana. So we ask two questions today: what fruit does my faith bear, and have I let myself be gathered under his wings?
outline: Opening
A tree is known by its fruit: what does my faith look like on an ordinary Monday?
Point 1 · Faith brought to completion
Abraham believed first and obeyed after; faith and works belong together.
Point 2 · The open door of Rahab
A stranger's living faith: welcome, risk and rescue.
Point 3 · Wings spread, children unwilling
The grief and tenderness of Jesus over Jerusalem; love that does not force.
Take-home line
“Faith without works is also dead.”
live: Let your faith be seen (James 2:22)
Choose one concrete act this week that your faith asks of you: a visit, a bill paid on time, a quarrel ended, a gift to someone in need. Do it quietly.
Come under the wings (Matthew 23:37)
Each evening this week, before sleep, say: “Lord, gather me under your wings,” and then name the people you want him to gather too.
fathers: St Clement of Rome (in substance)

Because of her faith and her hospitality Rahab the prostitute was saved. She received the spies and sent them out another way, and so she became a sign that those who trust in the Lord find redemption.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
When the Lord says “How often”, he shows not anger but a love wounded by refusal. These are the words of one who grieves over a city he would have saved, not of one who hates it.
magis: Catechism 1815 (in substance)

The gift of faith remains in one who has not sinned against it. But faith without works is dead: when it is deprived of hope and love, it does not fully unite the believer to Christ or make him a living member of his Body.
Catechism 597–598 (in substance)
It is not possible to lay responsibility for the Lord's Passion on the Jewish people as a whole. The Church sees the sins of all sinners as the cause of the sufferings of Christ.
Catechism 839 (in substance)
The Jewish people are the first to have heard the Word of God; theirs is the covenant and the promises, and God's gifts and call to them are irrevocable.
saints: Third Monday of Kaitha. In Kerala the monsoon is at its height and the fields are green: a good day to remember that faith, like a crop, is known by its fruit.

19–24 July: the third week of Kaitha. Mon 19 to Wed 21 and Sat 24: the Third Week of Kaitha, with the Epistle from the Letter of James (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat). Thu 22: Saint Mary Magdalene, apostle of the apostles, with readings of her own. Fri 23: the Third Friday of Kaitha (readings from the 2022–23 calendar, verify locally). Sat 24: in the Latin and Malankara calendars, Saint Sharbel Makhluf, a monk of the Maronite Church. Looking ahead: the Fourth Sunday of Kaitha on 25 July, and Saint Alphonsa on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-19.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you gathered your people under your wings, though they were not willing. Gather us today. Make our faith alive, like the faith of Abraham who obeyed and of Rahab who opened her door; let our hands do what our lips confess. Keep us from judging any people as you alone can judge, and teach us to grieve over the world as you grieved over Jerusalem. Welcome us when we come in your name, for you are blessed, you who come in the name of the Lord, now and for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord gathers his scattered children as a hen gathers her brood, around one altar, one bread and one cup. We come with the faith we confess in the Creed, and we are sent out to give it flesh in works of mercy, so that the Body we receive may live in the world through us.

2027-07-20.title: Third Tuesday of Kaitha
2027-07-20.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: A prophet is not accepted in his hometown
2027-07-20.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when the Church remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her field with their blood and keeps herself ready for the coming of the Lord. The calendar's own headings: “True wisdom is humble”; “Prophet is neglected in his hometown”. In the Syro-Malankara calendar today is the memory of the Prophet Elijah, who appears in the Gospel.
2027-07-20.verse: And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace for those who make peace.
theo: Who is wise? James asks the question as a teacher in a village school might ask it, and he gives an answer that surprises us: “Show by your good life that your works are done with gentleness born of wisdom.” For James wisdom is not cleverness, learning or a sharp tongue; it is a way of living that can be seen. He then sets two kinds of wisdom side by side. One is “earthly, unspiritual, devilish”, and it grows where there is “bitter envy and selfish ambition”. Its fruit is just as plain: “where there is envy and selfish ambition, there will also be disorder and wickedness of every kind.” Anyone who has sat on a parish committee, a family meeting or a village council knows how true this is. The other wisdom comes “from above”: “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, willing to yield, full of mercy and good fruits, without a trace of partiality or hypocrisy.” It is a portrait of Christ himself, and it begins with purity of heart and ends in good fruit.

The last verse carries the image of the Season of Kaitha: “And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace for those who make peace.” A farmer sows in the right season and in good soil; the seed of righteousness is sown in peace, and the harvest is gathered by those who make peace. It echoes the promise of Isaiah, “The effect of righteousness will be peace, and the result of righteousness, quietness and trust forever” (Isaiah 32:17), and the Beatitude of the Lord, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). The Fathers saw that envy is the root of much strife. Saint Basil (in substance) called it grief at the good of a neighbour, and Saint Augustine (in substance) called it hatred of another's happiness. The envious person is never at rest, because there is always someone who is doing better. The remedy is not to be less ambitious for good, but to rejoice with those who rejoice, and to ask God for the wisdom from above (James 1:5).

The Gospel shows envy at work in a small town. Jesus has come to Nazareth, “where he had been brought up”, and in the synagogue he reads from Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor.” At first all speak well of him and are amazed. Then comes the question that hides a doubt: “Is not this Joseph's son?” They cannot see beyond the carpenter's family they have known since he was a boy. Jesus answers with the proverb, “no prophet is accepted in the prophet's hometown”, and with two stories from their own Scriptures. In the great famine of Elijah's day, God sent the prophet to a widow of Zarephath in Sidon, a foreigner (1 Kings 17:9). In the time of Elisha, the one leper who was cleansed was Naaman the Syrian (2 Kings 5:14). God's mercy goes beyond every border, and the people of Nazareth, who wanted the miracles for themselves, cannot bear it. “All in the synagogue were filled with rage”: they drive him out of the town and lead him to the brow of the hill. This is the first of the rejections that end at the Cross, and yet, “he passed through the midst of them and went on his way”. His hour had not yet come.

For Kerala the lesson is close to home. We too can fail to see God in what is familiar: the parish priest we have known since he was a deacon, the sister who taught us, the neighbour's son who has become a teacher or a doctor, the grandmother whose prayer holds the house together. Familiarity can close our eyes. And we too can be angry when God is generous to someone we did not expect to be blessed. Today we ask for the wisdom from above: to see Christ in the ordinary, to welcome the blessing of others without envy, and to be, in our own homes and parishes, among those who make peace and gather a harvest of righteousness.
outline: Opening
Who is wise among you? A wisdom that can be seen in a good life.
Point 1 · Two kinds of wisdom
Earthly wisdom of envy and ambition; wisdom from above that is pure, peaceable and full of mercy.
Point 2 · Envy and its harvest
Disorder where envy rules; the harvest of righteousness sown in peace.
Point 3 · The prophet at home
Nazareth cannot see beyond Joseph's son, and cannot bear God's mercy to the stranger.
Take-home line
“A harvest of righteousness is sown in peace for those who make peace.”
live: Rejoice with others (James 3:14)
Think of someone whose success makes you uneasy. This week thank God aloud for the good that has come to that person, and congratulate them.
See the prophet at home (Luke 4:24)
Listen this week with new attention to someone you take for granted at home or in the parish, and thank them for what God has given through them.
fathers: St Basil the Great (in substance)

Envy is grief at the good fortune of a neighbour; therefore the envious man is never without pain, since the blessings of others never come to an end. Rejoice in your brother's good, and it becomes your own.
St Augustine (in substance)
Envy is hatred of another's happiness. It is the sin of the devil, who fell by pride and then envied the human being who was made to stand where he had fallen.
magis: Catechism 2539 (in substance)
Envy is sadness at the sight of another's goods and the immoderate desire to acquire them for oneself. It is a capital sin; the remedy is goodwill, humility and trust in God's providence.
Catechism 2305 (in substance)
Earthly peace is the image and fruit of the peace of Christ, the Prince of Peace; those who make peace share in his work.
Catechism 2582 (in substance)
Elijah, the father of the prophets, belongs to the generation that sought the face of the living God; the Church learns from the prophets to trust the word of God even when his people do not.
saints: Third Tuesday of Kaitha. In the Syro-Malankara calendar this is the memory of the Prophet Elijah, who appears in today's Gospel; in the Latin calendar it is the optional memorial of Saint Apollinaris.

19–24 July: the third week of Kaitha. Mon 19 to Wed 21 and Sat 24: the Third Week of Kaitha, with the Epistle from the Letter of James (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat). Thu 22: Saint Mary Magdalene, apostle of the apostles, with readings of her own. Fri 23: the Third Friday of Kaitha (readings from the 2022–23 calendar, verify locally). Sat 24: in the Latin and Malankara calendars, Saint Sharbel Makhluf, a monk of the Maronite Church. Looking ahead: the Fourth Sunday of Kaitha on 25 July, and Saint Alphonsa on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-20.prayer: God of wisdom, you give your wisdom from above to those who ask in faith. Make us pure in heart, peaceable, gentle, willing to yield and full of mercy. Heal in us the envy that grieves at another's good, and teach us to rejoice with those you bless. Give us eyes to see you in the people we know best, so that we may not drive you from our towns as Nazareth did. Make us peacemakers, and let the seed of righteousness we sow in peace bear a rich harvest in your Church. Through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord who was driven from Nazareth gives himself to us in the most ordinary things, bread and wine, and no one is a stranger at his table. We come with our small envies and our quarrels, we offer one another the sign of peace, and from one altar the seed of peace is sown in us for the harvest of the week.

2027-07-21.title: Third Wednesday of Kaitha
2027-07-21.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: In Christ God reconciled the world to himself
2027-07-21.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when the Church remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her field with their blood and keeps herself ready for the coming of the Lord. The calendar's own headings: “In Christ, God reconciled the world to himself”; “Jesus calls the first disciples”. In the Latin calendar today is the optional memorial of Saint Lawrence of Brindisi.
2027-07-21.verse: So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!
theo: Paul has just said why he cannot stay silent: “For the love of Christ urges us on, because we are convinced that one has died for all; therefore all have died.” Today's reading continues: “And he died for all, so that those who live might live no longer for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them.” The death and rising of Christ is not only something that happened to him; it is something that happened to us, and it changes how we live and how we see. “From now on, therefore, we regard no one from a human point of view”: the neighbour I have labelled by caste, party, income or an old quarrel is now seen as someone for whom Christ died. Then comes one of the great sentences of the New Testament: “So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!” For the Syro-Malabar faithful this is the language of the baptismal font, where we go down with Christ and rise to “walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4), and it is the language of every confession and every Qurbana in which the old is forgiven and the new begins. God had promised it long before through Isaiah: “I am about to do a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it?” (Isaiah 43:19).

The whole movement begins with God: “All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ, and has given us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting the message of reconciliation to us.” Reconciliation is not two parties meeting halfway; the offended party makes the first move, at his own cost. Then comes the astonishing title: “So we are ambassadors for Christ, since God is making his appeal through us; we entreat you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.” An ambassador lives in a foreign land, carries the word of the king, and is received as the king himself would be received. God makes an appeal, he does not command, and he makes it through human voices: a priest in the confessional, a mother who ends a family quarrel, a neighbour who says sorry first. The reading ends at the heart of the mystery: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” The sinless one took our place, and in his sacrifice we are given a place in God's own righteousness.

The Gospel shows how this ministry began, with four fishermen. “As Jesus passed along the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and his brother Andrew casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And Jesus said to them, ‘Follow me and I will make you fish for people.’ And immediately they left their nets and followed him.” A little farther on he sees James and John “in their boat mending the nets”; “Immediately he called them; and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men, and followed him.” Nothing is said about their qualifications. Jesus does not call the learned of Jerusalem but men with the smell of fish and the habit of hard work, and he gives them a new work, to bring people out of the waters of death into life. This is the beginning of the apostolic Church which the Season of Kaitha honours. The fishermen of Galilee became the ambassadors of Paul's letter; the call was theirs, and the message was entrusted to them.

In Kerala, with its fishing villages along the coast, from Vypin to Vizhinjam, the picture needs no explanation: the early morning, the mended net, the boat pushed out into the waves. Every Christian has been called, in his or her own trade, to be an ambassador of reconciliation, in the home, at the workplace, in the parish and on the road. Gregory the Great (in substance) noticed that Peter and Andrew had little to leave, only a net and a boat, and yet the Lord accepted it as a great gift, because the kingdom of God is worth exactly as much as we have, and we give what we have. The first step is the same for all of us: be reconciled to God, and then go and be reconciled to the brother or sister whom we have not spoken to for years.
outline: Opening
The love of Christ urges us on: he died for all, and so we live for him.
Point 1 · New creation
From now on we see no one from a merely human point of view; everything has become new.
Point 2 · Ambassadors of reconciliation
God made the first move; he appeals through human voices; he made the sinless one to be sin for us.
Point 3 · Follow me
Four fishermen, immediate answers, nets left behind; the apostolic Church begins.
Take-home line
“Be reconciled to God.”
live: Make the first move (2 Corinthians 5:18)
Think of the person with whom you have not spoken for a long time. This week make the first move: a message, a call, a visit.
Leave one net (Mark 1:18)
Name one habit or possession that holds you back from following Christ more closely, and take one concrete step to let it go.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

Peter and Andrew had left only a net and a boat, yet they had left everything, because the Lord does not weigh what is given but the heart that gives it. The kingdom of God is worth as much as you have.
St Augustine (in substance)
He who knew no sin was made sin for us, that is, a sacrifice for sin, so that we, who were sinners, might be made the righteousness of God, not in ourselves but in him.
magis: Catechism 1442 (in substance)
Christ gave his apostles the ministry of reconciliation; the Church continues it in the sacrament of Penance, where bishops and priests act in the name of Christ.
Catechism 787 (in substance)
From the beginning Jesus associated his disciples with his own life, revealed the mystery of the kingdom to them, and gave them a share in his mission, his joy and his sufferings.
Catechism 1989 (in substance)
The first work of the grace of the Holy Spirit is conversion, which brings the forgiveness of sins and reconciles us to God.
saints: Third Wednesday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar, the optional memorial of Saint Lawrence of Brindisi, a Capuchin preacher and Doctor of the Church.

19–24 July: the third week of Kaitha. Mon 19 to Wed 21 and Sat 24: the Third Week of Kaitha, with the Epistle from the Letter of James (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat). Thu 22: Saint Mary Magdalene, apostle of the apostles, with readings of her own. Fri 23: the Third Friday of Kaitha (readings from the 2022–23 calendar, verify locally). Sat 24: in the Latin and Malankara calendars, Saint Sharbel Makhluf, a monk of the Maronite Church. Looking ahead: the Fourth Sunday of Kaitha on 25 July, and Saint Alphonsa on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-21.prayer: Father of mercy, in Christ you reconciled the world to yourself and did not count our trespasses against us. Make us a new creation. Give us the courage of the fishermen of Galilee, who left their nets at your word, and make us ambassadors of your peace in our homes, our parish and our land. Where there is a quarrel, let us be the first to speak; where there is a wound, let us bring your healing. Through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the one who died for all and rose for all gives himself to us as the sign and the cost of our reconciliation. Before we approach the altar we exchange the sign of peace, because the Lord's offering and our quarrel cannot stand side by side; and as the nets were left on the shore, so we leave our old selves here and are sent out as his ambassadors.

2027-07-22.title: Third Thursday of Kaitha · Saint Mary Magdalene
2027-07-22.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Who can separate us from the love of Christ?
Mary Magdalene proclaims the risen Christ
The prayer offered in faith will make the sick person well
Jesus sends out the twelve disciples
2027-07-22.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when the Church remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her field with their blood and keeps herself ready for the coming of the Lord. The calendar gives the readings of Saint Mary Magdalene and the weekday readings of the Third Thursday of Kaitha; both sets are shown here (verify locally which are read). The Latin Church keeps her feast today, and the Syro-Malankara Church keeps her memory.
2027-07-22.verse: Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”; and she told them that he had said these things to her.
theo: Of all the women who followed Jesus, one is named in every Gospel: Mary of Magdala, a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Luke tells us who she was before the Lord met her: “Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out”, who with Joanna, Susanna and many others “provided for them out of their resources” (Luke 8:2–3). A woman who had been delivered from a great darkness spent the rest of her life giving back what she had received. We know her only through what the Gospels say: her healing, her service, her courage. She is among the women who watched “from a distance” (Mark 15:40), and John puts her “near the cross of Jesus”, standing with his mother (John 19:25). She saw where the body was laid (Mark 15:47). The Gospels do not say that she was the sinful woman of Luke 7 or Mary of Bethany; the Church today keeps these women distinct, and the older identification made in the Western Church is remembered only as a tradition, which the Eastern Churches never adopted. What the Gospels give is enough: she is the disciple who stayed when others fled.

Her whole story is an answer to the question of today's Epistle: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will hardship, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” Paul's answer is a cry of victory: “No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor rulers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Mary Magdalene did not read these lines, but she lived them. Not the soldiers, not the darkness, not even the closed tomb could separate her from the love she had received. Many Christians have heard in her search the voice of the bride in the Song of Songs: “I will seek him whom my soul loves” (Song of Songs 3:2).

John tells the Easter morning with a care that makes us see it: “Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed.” She runs to Simon Peter and the beloved disciple; they run to the tomb, see the linen wrappings, and the beloved disciple believes, and then “the disciples returned to their homes.” “But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb.” The angels ask, “Woman, why are you weeping?” and then the Lord himself, whom she does not recognise, asks the same question and adds, “Whom are you looking for?” She takes him for the gardener: “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.” She will carry the body of the Lord herself if she must. Then comes the shortest and greatest speech in the Gospel: “Jesus said to her, ‘Mary!’ She turned and said to him in Hebrew, ‘Rabbouni!’ (which means Teacher).” The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3), and she knows his voice. He is not recognised by his face but by the way he says her name.

Then the risen Lord gives her a mission: “Do not hold on to me, because I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’” She must not cling to the old way of being near him; a new nearness is coming, through the Ascension and the Spirit. And for the first time he calls the disciples “my brothers” and shares his Father with them. “Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord’.” Luke records how her message was received: the words seemed to the apostles “an idle tale” (Luke 24:11). Yet the Church's whole witness begins with her voice. This is why Saint Thomas Aquinas called her the apostle of the apostles, and why in 2016 the Church raised her memorial to a feast. In the Season of Kaitha, which honours the apostles, the Church places beside the Twelve the woman whom the Lord himself sent to tell the Twelve. The Eastern Churches honour her among the myrrh-bearing women who came to the tomb with their ointments.

The weekday readings, too, speak of prayer and mission. James teaches the prayer of the community: “Are any among you suffering? They should pray. Are any cheerful? They should sing songs of praise.” He mentions the anointing of the sick with oil, confession to one another, and the prayer of the righteous, which “is powerful and effective”: “Elijah was a human being like us, and he prayed fervently”. The prophet whom the Syro-Malankara Church remembered on Tuesday is held up as a man like us, so that we may pray as he did. The Gospel is the sending of the Twelve: “As you go, proclaim the good news, ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near.’ ... You received without payment; give without payment.” “As you enter the house, greet it. If the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it.” Mary Magdalene received without payment, from the Lord who drove out the seven demons, and she gave without payment, all she had. She entered the room of the frightened disciples with the first greeting of Easter on her lips. Today we ask for the same love that does not leave, the same ears that know his voice, and the same courage to announce, “I have seen the Lord.”
outline: Opening
A woman delivered from darkness who stayed when others fled.
Point 1 · Love that is not separated
At the cross and at the tomb; nothing in creation can separate us from the love of Christ.
Point 2 · “Mary!”
She seeks and weeps; the Good Shepherd calls his sheep by name.
Point 3 · Do not hold on, but go
A new nearness and a mission: “go to my brothers”.
Point 4 · Apostle of the apostles
“I have seen the Lord”: the first witness, and the word that was thought an idle tale.
Take-home line
“I have seen the Lord.”
live: Stay near (John 19:25)
Visit this week someone who is suffering or who is alone, and simply stay near them, as Mary stayed near the cross.
Listen for your name (John 20:16)
Each morning this week, after your prayer, stay silent for a minute and listen for the Lord calling you by name; then go and tell one person something good that you have seen of him.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)
Mary stayed at the tomb to seek him whom she had not found, and because she went on seeking she found him. So her desire grew by waiting, and by growing it became able to receive what it found.
St Thomas Aquinas (in substance)
She is rightly called the apostle of the apostles, for she announced to the apostles what they were to announce to the world.
magis: Catechism 641 (in substance)

Mary Magdalene and the holy women, who came to anoint the body of Jesus, were the first to encounter the Risen One; so women were the first messengers of Christ's Resurrection to the apostles themselves.
Catechism 640 (in substance)
The empty tomb is a first sign, not a proof; the apostles come to believe in the Resurrection through the encounter with the Risen Lord, and Mary Magdalene is the first to meet him.
Catechism 645 (in substance)
The risen body of Jesus is the same body that was crucified, yet it shares in the divine life; so he appears as he wishes and is not recognised at once, as Mary Magdalene took him for the gardener.
saints: Saint Mary Magdalene, disciple of the Lord and first witness of the Resurrection, called “apostle of the apostles”. The Latin Church has kept her feast since 2016, and the Syro-Malankara Church keeps her memory today; the Eastern Churches honour her among the myrrh-bearing women.

19–24 July: the third week of Kaitha. Mon 19 to Wed 21 and Sat 24: the Third Week of Kaitha, with the Epistle from the Letter of James (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat). Thu 22: Saint Mary Magdalene, apostle of the apostles, with readings of her own. Fri 23: the Third Friday of Kaitha (readings from the 2022–23 calendar, verify locally). Sat 24: in the Latin and Malankara calendars, Saint Sharbel Makhluf, a monk of the Maronite Church. Looking ahead: the Fourth Sunday of Kaitha on 25 July, and Saint Alphonsa on Wednesday 28 July.
