2027-07-22.prayer: Risen Lord Jesus Christ, you called Mary Magdalene by her name in the garden and sent her to your brothers. Call us by name, and make us hear your voice. Give us her love that stayed at the cross and her courage that sought you in the dark. Let nothing in creation separate us from your love, and make us witnesses who can say, “I have seen the Lord.” Hear us through the prayers of Saint Mary Magdalene, apostle of the apostles, for you live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the risen Lord is present, and he calls each of us by name as he called Mary in the garden. We do not hold on to him as Mary tried to do; he gives himself to us in the Bread and the Cup and then sends us, as he sent her, to tell our brothers and sisters, “I have seen the Lord.”

2027-07-23.title: Third Friday of Kaitha
2027-07-23.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Christ dwells in your hearts through faith
Jesus heals a blind man at Bethsaida
2027-07-23.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when the Church remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her field with their blood and keeps herself ready for the coming of the Lord. The calendar's own headings: “Christ is in your heart through faith”; “Jesus heals the blind”. These readings are taken from the official First Set calendar of 2022–23 for the Third Friday of Kaitha, because the 2025 calendar has a different feast on the matching day (verify locally). In the Latin calendar today is the optional memorial of Saint Bridget of Sweden.
2027-07-23.verse: and that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, as you are being rooted and grounded in love.
theo: On this Friday, the day on which the Church remembers the Lord's death, the Epistle gives us a prayer of Saint Paul on his knees: “For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth takes its name.” In a land where the family is so dear, it is a joy to hear that every family, in heaven and on earth, takes its name from the Father of Jesus Christ. Paul then makes three requests. The first: “that, according to the riches of his glory, he may grant that you may be strengthened in your inner being with power through his Spirit.” The second: “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith.” The third: “as you are being rooted and grounded in love.” The heart in the Bible is not only the seat of feeling; it is the centre of the whole person, where we decide and where we meet God. Christ does not visit the heart as a guest who leaves; he dwells there. And Paul uses two images that a Kerala farmer and a builder understand at once: roots and foundations. A coconut palm that has sent its roots deep survives the monsoon storm; a house with a good foundation stands in the flood. The prophet had already said, “They shall be like a tree planted by water, sending out its roots by the stream” (Jeremiah 17:8).

Then comes the great prayer for understanding: “I pray that you may have the power to comprehend, with all the saints, what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.” Paul does not name what has breadth, length, height and depth; it is the love of Christ. Saint Augustine (in substance), in a letter, saw in these four dimensions the shape of the Cross: the breadth is the crossbeam where the Lord's hands were stretched out, the length is the upright on which his body hung, the height is the part that rises above the beam, and the depth is the part fixed in the earth and hidden. His love reaches to the whole world, to the whole of time, to the heights of God and to the depths of our sin. It “surpasses knowledge”, and yet we are asked to know it, not as we know a fact but as we know a person, with all the saints, within the Church. The reading ends with the song that every Christian sings: “Now to him who by the power at work within us is able to accomplish abundantly far more than all we can ask or imagine, to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever. Amen.”

The Gospel puts before us a blind man and a Lord who does not hurry. “They came to Bethsaida. Some people brought a blind man to him and begged him to touch him.” The man has friends who carry his need to Jesus. “He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village; and when he had put saliva on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, ‘Can you see anything?’” Jesus uses ordinary things, a hand and spittle, because he heals the whole person, body and trust together. The answer is the most honest sentence in the Gospel of Mark: “I can see people, but they look like trees, walking.” This is the only healing in Mark that comes in two stages. “Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he looked intently and his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly.” The Lord does not scold the man for seeing so little. He touches him again.

Mark has placed this story with great care. Right after it Jesus asks his disciples, “Who do you say that I am?” and Peter answers, “You are the Messiah” (Mark 8:29): he sees the shape, but not yet clearly, because he cannot yet accept the Cross. The disciples too are men who see people like trees walking. Saint Bede (in substance) and other Fathers saw in the two touches the way the Lord enlightens us gradually, and we should not be ashamed to be beginners. Today's two readings are about seeing with the heart: Paul prays that we may comprehend the dimensions of Christ's love, and the blind man is healed in stages. We do not understand the Cross all at once. We learn it year by year, in Qurbana, in sorrow, in prayer, until the day we see everything clearly. Let us bring our blind friends to Jesus, as the people of Bethsaida did, and let us let him take us by the hand, outside the village of our habits, and touch us again.
outline: Opening
A prayer on bended knees: every family in heaven and on earth takes its name from the Father.
Point 1 · Christ in the heart, roots in love
Strength in the inner being; the tree planted by the stream.
Point 2 · The breadth, length, height and depth
The love of Christ that surpasses knowledge; the shape of the Cross.
Point 3 · Sight in stages
The blind man of Bethsaida; the patient Lord who touches again.
Take-home line
“Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, as you are being rooted and grounded in love.”
live: Kneel for your family (Ephesians 3:14–15)
Each evening this week kneel for one minute and pray for every member of your family by name, in the words of Paul: that Christ may dwell in their hearts.
Bring a blind friend (Mark 8:22)
Think of someone who cannot yet see the way, in faith or in life, and bring them to Jesus by prayer and by a visit or a call.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The breadth is the crossbeam on which the hands are stretched; the length is the upright from the beam to the ground; the height is the part above the beam; the depth is the part hidden in the earth. The love of Christ is the Cross, in all its dimensions.
St Bede the Venerable (in substance)
The Lord heals the blind man in two stages to show how the mind is enlightened step by step; and he leads him out of the village so that the one who is healed may leave the crowd and its noise.
magis: Catechism 2563 (in substance)
The heart is the dwelling place where I am, where I live; it is the place of decision and of encounter with God, who is the one who searches it.
Catechism 1504 (in substance)
Jesus often asks the sick to believe, and uses signs to heal them: spittle and the laying on of hands, mud and washing. The sacraments continue his healing touch.
Catechism 1827 (in substance)
Charity is the form of all the virtues; it is the source and the goal of Christian life and raises human love to the divine love.
saints: Third Friday of Kaitha, a day on which the Church remembers the Lord's death. In the Latin calendar, the optional memorial of Saint Bridget of Sweden. No saint is commemorated in the Syro-Malabar calendar today, as far as the calendar of this season shows.

19–24 July: the third week of Kaitha. Mon 19 to Wed 21 and Sat 24: the Third Week of Kaitha, with the Epistle from the Letter of James (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat). Thu 22: Saint Mary Magdalene, apostle of the apostles, with readings of her own. Fri 23: the Third Friday of Kaitha (readings from the 2022–23 calendar, verify locally). Sat 24: in the Latin and Malankara calendars, Saint Sharbel Makhluf, a monk of the Maronite Church. Looking ahead: the Fourth Sunday of Kaitha on 25 July, and Saint Alphonsa on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-23.prayer: Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth takes its name, we bow our knees before you. Strengthen us through your Spirit in our inner being; let Christ dwell in our hearts through faith, and root and ground us in love. Give us the power to comprehend, with all the saints, the breadth and length and height and depth of the love of Christ, and fill us with all the fullness of God. Take us by the hand as you took the blind man, and touch us again where we see only dimly, until we see everything clearly. Glory to you in the Church and in Christ Jesus to all generations, for ever and ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana, on the day of the Cross, the love whose breadth and depth we cannot measure is given to us in the Bread and the Cup. Christ comes to dwell not only in the heart of the Church but in the heart of each one who receives him with faith, and he sends us out rooted in love.

2027-07-24.title: Third Saturday of Kaitha
2027-07-24.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Whoever is not against you is for you
2027-07-24.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when the Church remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her field with their blood and keeps herself ready for the coming of the Lord. The calendar's own headings: “Boasting is evil”; “He that is not against you is for you”. In the Latin and Syro-Malankara calendars today is the memory of Saint Sharbel Makhluf, a monk and hermit of the Maronite Church of Lebanon.
2027-07-24.verse: Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wishes, we will live and do this or that.”
theo: Saint James paints a scene from the market. A trader says, “Today or tomorrow we will go to such and such a town and spend a year there, doing business and making money.” There is nothing wrong with planning, and James does not forbid it. What he exposes is the presumption in the plan, the tone of a man who speaks as if he were the lord of tomorrow. “Yet you do not even know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes.” Anyone who has seen the morning mist on the hills of Idukki or Munnar in the monsoon knows how quickly it is gone when the sun rises. The psalmist prays the same truth: “So teach us to count our days that we may gain a wise heart” (Psalm 90:12). Then comes the remedy: “Instead you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wishes, we will live and do this or that.’” Many Kerala families keep the habit in their speech: ‘if God helps’. It is not a phrase to excuse laziness; it is the confession that every plan is made inside God's providence. “The human mind plans the way, but the Lord directs the steps” (Proverbs 16:9).

James adds two sharp sentences. “As it is, you boast in your arrogance; all such boasting is evil.” And then the line that every conscience hears: “Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, commits sin.” The Church teaches that sin is not only what we do but also what we fail to do, in thought, word, deed and omission. Every good examination of conscience asks not only what we have done but what we have left undone. The man in James's market had no plan to harm anyone. His fault was that God and the neighbour did not appear in the plan at all: the good he could do today he put off for a tomorrow that he does not own.

The Gospel begins with a small quarrel among the apostles. John says, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.” It is the voice of the group: he is not one of us. Jesus answers, “Do not stop him; for whoever is not against you is for you.” The same breadth of heart was in Moses when Joshua wished to silence Eldad and Medad, who were prophesying in the camp: “Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the Lord's people were prophets” (Numbers 11:29). The Church teaches, of course, that the fullness of the means of salvation is found in the Catholic Church. But she also teaches that “many elements of sanctification and of truth” are found outside her visible boundaries (Catechism 819), and that good done in the name of Christ by others is not to be forbidden with envy. This is the same lesson as on Tuesday: the spirit of rivalry is the opposite of the wisdom from above.

Then the Gospel turns toward the Cross: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” Isaiah's servant had said, “I have set my face like flint” (Isaiah 50:7). Jesus sends messengers ahead to a Samaritan village, and the villagers do not receive him because his face is set toward Jerusalem. James and John, whom the Lord called Sons of Thunder (Mark 3:17), say, “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” They remember Elijah, who once called down fire (2 Kings 1:10), and the Church has met this prophet more than once this week. But Jesus “turned and rebuked them. Then they went on to another village.” No fire, no argument, no revenge. He who has set his face to the Cross moves on to another village. It is the way of the Lamb. In many homes Saturday is kept in honour of the Mother of the Lord, and in her we see the opposite of the arrogant plan: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). Her whole life was an ‘if the Lord wishes’.
outline: Opening
A mist on the hills in the morning: our plans and the Lord who directs the steps.
Point 1 · A mist that vanishes
Plan, but with the words “If the Lord wishes”; the good not done is sin.
Point 2 · Whoever is not against you
The spirit of the group against the breadth of Jesus; good done in his name.
Point 3 · His face set toward Jerusalem
No fire from heaven; the Lamb moves on to the next village.
Take-home line
“If the Lord wishes, we will live and do this or that.”
live: Say it and mean it (James 4:15)
Before each important plan this week, say quietly: “If the Lord wishes”, and offer the plan to him. Do today the good thing that you have been putting off.
Welcome a good done by another (Luke 9:50)
Find one good work done by someone outside your own group, parish or association, and thank God for it and for the people who do it.
fathers: St Bede the Venerable (in substance)
James does not forbid us to make plans but teaches us to refer every plan to the will of God, who holds our life in his hand; the one who forgets God in his plans builds on a mist.
St Cyprian of Carthage (in substance)
Patience belongs to Christ; the disciple of the Lamb overcomes by gentleness, not by revenge.
magis: Catechism 1013 (in substance)
Death is the end of man's earthly pilgrimage, of the time of grace and mercy which God offers him; there is no return to another earthly life, and so we must be watchful.
Catechism 1853 (in substance)
Sins can be classed in thought, word, deed or omission (compare James 4:17: to know the good and not do it is sin).
Catechism 819 (in substance)
Many elements of sanctification and truth are found outside the visible structure of the Catholic Church; the Spirit of Christ uses them as means of salvation, and they call us toward unity.
saints: Third Saturday of Kaitha; in many homes Saturday is Mary's day. In the Latin and Syro-Malankara calendars, Saint Sharbel Makhluf (1828–1898), a monk and hermit of the Maronite Church in Lebanon, much loved by many Indian Catholics.

19–24 July: the third week of Kaitha. Mon 19 to Wed 21 and Sat 24: the Third Week of Kaitha, with the Epistle from the Letter of James (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat). Thu 22: Saint Mary Magdalene, apostle of the apostles, with readings of her own. Fri 23: the Third Friday of Kaitha (readings from the 2022–23 calendar, verify locally). Sat 24: in the Latin and Malankara calendars, Saint Sharbel Makhluf, a monk of the Maronite Church. Looking ahead: the Fourth Sunday of Kaitha on 25 July, and Saint Alphonsa on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-24.prayer: Lord God, our lives are like a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes, and our tomorrows are in your hands. Teach us to count our days and gain a wise heart. Let us make our plans in humility and say with sincere hearts, “If the Lord wishes.” Keep us from boasting, and move us to do today the good that we know. Give us the breadth of heart of Jesus, who did not forbid the stranger who cast out demons in his name; and give us his gentleness, who set his face toward Jerusalem and refused to call down fire. Through Mary, who said “Let it be with me according to your word”, and through Christ our Lord, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lamb of God who set his face toward Jerusalem makes present his one offering, and we place before him all our plans and our tomorrows. We receive the Bread of the journey, and we are sent out to do the good we know, in the company of all who work in his name.

2027-07-26.title: Fourth Monday of Kaitha · Saint Joachim and Saint Anne
2027-07-26.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: What is impossible for mortals is possible for God
Sts Joachim and Anne · First Reading
Sts Joachim and Anne · Second Reading
The genealogy of Jesus the Messiah
2027-07-26.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, summer), which began on 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when she remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her with their blood and waits in readiness for the Lord's coming. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar gives the weekday readings of the Fourth Monday of Kaitha and the readings of the commemoration of Saint Joachim and Saint Anne; both sets are shown here (verify locally which are read). The Latin Church keeps the memorial of Sts Joachim and Anne today.
2027-07-26.verse: He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor. For the pillars of the earth are the Lord’s, and on them he has set the world.
theo: Yesterday we honoured grandparents, and today the Church gives us the grandparents of Jesus. The Bible does not name the parents of the Virgin Mary. Their names, Joachim and Anne, come to us from an early Christian writing of the second century, the Protoevangelium of James, which is not part of Scripture but which the Church has treasured for its picture of the family into which Mary was born. By tradition, then, Joachim and Anne were an older couple who had long prayed for a child. The Eastern Churches kept their feast from early times, and the West followed. The name Anne is the Greek form of Hannah, which means grace, and in Kerala it lives on in the name Annamma, borne by countless grandmothers, while Joachim, in its Malayalam form Yoakim, is the name of many a grandfather. We honour them as the saints who handed on faith to the one who gave the Saviour to the world.

The Church puts the song of Hannah on their lips. Hannah, long barren, prayed in the temple at Shiloh, and when her son Samuel was born she sang: “My heart exults in the Lord; my strength is exalted in my God.” It is the song that Mary will sing again in the Magnificat. “The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble gird on strength. Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry are fat with spoil. The barren has borne seven.” And above all: “He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor.” God is the one who reverses the world's order. The couple who, according to tradition, bore the shame of childlessness became the grandparents of the Messiah.

Isaiah continues the theme in his word to Jerusalem: “Sing, O barren one who did not bear; burst into song and shout, you who have not been in labor! For the children of the desolate woman will be more than the children of her that is married, says the Lord.” Then comes the command that every grandmother and grandfather needs: “Enlarge the site of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out; do not hold back.” The family of faith grows wider than anyone could have imagined, because the Lord says, “with everlasting love I will have compassion on you.” The letter to the Hebrews shows the same pattern in Abraham and Sarah. Of Abraham the letter says that “he considered him faithful who had promised,” and that “from one person, and this one as good as dead, descendants were born.” Faith is trust in the one who keeps his promise when our own strength is gone.

Matthew's Gospel opens with a list of names: “An account of the genealogy of Jesus the Messiah, the son of David, the son of Abraham.” It is a long chain of ordinary people, some famous, some not, some sinners, who handed on a promise from one generation to the next. Jesus did not fall from the sky; he was born into a family and a history. Joachim and Anne belong to that chain. In every Kerala home, the names of grandparents, the lamp lit at dusk, the Our Father taught at a grandmother's knee are the links of the same chain. And the chain ends in the verse that matters most: “Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called the Messiah.”

The weekday readings add a sober word. James says to the rich: “Your riches have rotted, and your clothes are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be evidence against you.” The wages kept back by fraud “cry out.” In Luke, Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God. The disciples ask in despair, “Then who can be saved?” and he answers, “What is impossible for mortals is possible for God.” The same tradition that names Joachim also remembers him as a rich man, but one who gave his gifts to the poor and to the Temple, and who, when he was humiliated for having no child, did not turn bitter but fasted and prayed. Riches do not save, and neither does poverty by itself; the grace of God saves, and it asks for a heart that gives and trusts. Peter says: “Look, we have left our homes and followed you.” Jesus answers that no one who has left house or family for the kingdom “will not get back very much more in this age, and in the age to come eternal life.” Grandparents are the best witnesses of this: a long life given away in love comes back as a great family and a rich old age.
outline: Opening
Yesterday grandparents, today the grandparents of Jesus: Joachim and Anne.
Point 1 · The song of the barren
Hannah's song, Isaiah's tent: God turns shame into joy; Mary's Magnificat is already sung.
Point 2 · By faith
Abraham and Sarah, Joachim and Anne: a promise handed from one generation to the next.
Point 3 · Riches that rot and a gift that returns
James against hoarding; Luke's camel and the needle; what is impossible for mortals is possible for God.
Take-home line
“What is impossible for mortals is possible for God.” (Luke 18:27)
live: Thank your grandparents (Matthew 1:2)
Write down the names of your four grandparents and a quality of faith or character you received from each. Thank God for them tonight.
Do not hold back (Isaiah 54:2)
If you are an older person, tell one younger person this week how God carried you; if you are young, ask an older one.
Pay what is owed (James 5:4)
Check whether any wage, fee or debt you owe to a worker, a house help or a small trader is delayed. Settle it this week.
Pray with the Magnificat (1 Samuel 2:1)
Say the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55) slowly after the evening prayer this week, in the name of someone who is waiting for a miracle.
fathers: St John of Damascus (in substance)

O blessed pair, Joachim and Anne, all creation is in your debt. Through you the creation offered to the Creator the best of all gifts, a pure Mother, who alone was worthy to be the Mother of the Creator.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Hannah teaches us how to pray. She did not need a loud voice; her lips moved and her heart was heard. She poured out her soul before the Lord, and the Lord who looks at the heart gave her what she asked, and more.
St Basil the Great (in substance)

The bread that you keep is the bread of the hungry; the coat that you store is the coat of the naked; the money that you bury is the money of the poor. Those who have more than they need have a debt, not a prize.
magis: Catechism 489

Throughout the Old Covenant the mission of many holy women prepared for that of Mary. At the very beginning there was Eve; and, despite her disobedience, she receives the promise of a posterity that will be victorious over the evil one, and the promise that she will be the mother of all the living.
Catechism 146
Abraham thus fulfils the definition of faith in Hebrews 11:1: faith is the assurance of things hoped for. He is the model of faith, and the Church honours him as our father in faith.
Catechism 2219
Filial respect promotes harmony in all of family life; it also concerns relationships between brothers and sisters and respect toward grandparents and ancestors.
Catechism 2544
Jesus enjoins his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone, and bids them renounce all that they have for his sake and that of the Gospel.
saints: Fourth Monday of Kaitha. Saint Joachim and Saint Anne, the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary, according to tradition. In the Latin calendar, their memorial.

25–31 July: the fourth week of the Season of Kaitha. Sun 25: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha (St James the Apostle gives way to the Sunday; World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly). Mon 26: Sts Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Wed 28: St Alphonsa, the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised, an important feast. Thu 29: St Martha. Fri 30: Fourth Friday of Kaitha. Sat 31: St Ignatius of Loyola. In the Latin calendar the same days keep Sts Joachim and Anne (26), St Alphonsa (28, a memorial in India), Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus (29) and St Ignatius (31). Looking ahead: the month of August and the later weeks of Kaitha.
2027-07-26.prayer: Lord God, you gave your Son a mother and a family, and you chose Joachim and Anne to hand on the faith to the Virgin Mary. Bless our grandfathers and grandmothers, living and departed. Reward their patience, their prayers and the hope they kept for us. Make us grateful for the chain of faith that has reached us, and let us pass it on to our children. Teach us, like Hannah, to pour our hearts before you, and, like Abraham and Sarah, to trust your promise when our own strength is spent. Keep us from the love of money that rots, and give us hearts that give. Through the prayers of Saint Joachim and Saint Anne, grant to the old and the lonely a peaceful home. Amen.
altar: The Holy Qurbana is the table where generations meet. We stand with the faithful of every age: Abraham and Sarah, Hannah, Joachim and Anne, our own grandparents. The Body of Christ, who took flesh from Mary, the daughter of Joachim and Anne, is given to us, so that the chain of faith may pass from the altar into every home.

2027-07-27.title: Fourth Tuesday of Kaitha
2027-07-27.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Be patient until the coming of the Lord
The coming of the Son of Man
2027-07-27.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, summer), which began on 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when she remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her with their blood and waits in readiness for the Lord's coming. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “Be patient until the coming of the Lord”; “The Coming of the Son of Man”. In the Latin calendar today is the Tuesday of the seventeenth week in Ordinary Time (Exodus 33:7–11; 34:5b–9, 28; Matthew 13:36–43).
2027-07-27.verse: You also must be patient. Strengthen your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is near.
theo: Kerala knows how to wait for rain. The farmer who has prepared the field cannot make the monsoon come; he can only repair the bunds, keep the seed ready, and watch the sky. Saint James uses exactly this picture for the Church in the season of Kaitha, the time of growth and harvest: “Be patient, therefore, beloved, until the coming of the Lord. The farmer waits for the precious crop from the earth, being patient with it until it receives the early and the late rains.” The land of Palestine, like Kerala, had two rainy seasons, the early rain of autumn that softens the ground for sowing and the later rain of spring that fills the ears of grain; our own Edavappathi and Thulavarsham are their cousins. The farmer does not complain that the rain comes in its own time. “You also must be patient. Strengthen your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is near.”

Patience in James is not passivity. It is a strength of the heart, a holding firm. He gives the community three practical rules for the waiting time. First, “do not grumble against one another, so that you may not be judged. See, the Judge is standing at the doors!” Long waiting makes people short-tempered, in the parish as in the family, and the complaint against a neighbour is the first sign of a heart that has stopped looking for the Lord. Second, look at the prophets and at Job: “As an example of suffering and patience, beloved, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. Indeed we call blessed those who showed endurance. You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.” Job lost everything and said, “the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord”; and in the end the Lord's purpose showed itself as compassion. Third, keep your word: “let your ‘Yes’ be yes and your ‘No’ be no, so that you may not fall under condemnation.” People who are waiting for the Lord should be people whose word can be trusted, who do not need oaths to be believed.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks of the great coming. Mark's thirteenth chapter, often called the little apocalypse, uses the language of the prophets: the sun darkened, the moon not giving its light, the stars falling, the powers of heaven shaken. This is the language of the end of an age, the old world shaking to make room for the new. Out of the shaking comes the one sure thing: “Then they will see ‘the Son of Man coming in clouds’ with great power and glory. Then he will send out the angels, and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.” The elect are gathered from the ends of the earth, and no corner of the world, no village on a distant hill, is forgotten. The Church in India, which according to tradition received the Gospel from Mar Thoma at the edge of the known world, hears in this promise that nobody is too far to be gathered.

Then Jesus teaches by the fig tree, as the farmer teaches by the rain: “From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts forth its leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates.” The fig tree gives no timetable, only a sign that a season is turning. Elsewhere Jesus says plainly that “about that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” and tells us to “keep alert” (Mark 13:32–33). The Church does not read charts and dates of the end; she lives each day as a day of the Lord's nearness. And the promise that makes this possible is the last sentence of the reading: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” The monsoon passes, the year passes, a life passes; his word remains. For this reason we can wait without fear: the one who is coming is the one who has already come, who is with us in the Holy Qurbana, and who will come again.

The passage ends the day with a prayer for the patient heart. If the waiting seems long, remember that the farmer sows in the rain and reaps in the sun. The Lord is “compassionate and merciful,” and he knows how long a human being can wait. Let us use the waiting time as Kaitha teaches: to strengthen our hearts, to speak without complaint, to keep our word, to pray for those who are still far away, and to look for the signs of summer in the green leaves of every day.
outline: Opening
Waiting for rain: the Kerala farmer and the coming of the Lord.
Point 1 · Be patient
The farmer, the early and the late rains; strengthening the heart; no grumbling, no oaths.
Point 2 · Endurance
The prophets and Job: blessed are those who endure; the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
Point 3 · Keep alert
The Son of Man will gather his elect from the ends of the earth; the fig tree; his words will not pass away.
Take-home line
“Strengthen your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is near.”
live: Wait without grumbling (James 5:9)
For one day this week, do not complain about anyone. If a complaint rises, turn it into a prayer for that person.
Keep your word (James 5:12)
Make one promise you have delayed and keep it this week; make no promise you cannot keep.
Read the signs (Mark 13:28)
Take five minutes in the evening to read one gospel verse about the coming of the Lord, and pray ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’
fathers: St Cyril of Jerusalem (in substance)

We proclaim not only one coming of Christ, but a second one also, much more glorious than the first. The first showed his patience; the second brings the crown of the kingdom. Let us therefore be ready, and not merely hope.
St Augustine (in substance)
Patience is the companion of wisdom. The one who is patient does not lose the good that he already has because of an evil he suffers; he waits for the good that is promised.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Job lost his children, his herds and his health, and still he stood. The devil took everything but could not take his patience, and in this he was richer than before. A patient heart is the one treasure the thief cannot reach.
magis: Catechism 673
Christ's coming in glory is imminent, although it is not for us to know the times or the moments which the Father has fixed by his own authority.
Catechism 1817

Hope is the theological virtue by which we desire the kingdom of heaven and eternal life as our happiness, placing our trust in Christ's promises and relying not on our own strength, but on the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit.
Catechism 2153
The Lord teaches that every oath involves a reference to God, and that God's name is to be honoured; our word should be simple: Yes or No.
saints: Fourth Tuesday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar, the Tuesday of the seventeenth week in Ordinary Time.

25–31 July: the fourth week of the Season of Kaitha. Sun 25: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha (St James the Apostle gives way to the Sunday; World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly). Mon 26: Sts Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Wed 28: St Alphonsa, the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised, an important feast. Thu 29: St Martha. Fri 30: Fourth Friday of Kaitha. Sat 31: St Ignatius of Loyola. In the Latin calendar the same days keep Sts Joachim and Anne (26), St Alphonsa (28, a memorial in India), Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus (29) and St Ignatius (31). Looking ahead: the month of August and the later weeks of Kaitha.
2027-07-27.prayer: Lord Jesus, you are coming, and we do not know the day or the hour. Strengthen our hearts as you strengthened the prophets and Job, and as the farmer waits for the rain, teach us to wait for you without grumbling and without fear. Keep our word true and our hands busy while we wait. Gather your elect from the ends of the earth, and let us be among them, with all those who prayed and worked for us. Your words will not pass away; let them be our rock when the monsoon rains pour and the rivers rise. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbana we proclaim the Lord's death and resurrection until he comes. The bread and wine are the first fruits of the harvest that he will gather at the end; every Qurbana is a small coming of the Son of Man in clouds of incense and glory, and a promise of the great one. We wait, but we wait at the table.

2027-07-28.title: Fourth Wednesday of Kaitha · Saint Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception
2027-07-28.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Crucified in weakness, alive by the power of God
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few
Suffering that leads to the kingdom of God
Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies
2027-07-28.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, summer), which began on 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when she remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her with their blood and waits in readiness for the Lord's coming. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar gives the weekday readings of the Fourth Wednesday of Kaitha and the readings of the commemoration of Saint Alphonsa, an important feast among the commemorations of martyrs and saints; both sets are shown here (verify locally which are read). The calendar's own headings for the saint's readings: “Israel, God's portion”; “Suffering leads to the Kingdom of God”; “Be crucified with Christ”; “Be like the grain of wheat that is dropped into the ground and dies”. In the Latin calendar of India, today is the memorial of Saint Alphonsa.
2027-07-28.verse: Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
theo: Today the Church in Kerala, and with her the whole Church in India, keeps the feast of a daughter of our own soil. Anna Muttathupadathu was born on 19 August 1910 at Kudamaloor, in the Kottayam district, in a Syro-Malabar Catholic family. Her mother died when she was a few months old, and she was brought up by her mother's sister, at Muttuchira. She grew into a girl who loved prayer and who longed to belong wholly to Christ. When a marriage was being arranged for her, her biographers tell us, she did a terrible thing out of desperate love: she stepped into a pit of burning chaff, so as to be unfit for marriage, and she carried the injury to her feet for life. In 1927 she entered the convent of the Franciscan Clarist Congregation at Bharananganam, took the name Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception, and lived there a hidden life of prayer, teaching and humble work. Illness followed illness, and she bore them with a quiet smile. She died on 28 July 1946, at the age of thirty-five. Pope John Paul II beatified her at Kottayam on 8 February 1986, and Pope Benedict XVI canonised her in Rome on 12 October 2008. She is the first woman of Indian origin to be declared a saint, and the first canonised saint of the Syro-Malabar Church. Her tomb in the church at Bharananganam is visited by pilgrims of every faith, and the Syro-Malabar Church calls her Alphonsamma, as one calls a mother or an aunt.

The readings of her feast give the secret of her life. The first is from Deuteronomy: “The Lord will establish you as his holy people, as he has sworn to you, if you keep the commandments of the Lord your God and walk in his ways. All the peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by the name of the Lord.” A people consecrated to God is a visible sign to the nations; Alphonsa, in a small cell, became such a sign for Kerala and for the world. The same chapter promises blessing on the barns and on the land, and the reading closes with the rain in its season: “The Lord will open for you his rich storehouse, the heavens, to give the rain of your land in its season and to bless all your undertakings.” In July, in the monsoon, we see the sky open, and we remember that this reading is about a God who gives from heaven the gift that no field can produce for itself. Alphonsa never had a field to sow, and yet her life bore the harvest of a whole Church.

Isaiah's fourth song of the Servant goes to the heart: “Yet it was the will of the Lord to crush him with pain. When you make his life an offering for sin, he shall see his offspring, and shall prolong his days; through him the will of the Lord shall prosper. Out of his anguish he shall see light; he shall find satisfaction through his knowledge. The righteous one, my servant, shall make many righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities.” The Church reads the song in the light of Jesus, the Servant who gave himself for the many. Suffering by itself saves no one; only the suffering of Christ, offered in love, has redeeming power. But he lets his friends share in it. Saint Paul writes: “I am now rejoicing in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am completing what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church.” Alphonsa understood this. She did not look for pain, and she asked for healing as anyone would; but when the suffering came, she joined it to the cross of the Lord, and from her cell she prayed for the Church and for sinners. Her suffering was not a failure, but a kind of fruitfulness.

In the letter to the Galatians, Paul gives the words that every saint could say: “I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” That is what holiness means: Christ living in a person who has let go of herself. Alphonsa had nothing to boast of in the eyes of the world. She was a sick sister in a convent, who taught little children for a short time, who was often unable to work, and who died young. And yet, “it is Christ who lives in me.” The Gospel gives the picture that fits her best. Some Greeks come to Philip and say, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.” Jesus answers with a parable about a grain of wheat: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Those who love their life lose it, and those who hate their life in this world will keep it for eternal life. Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.” Alphonsa was a grain that fell into the ground of Bharananganam. In 1946 it seemed that a young nun had died unnoticed. Today the fruit is a shrine that receives thousands of pilgrims, and countless people in hospitals, at home and in prison who have learnt from her that suffering offered with love is not wasted.

The weekday readings add a word of encouragement. Paul says to the Corinthians: “he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.” Weakness and power are not enemies in the Christian life: the cross is where God's power is hidden. In the Gospel Jesus goes about the villages, and when he sees the crowds, “he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.” Then he says to the disciples: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.” We are in Kaitha, the season of harvest. Alphonsa was one of those laborers whom the Lord sent into his field, though from a sickbed. Let us ask the Lord today to send more of them, women and men who love the poor and the sick, and let each of us ask what part of the harvest is ours: a sick neighbour to visit, a child to teach, a pain to offer.
conn: Sharing in Christ's sufferings.
“I am now rejoicing in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am completing what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church” (Colossians 1:24).
Carrying the death of Jesus.
“Always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our bodies” (2 Corinthians 4:10).
The cross and following.
“If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).
The Servant who heals.
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).
Love that gives life.
“No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends” (John 15:13).
Drawn to himself.
“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the grain of wheat is on the altar: the bread that is broken and the Lord who died and rose to bear much fruit. Saint Alphonsa gave her whole life to this mystery; she asked to be joined to the sacrifice of Christ every day. Whoever kneels at this altar with a pain or an illness may place it there, beside the Body and Blood of the Lord, and so make it a gift to the Father.

The blessing of the Qurbana does not stay in the church. As the grain was broken for us, we are sent out to be broken bread for others, in the hospital ward, in the sickroom at home, in the long hours of care for a parent. There, in hidden service, the harvest of Kaitha is ripening.
outline: Opening
A daughter of Kerala at the altar of the Church: Alphonsa, the grain of wheat of Bharananganam.
Point 1 · A holy people, a visible sign
Deuteronomy: God's people called by his name; Alphonsa's hidden life made her a sign for the nations.
Point 2 · The Servant and the suffering offered
Isaiah 53 and Colossians 1:24: suffering united to Christ's offering bears fruit for many.
Point 3 · Crucified with Christ, a grain that dies
Galatians 2:20 and John 12:24: Christ lives in her; the grain of wheat bears much fruit.
Point 4 · The harvest and the laborers
Matthew 9:37–38: the Lord of the harvest sends laborers, even from a sickbed.
Take-home line
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
live: Offer one pain (Colossians 1:24)
When you have a headache, a long wait, or a hurt, say: “Lord, I offer this with your cross for someone who needs it,” and name the person.
Visit one who suffers (Matthew 25:36)
This week visit a sick or lonely person, in a hospital, a home or a care centre, and stay a little longer than is comfortable.
Be a grain (John 12:24)
Choose one hidden thing that you will do for others without being noticed: washing the dishes, helping a child with homework, giving up a seat.
Pray for vocations (Matthew 9:38)
Pray the Lord of the harvest to send laborers, and say a prayer for the sisters of your parish.
fathers: Tertullian (in substance)
The blood of Christians is seed. The more you cut us down, the more we grow; the death of the faithful is the seed of the Church. What looks like loss is the Lord's sowing.
St Augustine (in substance)

Christ is the grain of wheat that died and was multiplied. He fell into the earth and rose to bear much fruit, which is the whole Church. Let every disciple die to self so that the harvest may be great.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
Paul does not say that he has Christ with him, but that Christ lives in him, as the soul lives in the body. A person whom Christ has taken into himself carries Christ wherever she goes.
magis: Catechism 618

The Cross is the unique sacrifice of Christ; he invites his disciples to take up their cross and follow him, for he wants to associate with his redeeming sacrifice those who are to be its first beneficiaries.
Catechism 1505
By his passion and death on the Cross Christ has given a new meaning to suffering: it can henceforth configure us to him and unite us with his redemptive Passion.
Catechism 956
The intercession of the saints is their most exalted service to God's plan; we may and we should ask them to intercede for us and for the whole world.
Catechism 2013
All Christians in any state or walk of life are called to the fullness of Christian life and to the perfection of charity; holiness is for everyone.
saints: Fourth Wednesday of Kaitha. Saint Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception (1910–1946), Franciscan Clarist sister of Bharananganam, canonised on 12 October 2008, the first woman of Indian origin to be declared a saint, and the first canonised saint of the Syro-Malabar Church. In the Latin calendar of India, her memorial.
Her tomb at Bharananganam, in the Pala diocese, receives pilgrims of every faith, especially during the novena before her feast in the monsoon. Many people in Kerala carry her name.

25–31 July: the fourth week of the Season of Kaitha. Sun 25: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha (St James the Apostle gives way to the Sunday; World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly). Mon 26: Sts Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Wed 28: St Alphonsa, the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised, an important feast. Thu 29: St Martha. Fri 30: Fourth Friday of Kaitha. Sat 31: St Ignatius of Loyola. In the Latin calendar the same days keep Sts Joachim and Anne (26), St Alphonsa (28, a memorial in India), Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus (29) and St Ignatius (31). Looking ahead: the month of August and the later weeks of Kaitha.
2027-07-28.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, grain of wheat fallen into the earth, you died and rose to bear much fruit. We thank you for Saint Alphonsa, your faithful daughter of Kerala, who offered her suffering in love for the Church and for sinners. Grant, through her prayers, that all who are sick, lonely or in pain may find strength, and may offer what they bear with your cross. Send more laborers into your harvest, sisters, priests and lay people who love the poor. Teach us to die to ourselves so that you may live in us. Let the grain that fell at Bharananganam bear fruit in every home of our land, and let all our people come to see you. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.

2027-07-29.title: Fourth Thursday of Kaitha · Saint Martha
2027-07-29.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: I came to bring fire to the earth
Whoever lives in love lives in God
Jesus, the resurrection and the life
2027-07-29.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, summer), which began on 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when she remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her with their blood and waits in readiness for the Lord's coming. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar gives the weekday readings of the Fourth Thursday of Kaitha and the readings of the commemoration of Saint Martha; both sets are shown here (verify locally which are read). The calendar's own headings: “Humble yourselves before God”; “I came to bring fire to the earth”; “He who lives in love lives in God”; “Jesus the Life and Resurrection”. The Latin Church keeps today the memorial of Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus, the friends of Jesus at Bethany.
2027-07-29.verse: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”
theo: Of all the friends of Jesus, the house at Bethany seems to have been the one where he felt most at home. The Gospel of John says it in a single sentence: “Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.” Bethany lay about two miles from Jerusalem, on the road he walked on his way to the feast, and there a woman named Martha welcomed him into her home. We know her from three scenes. In Luke she is the one busy with “many tasks,” who comes to the Lord and says: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to do all the work by myself?” In John, at the death of her brother, she is the one who runs out to meet him on the road and makes a confession of faith. And at the supper in Bethany six days before the Passover, “Martha served.” Today the Church honours her as a saint, a woman who loved the Lord in the practical ways of the kitchen and the road, and who also found the words of faith.

The reading from John is one of the greatest passages of the Gospel. Lazarus “had already been in the tomb four days,” and “many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them about their brother.” When Martha hears that Jesus is coming, she goes out to meet him, while Mary stays at home. Her first words are full of grief and of trust: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that God will give you whatever you ask of him.” Jesus says, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha answers with the faith of her people, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.” And then Jesus lifts her faith higher: “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” The resurrection is not only an event of the last day; it is a person standing on the road in front of her. Martha's answer, in the verse that follows the reading, belongs among the great confessions: “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.” It is the faith that Peter confesses at Caesarea Philippi, and it is spoken by a woman, before Lazarus has been raised, in the middle of her tears.

The reading from the First Letter of John explains why Martha's service and her faith belong together: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God; everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love.” Love is not first our achievement. “In this is love, not that we loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins.” Martha's kitchen, her bread and her fire were an answer to a love that had come first. “No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God lives in us, and his love is perfected in us.” And the letter ends with the words that could stand over every Christian home: “God is love, and those who abide in love abide in God, and God abides in them.” Kerala is famous for its hospitality, for the cup of tea and the rice offered to every guest; the letter to the Hebrews says that “some have entertained angels without knowing it.” Martha was a woman who knew how to welcome Christ in a guest.

The weekday readings meet her at the same door. James says: “Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.” In John, Martha does precisely this: when Jesus comes, she draws near, runs to meet him, and speaks to him without fear. James also says, “Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you,” and he warns against speaking evil of one another and judging a neighbour. In Luke 10 the two sisters are tempted to judge each other, one for being busy, the other for being idle; the Lord does not tell Martha to stop serving, but to stop being “worried and distracted by many things.” He says, “there is need of only one thing,” and Mary has chosen it. The Gospel of the day then speaks with an unexpected voice: “I came to bring fire to the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled! I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and what stress I am under until it is completed!” The fire is the love of God that Jesus came to set alight, and the baptism is his death. Even at Bethany, the raising of Lazarus will lead directly to the chief priests' decision to put Jesus to death (John 11:53). Love of this kind is costly, and it divides households between those who accept it and those who refuse it.

We are in Kaitha, the season of harvest, and Martha is a saint of the harvest. The work of the harvest is also the work of serving: of feeding the workers, washing the pots, welcoming the guest, and keeping the household going. The Gospel does not tell us that this work is a lesser thing; it says that it must be done with the heart of Mary, sitting at the feet of the Lord. In the Holy Qurbana we do both: we sit and listen to the word, and then we rise and serve at the table of the poor. Let us ask Saint Martha to teach us both how to run and meet the Lord, and how to sit and listen; and let us answer in our own lives the question that Jesus asked her: “Do you believe this?”
outline: Opening
The house at Bethany where Jesus loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus.
Point 1 · Martha's faith
Grief and trust on the road; “I am the resurrection and the life”; a confession by a woman.
Point 2 · Love that serves
First John: God loved us first; hospitality as welcoming Christ; Martha served.
Point 3 · Draw near, and keep the fire
James: submit, draw near, humble yourselves; Luke: the fire Jesus came to kindle.
Take-home line
“I am the resurrection and the life… Do you believe this?”
live: Welcome someone (Hebrews 13:2)
Invite a neighbour, a newcomer or someone who is lonely to share a meal or a cup of tea this week.
Sit before you serve (Luke 10:39)
Before the busiest part of your day, take five minutes to sit in silence before the Lord, then go to your work.
Answer his question (John 11:26)
Say aloud in prayer, “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God,” and name one grief you place in his hands.
Do not judge (James 4:11)
Think of the person whose work or way of life you judge most easily, and pray a blessing for them instead.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Martha was busy in a good work, serving the Lord; but Mary chose the one thing that will not be taken away. The labour of Martha will pass when hunger and thirst pass; the sweetness of Mary will remain for ever. Martha, do not be anxious: what you now give in service, you will receive in the kingdom.
St Gregory the Great (in substance)

The two sisters are the two kinds of life, the active and the contemplative, and neither is rejected. Martha is not blamed for her service but for her anxiety, and Mary is praised because she chose the better part, in which the other will end.
St Cyril of Alexandria (in substance)

When the Lord says, ‘I am the resurrection,’ he shows that he is the source of life in himself. He does not only say that the dead will rise; he is the one by whom they rise. Martha was asked to believe this, and in believing she saw the glory of God.
magis: Catechism 994
In the Gospel Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: ‘I am the Resurrection and the life.’ It is Jesus himself who on the last day will raise up those who have believed in him.
Catechism 1822
Charity is the theological virtue by which we love God above all things for his own sake, and our neighbour as ourselves for the love of God.
Catechism 2447
The works of mercy are charitable actions by which we come to the aid of our neighbour in his bodily and spiritual necessities; they include welcoming the stranger and feeding the hungry.
saints: Fourth Thursday of Kaitha. Saint Martha of Bethany, friend of Jesus. In the Latin calendar, the memorial of Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus.

25–31 July: the fourth week of the Season of Kaitha. Sun 25: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha (St James the Apostle gives way to the Sunday; World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly). Mon 26: Sts Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Wed 28: St Alphonsa, the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised, an important feast. Thu 29: St Martha. Fri 30: Fourth Friday of Kaitha. Sat 31: St Ignatius of Loyola. In the Latin calendar the same days keep Sts Joachim and Anne (26), St Alphonsa (28, a memorial in India), Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus (29) and St Ignatius (31). Looking ahead: the month of August and the later weeks of Kaitha.
2027-07-29.prayer: Lord Jesus, you loved Martha and her sister and her brother, and you were at home in their house. You are the resurrection and the life; teach us to answer, as Martha did, ‘Yes, Lord, I believe.’ Give us hearts that run to meet you, hands that serve in love, and ears that listen at your feet. Heal our worry and our distraction; keep us from judging one another. Light in our hearts the fire of your love, and let our homes in Kerala be houses of welcome where you are loved in every guest. Through the prayers of Saint Martha, comfort all who grieve, and raise us with all your friends to the life that does not end. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord comes to a house like Bethany's. The same Jesus who stood on the road before Martha says to us, “I am the resurrection and the life,” and gives himself as bread. We sit to listen and rise to serve; the table of the altar sends us to the table of the guest and the poor.

2027-07-30.title: Fourth Friday of Kaitha
2027-07-30.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The lowly boast in being raised up; the rich will fade like the flower
2027-07-30.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, summer), which began on 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when she remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her with their blood and waits in readiness for the Lord's coming. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation”; “The most important commandments”. The Fridays of Kaitha are kept in memory of the martyrs and saints of the Church (verify locally for today). In the Latin calendar, today is the optional memorial of St Peter Chrysologus, bishop and Doctor of the Church; the Mass readings are Leviticus 23:1, 4–11, 15–16, 27, 34b–37 and Matthew 13:54–58.
2027-07-30.verse: He said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the greatest and first commandment. And a second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
theo: On the Friday that closes the fourth week of Kaitha, the Church gives us the shortest reading of the week and one of the most demanding. James writes only three verses, and in them turns the world's scale upside down: “Let the believer who is lowly boast in being raised up, and the rich in being brought low, because the rich will disappear like a flower in the field.” The lowly believer, the one whom the world overlooks, is told to boast, because in Christ he has been raised to the dignity of a child of God. The rich believer is told to boast too, but in being brought low, in the humility of seeing that wealth does not last. James is not praising poverty or condemning money; he is changing the place where we stand to measure our worth. Elsewhere he asks: “Has not God chosen the poor in the world to be rich in faith and to be heirs of the kingdom that he has promised to those who love him?”

The picture he uses is one that every Malayali knows from July: “For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the field; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. It is the same way with the rich; in the midst of a busy life, they will wither away.” After weeks of rain the grass is thick and green, and the flowers are everywhere; then a few days of hot sun in a break of the monsoon, and the tender growth dries and turns brown. So it is with human strength and success. Isaiah says it in the same way: “All people are grass, their constancy is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, when the breath of the Lord blows upon it.” The point is not despair, but relief: what fades should not be the foundation of a life. Jesus puts it simply: “Take care! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; for one's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.”

The Gospel gives the foundation that does not fade. Pharisees gather after Jesus has silenced the Sadducees, and one of them, a lawyer, asks him a question to test him: “Teacher, which commandment in the law is the greatest?” Jesus answers from the Scriptures that every devout Jew knew by heart. The first words come from the Shema, the prayer of Israel: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord is our God, the Lord alone. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.” The second comes from Leviticus: “you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Jesus is not setting aside the law of Israel; he is showing its centre. This answer belongs to the heart of Jewish faith and is shared with the Church, and it should make us look with respect at the people to whom we owe it.

“On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.” A door hangs on its hinges, and a garment hangs on its peg; the whole of Scripture hangs on love. The two commandments are one love: the second is “like” the first, and the First Letter of John joins them with an edge: “Those who say, ‘I love God,’ and hate their brothers or sisters, are liars; for those who do not love a brother or sister whom they have seen, cannot love God whom they have not seen.” Paul adds: “Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore, love is the fulfilling of the law.” The rich and the lowly of James's letter are both neighbours to each other, and the love of neighbour is what makes the rich man's fading wealth useful: shared, it becomes a treasure in heaven. Alphonsa, Martha and Joachim and Anne, whom we have remembered this week, each lived these two commandments in their own way.

As Kaitha continues, we are at the heart of the monsoon, and the great rivers are rising. A river does not ask whose compound it is; the water goes where it goes and shows that no human house is the foundation of anything. The only foundation that does not wash away is the love of God and neighbour. The prayer of the Holy Qurbana puts us in this love: we stand before God with the whole heart, and then we turn to give the sign of peace to our neighbour. Let us ask that, on the day when the flower fades and the grass dries, the Lord may find in us what he asked of the lawyer: the love that is the fulfilling of the law.
outline: Opening
Three verses that turn the scale upside down: the lowly raised, the rich brought low.
Point 1 · Boast in the right place
The lowly boast in their dignity; the rich in their humility; wealth fades like the flower of the field.
Point 2 · The foundation that does not fade
The lawyer's question; the Shema and Leviticus; the whole of Scripture hangs on love.
Point 3 · One love, two commandments
Love of God cannot be separated from love of neighbour; shared wealth becomes lasting.
Take-home line
“You shall love the Lord your God… and your neighbor as yourself.”
live: Boast rightly (James 1:9)
If you feel small, remember your dignity as a child of God; if you feel secure, remember how little of it you will keep. Say a short prayer for each state.
Loosen your grip (Luke 12:15)
Choose one possession or sum that you can share with a person in need this week, and give it.
Say the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–5)
Each morning this week, say: “Lord, you alone are God; I love you with my whole heart,” then name one neighbour whom you will love in a concrete way that day.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Love, and do what you will. If you keep silent, keep silent out of love; if you speak, speak out of love; if you correct, correct out of love; if you spare, spare out of love. Let the root of love be within you, and nothing but good can grow from it.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Why do you take pride in riches, which pass like the flowers of spring? The rich man shines for a short time and then withers; but the one who loves the poor stores up what does not wither. Make your wealth a bridge to heaven by giving it to Christ in the poor.
St Basil the Great (in substance)
God gave us two commandments in one: whoever loves God will love his neighbour, because God has commanded it. Whoever loves his neighbour also loves God, to whom the love is offered.
magis: Catechism 2055

When someone asks Jesus which commandment in the Law is the greatest, he replies: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind; the second is like it: you shall love your neighbour as yourself.
Catechism 2196
In response to the question about the first of the commandments, Jesus says: the love of God and the love of neighbour are inseparable; on these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.
Catechism 2443
God blesses those who come to the aid of the poor and rebukes those who turn away from them; love for the poor is incompatible with immoderate love of riches or their selfish use.
saints: Fourth Friday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar, the optional memorial of St Peter Chrysologus, bishop and Doctor of the Church (about 380–450), known for his short and loving sermons.

25–31 July: the fourth week of the Season of Kaitha. Sun 25: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha (St James the Apostle gives way to the Sunday; World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly). Mon 26: Sts Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Wed 28: St Alphonsa, the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised, an important feast. Thu 29: St Martha. Fri 30: Fourth Friday of Kaitha. Sat 31: St Ignatius of Loyola. In the Latin calendar the same days keep Sts Joachim and Anne (26), St Alphonsa (28, a memorial in India), Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus (29) and St Ignatius (31). Looking ahead: the month of August and the later weeks of Kaitha.
2027-07-30.prayer: Lord God, you alone are God, and you ask us to love you with our whole heart and our neighbour as ourselves. Teach us to measure our lives by your love and not by what fades. Raise up those who are lowly and teach the rich to be humble, so that all may boast in you. When the sun scorches and the flower falls, let us stand on the one foundation that does not wash away. Make our homes and our parishes places where the love of God and neighbour is one love. Through the prayers of your martyrs and saints, whom we remember in these days of Kaitha, keep us in your love. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the two commandments become one action. With our whole heart we offer ourselves to God, and then we turn to our neighbour with the sign of peace. The Bread of life is the love of God made flesh, and whoever receives it is sent to love in the same way.

2027-07-31.title: Fourth Saturday of Kaitha · Saint Ignatius of Loyola
2027-07-31.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Those who refused to love the truth
Do everything for the glory of God
A disciple must give up everything
2027-07-31.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, summer), which began on 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when she remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her with their blood and waits in readiness for the Lord's coming. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar gives the weekday readings of the Fourth Saturday of Kaitha and the readings of the commemoration of Saint Ignatius of Loyola; both sets are shown here (verify locally which are read). The calendar's own headings: “Those who have delighted in wickedness will be condemned”; “Woe on unrepentant people”; “Everything for the glory of God”; “A disciple of Jesus must give up everything”. The Latin Church keeps today the memorial of St Ignatius of Loyola, priest.
2027-07-31.verse: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.
theo: On the last day of July the Church remembers a soldier who became a saint. Ignatius was born in 1491 in the castle of Loyola in the Basque country of Spain, the youngest of a large family, and was brought up to be a knight, with dreams of fame and glory. In 1521, at the siege of Pamplona, a cannonball broke his leg. During the long months of recovery he asked for novels of chivalry, but the house had only a Life of Christ and a book on the lives of the saints. He read them, and he noticed that when he thought about the saints, he was left joyful and peaceful, whereas his dreams of worldly glory left him dry. That was the beginning of a conversion. He laid down his sword before the altar of Our Lady at Montserrat, lived in prayer in a cave at Manresa, and wrote the notes which became the Spiritual Exercises. As a student in Paris he gathered companions, among them Francis Xavier and Peter Faber, and in 1540 the Pope approved their Society of Jesus. He died in Rome on 31 July 1556 and was canonised in 1622. His motto has gone round the world: Ad maiorem Dei gloriam, “for the greater glory of God.”

That motto comes from today's reading from Paul: “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God. Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, so that they may be saved. Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.” Everything: eating and drinking, work and rest, prayer and the market. Ignatius taught that God can be found in all things and that every action can be offered to him; he built a whole spirituality out of the morning offering of the day. One of his companions, Francis Xavier, came to India in 1542, working first at Goa and then among the fishing communities of the coast of southern India and Travancore; Jesuit schools and colleges have since served many families in Kerala. The Holy Qurbana in our Church shows the same principle in another form: the bread and the wine, ordinary things of the table, are lifted up so that God may be glorified in them.

The Gospel is one of the strongest of Luke. Large crowds travel with Jesus, and he turns and says what no recruiting officer would say. “Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple.” In the language of Jesus, “hate” means to put in second place: Matthew has it plainly, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.” The family is not despised; but Christ must come first. Then two small parables: a man who wants to build a tower sits down first and counts the cost, and a king going out to war considers whether he has ten thousand men to meet twenty thousand. “So therefore, none of you can become my disciple if you do not give up all your possessions.” Ignatius did precisely that. When he put his sword on the altar of Montserrat, and when he left his family's wealth and a possible career at court, he was not despising the world; he was counting the cost and choosing the better kingdom. His prayer, which is known in many languages as the Suscipe, runs in substance: Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding and my entire will; all that I have and possess you have given me, and to you I give it back; give me only your love and your grace, and I am rich enough.

The weekday readings are quieter and harder. In the Gospel, Jesus and the disciples pass the fig tree in the morning and find it “withered away to its roots.” Peter remembers and says, “Rabbi, look!” Jesus answers, not with an explanation but with a call: “Have faith in God.” And he adds the sentence about the mountain: “if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and if you do not doubt in your heart, but believe that what you say will come to pass, it will be done for you. So I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.” The Church has always understood this as a promise that faith and prayer, joined to the will of God, can move what looks immovable. A lame ex-soldier with a handful of friends started a movement that now serves in nearly every country; that is a mountain moved. In Kaitha, the harvest season, we pray in faith for the harvest of the Lord.

Paul's words to the Thessalonians have a darker edge, and they must be read with care. He speaks of “the mystery of lawlessness” that is already at work, of a power of lies, signs and wonders that deceives “those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.” The apostle does not give a timetable; he gives a warning that deception is real, and that the defence against it is the love of truth. A little further on he gives thanks that God chose the Thessalonians “as the first fruits for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and through belief in the truth.” Ignatius made this into the art of discernment: not every light, not every wonder and not every fervour comes from God, and we must test the spirits and hold to what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). A believer in the world of the mobile phone and the news feed, where false things are quickly spread, needs this love of the truth as much as any Thessalonian. Tomorrow we begin August; let us offer to God the whole of the month, and say with Ignatius: for the greater glory of God.
outline: Opening
A knight with a broken leg, two books, and a conversion: Ignatius of Loyola.
Point 1 · Everything for the glory of God
Paul's rule and Ignatius's motto; finding God in all things; Francis Xavier in India.
Point 2 · Count the cost
Luke 14: put Christ first; tower and king; give up all; the Suscipe.
Point 3 · Have faith, and love the truth
Mark 11: faith and prayer move mountains; 2 Thessalonians: love the truth and test the spirits.
Take-home line
“Whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.”
live: Offer the day (1 Corinthians 10:31)
Each morning this week say a short offering: “Lord, all that I do today, for your glory.” Add one concrete task you will do with special care.
Count the cost (Luke 14:28)
Think of one decision you have been postponing for the sake of Christ, and write down what it would cost and what it would gain.
Test the spirits (1 Thessalonians 5:21)
Before sharing a message or a news item on your phone, ask: is it true, is it kind, does it serve the truth?
Ask in faith (Mark 11:24)
Pray daily this week for one specific good intention, with trust that God hears.
fathers: St Ignatius of Loyola (in substance)

Man is created to praise, reverence and serve God our Lord, and by this means to save his soul. All other things on the face of the earth are created for man, to help him in the pursuit of the end for which he is created.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
