For those who feel overlooked or unwanted by their own people.
For ourselves, that we may rejoice with those who rejoice.
pm.close: God of peace, sow in us the seed of righteousness, and let the harvest of peace grow in our homes and parishes, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Paul: Christ died for all, so we live no longer for ourselves; in Christ there is a new creation; God reconciled the world to himself and made us ambassadors of reconciliation.
Mark: Jesus calls Simon and Andrew, James and John, fishermen, and they leave their nets and follow him immediately.
Together: reconciliation and mission start with God's call; we answer by leaving something behind and going to others.
2027-07-21.action: Make the first move toward someone with whom you are at odds, and leave one net behind.
2027-07-21.question: Whom do I need to reconcile with, and what net am I still holding?

family.explain: Jesus saw fishermen mending their nets by the lake and said: follow me! And they did, right away. Saint Paul says that those who belong to Christ are like new people, and that God has made us his messengers of peace. An ambassador is a messenger who speaks for the king. We can be God's messengers when we say sorry first, when we forgive, and when we help friends make up after a fight.
family.intention: We thank God who forgives us, and we pray for all who are quarrelling in our families and villages.
family.ask: Ask: “Who can we be messengers of peace to this week?”

illus: An illustration

Two brothers who shared a fishing boat at Vypin (a story told to illustrate the reading) had not spoken to each other for six years, since a quarrel about the engine. One Wednesday the elder went to confession before dawn. The priest said only, ‘Before you offer anything at the altar, go and be reconciled.’ He walked to the shore, where his brother sat mending a net. He did not speak; he picked up the other end of the net and began to mend. After a long silence the younger one said, ‘It always tears in the same place.’ The elder answered, ‘Then we will mend it together.’ They went out in the same boat that evening.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you called fishermen and made them messengers of reconciliation. Call us now, and make us listen and follow. Amen.
share: The love of Christ urges us on (2 Corinthians 5:14). What does the love of Christ ask of me today?
In Christ there is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). What old thing in me needs to pass away?
We are ambassadors for Christ (2 Corinthians 5:20). In what place am I called to speak for his peace?
They left their nets and followed him (Mark 1:18). What is my net, and how can I loosen my hold on it?
pm.resp: Lord, make us new in you.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a sign and instrument of reconciliation in the world.
For priests who hear confessions, that they may be ministers of God's mercy.
For fishing families and all who work on the sea, that they may be safe and their work fruitful.
For families, parishes and nations divided by quarrels, that God's appeal may be heard.
For ourselves, that we may answer the call of Christ without delay.
pm.close: Father, in Christ you make all things new. Reconcile us to yourself and to one another, and send us out as your ambassadors, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Mary Magdalene was healed by the Lord, served him, stood near the cross with his mother, and came to the tomb in the dark; the risen Lord called her by name and sent her to the apostles.
Paul: nothing in creation can separate us from the love of Christ; James: pray in suffering, praise in joy, confess and be healed; Matthew: the Twelve are sent to proclaim and to bring peace.
Together: love that stays, a name that is called, and a mission to tell.
2027-07-22.action: Go to someone who is suffering and stay near them, then tell one person that you have seen the Lord at work.
2027-07-22.question: Where is the Lord calling me by name, and whom must I tell?
kidsaint: Saint Mary Magdalene

Mary Magdalene was a friend and follower of Jesus. Jesus had made her well, and she loved him very much. When Jesus died she stayed near the cross. On Easter morning, while it was still dark, she went to the tomb and cried because she could not find Jesus. Then someone said her name: “Mary!” It was Jesus, alive! He asked her to go and tell his friends, and she ran to tell them: “I have seen the Lord!” Lesson: Jesus calls each of us by name. Stay near him, and tell others the good news!
term: Apostle of the apostles

A title given to Saint Mary Magdalene since the early centuries and by Saint Thomas Aquinas, because the risen Lord sent her to announce the Resurrection to the apostles. The word apostle means one who is sent. In 2016 the Church raised her memorial to a feast.

family.explain: Mary was crying outside the empty tomb because she could not find Jesus. Then Jesus said just one word: “Mary!” and she knew his voice at once. He told her to go to his friends and tell them the good news, and she ran and said: “I have seen the Lord!” God knows each of us by name, and he sends us to tell good news too.
family.intention: We thank God for calling us by name at baptism, and we pray for all who are sad or lonely today.
family.ask: Ask: “What good news can we tell someone in our village or school this week?”

illus: An illustration

In a parish near Pala (a story told to illustrate the reading) a widow named Annamma came every day before dawn to sweep the church courtyard and light the lamp, long before the first bell. When asked why she came in the dark, she said, ‘On the first Easter someone came while it was still dark. I want to be there when he calls my name.’ On Easter morning the children found her kneeling with the lamp at the open door, and the old priest began the Easter greeting by naming her first: ‘Annamma, the Lord is risen.’ She answered, as the parish does, ‘He is risen indeed,’ and went to tell the whole village.

pm.open: Risen Lord, you called Mary by name in the garden. Call us by name too, and let us hear your voice as we gather. Amen.
share: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? (Romans 8:35). What do I fear might separate me from him?
Mary stood weeping outside the tomb (John 20:11). Where do I stand and weep, and what am I looking for?
Jesus said to her, “Mary!” (John 20:16). How does the Lord call me by name?
Go to my brothers and say to them (John 20:17). To whom does the Lord send me, and what shall I say?
pm.resp: Lord, we have seen you; send us.
interc: For the Church, that she may always proclaim the Resurrection with the courage of Saint Mary Magdalene.
For women who serve the Church in quiet ways, that their witness may be valued and their gifts used.
For those who weep because they cannot find the Lord, that he may call them by name.
For the sick and those who are anointed in this season of rains and fevers, that the prayer of faith may heal them.
For ourselves, that we may stay near the Lord in the dark and tell others what we have seen.
pm.close: Father, you raised your Son and sent Mary Magdalene to tell his brothers. Make us faithful witnesses of the Resurrection, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Paul: he kneels before the Father and prays that Christ may dwell in our hearts, that we may be rooted in love and know the breadth, length, height and depth of Christ's love.
Mark: friends bring a blind man to Jesus; he heals him in two stages, and the man first sees people like trees walking, then everything clearly.
Together: the heart is the place where Christ dwells, and our sight of him grows step by step.
2027-07-23.action: Kneel for your family this week, and bring one person who is spiritually blind to Jesus.
2027-07-23.question: Where do I see only dimly, and where do I ask the Lord to touch me again?

family.explain: Some friends brought a blind man to Jesus. Jesus took him by the hand and led him out of the village. He touched his eyes, and the man could see, but not clearly: people looked like trees walking! So Jesus touched his eyes again, and then he saw everything clearly. Jesus is very patient with us. Saint Paul prays that Jesus may live in our hearts and that we may be rooted in love, like a strong tree beside a river.
family.intention: We thank God for our family and for every person who has helped us to see the way, and we pray for all who cannot see.
family.ask: Ask: “Who is a friend we could take to Jesus by our prayers?”

illus: An illustration

A grandmother in Idukki (a story told to illustrate the reading) had her cataract operated on. The next morning the doctor lifted the bandage, and she said, ‘I see shapes, like trees walking.’ The doctor smiled and said, ‘Come back after a week.’ A week later she looked at her granddaughter's face and cried. ‘I thought I had seen you all these years,’ she said, ‘but now I see you.’ The old woman told the parish women afterwards, ‘The doctor did not scold me for seeing so little. Our Lord is like that. He touches again and again until we see.’

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you take us by the hand and touch us again. Come and dwell in our hearts through faith, and open our eyes to the depth of your love. Amen.
share: I bow my knees before the Father (Ephesians 3:14). Whom do I bring before the Father on my knees?
Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith (Ephesians 3:17). What would it mean today to let him live in my heart and not just visit?
The breadth and length and height and depth (Ephesians 3:18). Where do I need to understand more the love of Christ, especially in the Cross?
I can see people, but they look like trees, walking (Mark 8:24). Where do I see only dimly, and what do I ask the Lord to touch again?
pm.resp: Lord, root us in your love.
interc: For the Church, that she may know and show the breadth and depth of the love of Christ.
For families, that every family may be strengthened in the Spirit and rooted in love.
For all who are blind or whose sight is failing, and for those who care for them.
For those who see their faith only dimly, that the Lord may touch them again.
For ourselves, that Christ may dwell in our hearts through faith.
pm.close: Father, you are able to do more than we can ask or imagine. Strengthen us in your Spirit, let Christ dwell in our hearts, and bring us to the day when we see you face to face. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: James: our life is a mist; say “If the Lord wishes”; boasting is evil; to know the good and not do it is sin.

Luke: John tries to stop someone who is not of their group, and Jesus says whoever is not against you is for you; Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem and rebukes his disciples who want to call down fire.
Together: humility in our plans, breadth in our hearts, gentleness toward those who refuse us.
2027-07-24.action: Offer one plan this week to God with the words “If the Lord wishes”, and do one good thing you have been putting off.
2027-07-24.question: What good do I know and still not do, and whom do I try to stop because he is not one of us?

family.explain: In the morning the mist on the hills is thick, but when the sun comes up it vanishes. Saint James says that our life is like that, and so we should say, “If God wishes”, when we plan something. Then Jesus' friend John saw a man doing good in Jesus' name and told him to stop, because he was not in their group. Jesus said: do not stop him! Whoever is not against us is for us. God is happy when anybody does good.
family.intention: We thank God for all the good people we know, even if they do not belong to our group, and we pray for those who are in trouble.
family.ask: Ask: “Whom can we thank for doing good in our village, and how?”

illus: An illustration

In a town parish (a story told to illustrate the reading) some members of the choir complained that a group of young people from another parish were teaching the Our Father and a few songs to street children near the bus stand. ‘They are not ours,’ they said. The old vicar went and sat on the bench to listen. The children were saying the Our Father, the same prayer the parish teaches in its own catechism class. He came back and said, ‘Whoever is not against us is for us.’ In the next rains, when the bus stand was flooded, he lent the young people the parish hall for the classes, and the choir members brought tea.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you set your face toward Jerusalem and you did not call down fire. Make our plans humble and our hearts wide. Amen.
share: You are a mist that appears for a little while (James 4:14). How do I live as one who is only passing through?
If the Lord wishes (James 4:15). What plan do I need to offer to him today?
Anyone who knows the right thing to do and fails to do it commits sin (James 4:17). What good do I know, and not do?
Do not stop him; for whoever is not against you is for you (Luke 9:50). Whom do I try to stop because he is not one of us?
pm.resp: Lord, make our hearts wide and our plans humble.
interc: For the Church, that she may rejoice in every good done in the name of Christ.
For those who plan our towns and villages, that they may plan with humility and care for the poor.
For all who are tempted to answer refusal with anger, that they may follow the gentleness of the Lamb.
For those who think they have many tomorrows, that they may do the good that they can do today.
For ourselves, that we may say “If the Lord wishes” and mean it.
pm.close: Father, our days are in your hands. Teach us to count them wisely, and to follow your Son who set his face toward Jerusalem. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Hannah's song: the Lord raises the poor from the dust and turns the shame of the barren into joy; Mary will sing it again.
Isaiah and Hebrews: enlarge your tent; Abraham and Sarah, too old to have a child, trusted the one who promised.
Matthew: the genealogy of Jesus, a family chain; by tradition Joachim and Anne stand in it as Mary's parents.
Weekday: James warns the rich; Jesus says what is impossible for mortals is possible for God.
2027-07-26.action: Thank God for your grandparents by name tonight, and call or visit an elderly person this week.
2027-07-26.question: What faith did I receive from my grandparents, and what will I hand on to the next generation?
kidsaint: Sts Joachim and Anne

Joachim and Anne were the mother and father of Mary, so they were the grandparents of Jesus. We do not know much about them, but the old stories say they loved God and prayed for a child for a long time. God heard their prayer and gave them Mary. Lesson: our grandparents are God's gifts; let us love them, listen to their stories and ask them to pray for us.
term: Protoevangelium of James

An early Christian writing of the second century, not part of the Bible, that tells of the birth of Mary and names her parents Joachim and Anne. The Church does not teach it as Scripture, but it has long treasured the names and the feasts that grew from it.

family.explain: Hannah was a woman who wished for a child for many years, and she prayed and prayed. God gave her a son, Samuel, and she sang a song of thanks. Later Joachim and Anne, the parents of Mary, prayed in the same way, so the old stories say. God gives gifts to those who trust him. Jesus also had a family: a mother, a foster father, and grandparents. Let us thank God for ours.
family.intention: We pray for our grandparents, those who live with us and those in heaven.
family.ask: Ask: “Which story of a grandparent does our family like to tell? Let us tell it tonight.”

illus: An illustration

In a village near Kottayam (a story told to illustrate the reading) the power failed every evening during the monsoon, and a grandmother, Annamma, gathered the children round the oil lamp. With no television to watch, they said the rosary, and then she told them one story: how she had waited eleven years for a child, praying in a small chapel, and how her son was born on the feast of St Anne. The children grew up, went to Gulf cities and to Europe, and many forgot the stories of other nights. But on the evening of her funeral, a grandson, now a grown man, found himself saying the Hail Mary in the very rhythm of that lamplit room, and wept, because he understood that the faith in his house had a grandmother's name.

pm.open: Lord of all generations, you gave Joachim and Anne to the Virgin Mary as parents and teachers. Gather us now; open our ears to the faith of our grandparents. Amen.
share: My heart exults in the Lord (1 Samuel 2:1). What do I thank God for in a quiet, hidden way?
Enlarge the site of your tent (Isaiah 54:2). Whom can I make room for in my home or heart?
By faith Abraham obeyed (Hebrews 11:8). Whom has God asked me to trust without seeing the way?
Your riches have rotted (James 5:2). What do I keep that should be given?
pm.resp: Lord, what is impossible for us is possible for you.
interc: For grandparents and the elderly, that they may be honoured and cared for, and may see their children's children in the faith.
For couples who long for a child, that God may hear their prayer.
For the Church, that she may hand on the faith from one generation to the next.
For the rich, that they may share, and for workers whose wages are withheld, that justice may be done.
For our departed grandparents, that they may rest in the peace of Christ.
pm.close: Father, you made Joachim and Anne the parents of the Mother of your Son. Hear our prayer through their intercession and bless every home with faith and love. Amen.

quick: James: be patient like the farmer who waits for the early and late rains; strengthen your hearts; do not grumble; keep your word.
Examples of endurance: the prophets and Job; the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
Mark: the Son of Man will come in glory and gather his elect from the ends of the earth; learn from the fig tree; his words will not pass away.
2027-07-27.action: Pick one thing you are waiting for, and wait for it this week without complaining, and with a prayer.
2027-07-27.question: Do I wait for the Lord like a farmer who is working and trusting, or like someone who has stopped expecting him?

family.explain: A farmer plants his seeds and then must wait for the rain. He cannot make it come, but he trusts that it will, and he keeps working while he waits. Jesus told us to learn from a fig tree: when its leaves come, we know that summer is near. We know that Jesus will come again, and we do not know when. So we wait with patience, we are kind to each other, we do not grumble, and we say, “Come, Lord Jesus.”
family.intention: We pray that we may be patient and kind while we wait.
family.ask: Ask: “What is the hardest thing for us to wait for? How can we wait in a good way?”

illus: An illustration

A paddy farmer in Kuttanad (a story told to illustrate the reading), whom we may call Chacko, lost one whole crop to a breached bund. The next year, before the rains, he did not sit idle: he mended the bund with his sons and kept the seed dry in the old kitchen. The monsoon was late that year, and his neighbours began to say it would not come. He told his wife, ‘You do not sow only when it rains. You get ready, and the rain finds you ready.’ When the rains finally came, his field was the first to be sown. In the evening prayers that year the family added a line: ‘Lord, find us ready.’

pm.open: Lord Jesus, the Son of Man who will come in glory, gather us now in patience and hope; strengthen our hearts as we wait for you. Amen.
share: Be patient, therefore, beloved, until the coming of the Lord (James 5:7). Where am I impatient with God, with others, with myself?
Do not grumble against one another (James 5:9). Whom do I complain about most?
Let your ‘Yes’ be yes and your ‘No’ be no (James 5:12). Is my word reliable?
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Mark 13:31). What of mine will last?
pm.resp: Come, Lord Jesus; strengthen our hearts.
interc: For the Church, that she may wait for the Lord with a faithful and joyful heart.
For farmers, fishermen and all who wait for the rain, the harvest or the catch, that they may be provided for and not lose hope.
For those who suffer long illness or unemployment, that they may be patient and receive help.
For those who have been unfaithful to their word, that they may keep their promises.
For the dead, that they may be gathered with all the elect at the coming of the Lord.
pm.close: Father, you have sent your Son and promised that he will come again. Make us ready and hopeful, and keep us until that day. Amen.

quick: Deuteronomy: God's holy people, called by his name, are a sign to the nations; he opens the heavens to give rain in its season.
Isaiah: the Servant, crushed by the will of the Lord, offers his life for sin and makes many righteous.
Paul: “I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.”
John: the Greeks wish to see Jesus; he speaks of the grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit.
Weekday: Christ crucified in weakness lives by God's power; the harvest is plentiful and the laborers are few.
2027-07-28.action: Offer one small pain or inconvenience today for a person you name, and do one hidden act of service.
2027-07-28.question: Is there a place where God is asking me to fall like a grain into the earth so that others may have life?
catechism: The call of all to holiness.
kidsaint: St Alphonsa

Alphonsa was a girl from Kerala who lost her mother when she was a baby. She loved Jesus very much and wished to become a sister. She was often sick, but she smiled and offered it all to Jesus. She lived in the convent at Bharananganam and died when she was only thirty-five. Now she is a saint, and many people go to pray at her tomb. Lesson: when something hurts, you can give it to Jesus as a present, and do small things with love.
2027-07-28.special: Saint Alphonsa, the first woman of Indian origin to be declared a saint. Her tomb is at Bharananganam.
term: Offering up suffering

The Christian practice of uniting one's pains and troubles to the sacrifice of Christ on the cross, for the good of the Church and of others. It does not mean that suffering is good in itself, but that, joined to Christ's love, it can be fruitful. Saint Paul speaks of it in Colossians 1:24.

family.read: Read together: John 12:23–26 and 1 John 4:11–12, if you wish.
family.explain: Jesus told us about a seed. If a seed stays in a bag, it stays a seed. But if it falls into the earth and seems to die, it grows into a plant that gives many seeds. Saint Alphonsa lived a hidden life and was often ill, but she gave everything to Jesus, and now many people in the world have been helped by her. When we do small things with love, even things nobody sees, they are like seeds that God makes grow.
family.intention: We pray for sick people and for those who care for them, and we ask Saint Alphonsa to pray for us.
family.ask: Ask: “What seed of love can each of us plant today? What can we offer to Jesus when something is hard?”

illus: An illustration

A schoolteacher from the Pala area (a story told to illustrate the reading), who had suffered from a painful illness for many years, went each year on 28 July to the tomb at Bharananganam. In the early years she prayed to be healed. As the years passed she prayed more simply: ‘Alphonsamma, teach me to carry it.’ She was never healed, but her colleagues noticed that the more her body failed the gentler she became with the children, and her class, which had once been the noisiest in the school, became the most peaceful. At her funeral a former pupil said: ‘Miss taught us arithmetic, but what she really taught us was how to hurt without hurting others.’ The family put on her grave a small stalk of wheat carved in stone.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are the grain of wheat who died and rose. Gather us in the name of Saint Alphonsa; teach us to carry our crosses with you and to bear fruit for others. Amen.
share: I have been crucified with Christ… it is Christ who lives in me (Galatians 2:19–20). Where do I see Christ living in me?
Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies (John 12:24). What must I let go of so that it bears fruit?
I am completing what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions (Colossians 1:24). What suffering can I offer for someone else?
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few (Matthew 9:37). What part of the harvest is mine?
pm.resp: Lord of the harvest, send laborers into your harvest.
interc: For the Church in India, that the example of Saint Alphonsa may lead many to holiness through hidden love.
For the sick, the disabled and those in long pain, that they may find strength and be united to the cross of Christ.
For hospital workers, nurses, doctors and caregivers, that they may serve with compassion.
For the Clarist sisters of Bharananganam and all religious sisters of our land, and for new vocations.
For those who suffer without being noticed, that they may know they are loved.
pm.close: Father, you glorified Saint Alphonsa in the Church of our land. Through her prayers help us to carry our crosses with love, and bring us to the joy of your kingdom. Amen.

quick: Martha of Bethany welcomed Jesus, served him, and in her grief confessed him as the Messiah, the Son of God.
Jesus: “I am the resurrection and the life… Do you believe this?”
First John: God loved us first; whoever loves abides in God.
Weekday: draw near to God; humble yourselves; do not judge; Jesus has come to kindle fire on the earth.
2027-07-29.action: Welcome one person into your home or your day this week as you would welcome the Lord.
2027-07-29.question: When Jesus asks me, “Do you believe this?”, what is my answer in the middle of my own grief?
kidsaint: St Martha

Martha lived in a village called Bethany with her sister Mary and her brother Lazarus. Jesus often visited their home, and Martha cooked and served for him. When Lazarus died, Martha ran to meet Jesus and said, ‘I believe that you are the Son of God.’ Then Jesus raised Lazarus to life. Lesson: welcome guests with joy, serve with love, and always say to Jesus, ‘I believe.’
term: Bethany

A village about two miles east of Jerusalem, on the slope of the Mount of Olives. It was the home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus, and Jesus often stayed there. It is also where he raised Lazarus from the dead. The village is called al-Eizariya today, after Lazarus.

family.explain: Martha and her sister Mary lived in a village called Bethany. Jesus was their friend and visited their home. Martha worked hard to make a meal for him. Mary sat quietly to listen to Jesus. Jesus loved them both. He told Martha, ‘Do not be worried about so many things. Listen to me, too.’ Later Martha's brother Lazarus died, and Martha told Jesus, ‘I believe that you are the Son of God.’ Jesus brought Lazarus back to life! We can work for Jesus, and we can sit with him in prayer.
family.intention: We pray for our family's guests, and for all who have lost someone they love.
family.ask: Ask: “What can we cook or give for someone in need this week? When can we also sit quietly with Jesus?”

illus: An illustration

Aleyamma (a story told to illustrate the reading) cooked every year for the parish feast: rice for four hundred, the beef and fish curries, the payasam. Everyone praised her, and she was proud of it. But she never came to the Qurbana on feast day; she was always in the kitchen, with the pots. One year the vicar came into the kitchen at the time of the Gospel and found her alone with the steam. ‘Aleyamma,’ he said gently, ‘today the Lord himself is waiting for his cook.’ She stood, wiped her hands, and went in to the back of the church. After that she planned so that the rice was on the fire before the Qurbana and the last dishes were done after it. ‘I used to cook for the Lord,’ she said later, ‘and forget to see him.’

pm.open: Lord Jesus, resurrection and life, friend of Martha and Mary and Lazarus, gather us in your name. Teach us to run to meet you and to sit and listen to you. Amen.
share: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died (John 11:21). Where do I feel that the Lord was absent?
I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25). What does this mean for me and for those I have lost?
Let us love one another, because love is from God (1 John 4:7). Whom is it hard for me to love?
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you (James 4:8). How do I draw near each day?
pm.resp: Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a house of welcome like the house at Bethany.
For those who grieve, that they may hear the Lord say, ‘I am the resurrection and the life.’
For women who serve in homes, kitchens, hospitals and parishes, that their work may be honoured.
For those who are anxious and worried, that they may find the one thing necessary.
For our departed, that they may rise with Christ on the last day.
pm.close: Father, you gave your Son to be the resurrection and the life. Strengthen our faith, as you strengthened Martha's, and bring us to the table of your kingdom. Amen.

quick: James: the lowly may boast in being raised up; the rich must be brought low, for they will fade like the flower of the field.
Matthew: the lawyer's question; Jesus answers with the love of God and the love of neighbour, on which hang the whole law and the prophets.
Both: only love lasts; wealth and success fade like grass.
2027-07-30.action: Give something away this week that you would normally keep, and say the Shema each morning.
2027-07-30.question: What am I building my life on: something that will fade like the flower, or the love of God and neighbour?

family.explain: A man asked Jesus, ‘Teacher, which is the greatest of all God's commands?’ Jesus said, ‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart. And the second is like it: love your neighbour as yourself.’ When we love God and our neighbour, we keep everything God asks. James says that money and fine things are like a flower in the field: pretty for a while, and then gone. But love never goes away.
family.intention: We pray for people who are poor and for people who have much, that all may share and love.
family.ask: Ask: “Who is our neighbour this week? What can we share with them?”

illus: An illustration

One year in the heavy monsoon (a story told to illustrate the reading) the water rose in a village near Alappuzha. The richest man in the village had a big compound and a car, and his gate was locked, because he was afraid of thieves. When the water came up to the veranda, his car stalled in the road, and the only man who came to push it was Kunjan, the coconut-climber, whom he had underpaid for years. Standing waist-deep in the water the rich man said, ‘Kunjan, why do you help me?’ Kunjan answered, ‘Saar, the water does not ask whose house it is. Why should I?’ When the water went down, the rich man paid Kunjan all the wages he owed, and opened the gate. He told the vicar later: ‘That day I learned that my wealth could float away like a leaf.’

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you gave us the greatest commandment. Gather us now in your love; teach us to love God with all our heart and our neighbour as ourselves. Amen.
share: Let the believer who is lowly boast in being raised up (James 1:9). How do I see my dignity as a child of God?
The rich will disappear like a flower in the field (James 1:10). What do I trust more than God?
You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart (Matthew 22:37). Is God first in my day?
You shall love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:39). Whom do I find hardest to love?
pm.resp: Lord, teach us to love.
interc: For the Church, that she may be known by love of God and neighbour.
For the poor and the lowly, that they may know their dignity and be helped.
For the rich and powerful, that they may be humble and generous.
For those hit by the monsoon floods and landslides, that they may find help and shelter.
For all whom we find hard to love, that God may bless them and us.
pm.close: Father, your Son taught us that love is the fulfilment of the law. Pour your love into our hearts and keep us in it until the day when the flower fades and your kingdom comes. Amen.

quick: Paul to the Thessalonians: the mystery of lawlessness is at work; those who refuse to love the truth are deceived; God chose you through belief in the truth.
Mark: the fig tree withered; Jesus says, “Have faith in God”; believe that what you ask for in prayer will be yours.
Ignatius's readings: do everything for the glory of God; a disciple counts the cost and gives up all.
2027-07-31.action: Offer your whole day to God each morning, saying, “for your glory,” and test one message you receive before you pass it on.
2027-07-31.question: What would I do differently today if everything I did were for the glory of God?
kidsaint: St Ignatius

Ignatius was a brave soldier in Spain. A cannonball hurt his leg, and he had to stay in bed for months. He had nothing to read except a book about Jesus and a book about saints. He read them and thought, ‘I want to be a brave soldier for Jesus!’ He started the Jesuits, and his friend Francis Xavier came to India. Ignatius's motto was: for the greater glory of God. Lesson: do even small things for God, and use your mind and your heart for him.
term: AMDG (Ad maiorem Dei gloriam)

Latin for “for the greater glory of God.” It is the motto of Saint Ignatius and the Society of Jesus, and it comes from Paul's rule in 1 Corinthians 10:31: whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God. Jesuits often write the letters AMDG at the end of letters and on books and buildings.

family.explain: Saint Ignatius was a soldier who loved to dream about being famous. When he was hurt and in bed, he read about Jesus and the saints, and he decided to work for God. Paul says: whatever you do, do it for God's glory, even eating and playing and studying. Jesus says: have faith in God, and pray; he hears you. So we can offer our whole day to God each morning and ask him for what we need.
family.intention: We pray for all teachers and students in schools and colleges, and for the Jesuits who serve in India.
family.ask: Ask: “What can each of us do today just for God's glory? What shall we ask God with faith?”

illus: An illustration

A carpenter near Changanassery (a story told to illustrate the reading) cut, under every table or door that left his shop, three small letters in a hidden place: AMDG. A customer once found them and asked what they meant. ‘For the greater glory of God,’ said the carpenter. ‘A hidden mark?’ asked the customer. ‘Nobody will see it.’ ‘That is the point,’ he replied. ‘God sees it, and the joint I make where nobody will look must be as good as the one in front.’ Later, a builder asked him to put cheaper wood in the back of a cupboard to save money. The carpenter refused, and offered to work a day longer without being paid for it. ‘I could not sign it,’ he said. The cupboard still stands in a house at Kuttanad after two floods.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you call us to follow you and to do everything for your glory. Gather us now, and teach us to find you in all things. Amen.
share: Do everything for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). What in my day is hardest to offer to God?
Which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and estimate the cost? (Luke 14:28). What would following Christ more fully cost me?
Have faith in God (Mark 11:22). What do I need to ask with more faith?
Test everything; hold fast to what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). How do I test what I hear and read?
pm.resp: Lord, take and receive; for your greater glory.
interc: For the Church, that she may do all things for the glory of God.
For the Society of Jesus, for teachers and students in our schools and colleges, and for all missionaries.
For those who are deceived by lies and wonders, that they may love the truth.
For those who are struggling with a great decision, that they may count the cost and choose well.
For the month of August, that we may offer every day to God.
pm.close: Father, you gave Saint Ignatius to the Church as a servant of your glory. By his prayers, help us to offer you everything we do, and bring us to your kingdom. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today is the Dukhrana of Mar Thoma, Saint Thomas the Apostle, our father in faith. The word Dukhrana means remembrance. Today the Church remembers him, and we remember that the faith of our families and our parish comes, according to our oldest tradition, from an apostle of Jesus.

Thomas is often called the doubter, but he was much more. When Jesus went toward danger, Thomas said to the others, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16). When he did not understand, he asked: “How can we know the way?” (John 14:5). He was brave, and he was honest.

On Easter evening Thomas was not with the others. They told him, “We have seen the Lord.” He said that he could not believe unless he saw the wounds. A week later Jesus came again, through closed doors, and said, “Peace be with you.” Then Jesus turned to Thomas: “Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe” (John 20:27). Thomas did not need to touch. He said, “My Lord and my God!” This is the highest confession in the whole Gospel.

And Jesus said: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe” (John 20:29). That is us. We have not seen Jesus with our eyes. But we have seen the faith of our parents, and we have received the Body of the Lord in the Qurbana. Saint Paul says that we are built on the foundation of the apostles, with Christ as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). Thomas is one of those foundation stones for our Church in India.

The calendar also gives us the Garden of Eden and the Book of Proverbs. In Eden God puts the man in a garden “to till it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Thomas was given a garden in the east to till and keep. And Proverbs says, “Keep hold of instruction; do not let go; guard her, for she is your life” (Proverbs 4:13). Our ancestors kept hold of the faith for nearly two thousand years. What are we keeping hold of, and what are we handing on?

Today in the Saturday readings, Jesus and Saint Paul speak about marriage and peace in the home. The faith came to India in families and lives in families. Let us pray for our homes: “It is to peace that God has called you” (1 Corinthians 7:15). And let us say this week, at the elevation of the Holy Qurbana, the prayer of Thomas: “My Lord and my God.” Amen.
kids: Children, today is the feast of Saint Thomas, who came to our India with the good news of Jesus. Thomas was brave and he asked honest questions. When Jesus came back after Easter, Thomas said the most beautiful words: ‘My Lord and my God!’
You can say those words, too! When you see the priest lift the Body of Jesus at the Holy Qurbana, say in your heart: ‘My Lord and my God!’ And thank God for the people who taught you to pray.

homily: Dear friends, today is the First Sunday of Kaitha, and our Church celebrates the Feast of the Twelve Apostles. Yesterday we remembered Mar Thoma. Today we remember all the twelve friends of Jesus. “He called his disciples and chose twelve of them, whom he also named apostles” (Luke 6:13).

In the first reading the prophet Elijah builds an altar. He takes twelve stones, one for each tribe of Israel, and the people are one again before the Lord. Then the fire falls from heaven and the people say, “The Lord indeed is God” (1 Kings 18:39). The Church has always seen in those twelve stones the twelve apostles, on whom the altar of our Church is built, and in the fire the fire of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.

In the Acts the apostles are very busy and very happy. Many people are healed, and more and more believe. The authorities arrest them, but during the night an angel opens the prison and says, “Go, stand in the temple and tell the people the whole message about this life” (Acts 5:20). The Church is sent to say all of the message, not just the parts that are pleasant to hear.

Saint Paul tells the Corinthians that some say, “I belong to Paul”, and others “I belong to Apollos” or “to Cephas”. He asks, “Has Christ been divided?” (1 Corinthians 1:13). The Twelve are many, but Christ is one. Let us pray for unity in our families and parishes, and among all who are baptised in Christ.

In the Gospel Jesus is a guest at a meal and sees people choosing the best seats. He says: sit in the lowest place, “for all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). And invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind, who cannot pay you back. The apostles themselves once argued about who was the greatest, and Jesus taught them to serve. In the Kaitha season the full ears of rice bow down. Let us bow, too: let us take the last seat, serve first the one who cannot repay us, and so bring fruit that will last. Amen.
kids: Children, today we remember Jesus' twelve special friends, the apostles. Jesus asked them first to be with him, and then to go and tell everyone about God. They were ordinary people: fishermen, farmers and a tax collector.

Jesus also teaches us today: do not rush for the best seat. Take the last seat and let your friend sit first! And when you have a party, invite someone who is alone. That is how the apostles learned to love, and that is how we can too!

homily: Dear friends, today Moses asks Israel: has anything so great as this ever happened? And he gives the answer: God loved your ancestors, and he chose their children after them (Deuteronomy 4:37). Before there is any law, there is love. Before we do anything, we are loved. That is the first message of today.

The prophet Isaiah says that God will spread over his people a canopy, “a shade by day from the heat, and a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain” (Isaiah 4:6). In these July days, when the rain is heavy in Kerala and the sun is hot between the clouds, we know what a good roof means. The Church is that roof, which God himself has put over us.

Saint Paul says that we have a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit: “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). God does not want us only to obey rules. He wants to write his love on our hearts.

And the Gospel gives us the picture of that love, in the father who runs. The younger son asks for his share and goes away and loses everything. But he comes to himself and says, ‘I will go back to my father.’ And before he even finishes his speech, the father sees him far off, is filled with compassion, runs, embraces and kisses him. He gives him the best robe, a ring and sandals and holds a feast. “This son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!” (Luke 15:24).

But there is also the elder son, who is angry. He has been working faithfully, and he cannot bear the party. The father goes out to him as well: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31). We do not know if he went in. That is the question left for us.

Whether we are the younger or the elder, the Father is waiting at the gate. This week, if you have been far away, go back, and go to confession. If you have stayed, go out and welcome your brother and sister. Let the lamp be lit for those who have not yet come home. Amen.
kids: Children, in today's story a father had two sons. One went away and lost everything, but when he came back the father ran to hug him! God is like that father. If you do something wrong, do not hide. Say sorry and go to him, and he will run to meet you. And if your brother or sister is forgiven, be happy for him or her too, as the father wanted the elder son to be. Let us all come to the party!

homily: Dear friends, today the Church remembers a mother and her little son. Julitta and her three-year-old Kuriakose were arrested at Tarsus, about the year 304, at the time of Emperor Diocletian. The ancient Acts tell us that the mother confessed Christ, and the little boy said the same: “I am a Christian.”

How can a child be so brave? Jesus himself answers: “When they hand you over, do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say; for what you are to say will be given to you at that time; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you” (Matthew 10:19–20). The courage of the martyrs is the Spirit's gift.

And their courage is not so far from our own life. James says today, “Whenever you face trials of any kind, consider it nothing but joy” (James 1:2). He does not say that trials are pleasant. He says that faith tested produces endurance. If we lack wisdom, we are to ask God, who gives generously and ungrudgingly.

In the Gospel Jesus teaches us to pray with faith and to forgive: “Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone; so that your Father in heaven may also forgive you” (Mark 11:25). A grudge is a mountain that no prayer can move.

This week let us forgive one person and say one plain word of faith. “Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven” (Matthew 10:32). Saint Julitta and Saint Kuriakose, pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, Kuriakose was only three years old, but he said bravely, “I am a Christian.” When someone asks you about Jesus, you can say it too, kindly and happily. Jesus says that he knows each of us, even every hair on our head!

homily: Dear friends, today the Church opens with the Ten Commandments. But notice the first word: not “Do this”, but “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Deuteronomy 5:6). God saves first, and then he asks us to live as people he has saved.

Among the commandments, the Sabbath: a day of rest for everyone, even for those who work for us. For us Christians, Sunday is the Lord's Day, the day of the Resurrection. Let us keep it: come to the Qurbana, rest, spend time with the family. And let us honour our fathers and mothers, who gave us life.

Isaiah sings of a vineyard. The owner did everything: dug it, cleared the stones, planted choice vines, built a tower. He expected grapes, and got wild grapes (Isaiah 5:2). He asks, “What more was there to do for my vineyard that I have not done in it?” God has done everything for us. What fruit does he find in our families, our parishes, our streets? Justice, or bloodshed? Righteousness, or a cry?

Paul tells us how to bear fruit again: with a godly grief. Worldly grief is sorry for being caught. Godly grief is sorry for having hurt God and others, and it turns us back (2 Corinthians 7:10). Peter wept and was restored. We too can go to confession and begin again.

And in the Gospel Jesus opens the eyes of a man born blind. The man did what Jesus told him, and he saw. And when Jesus found him again, he said, “Lord, I believe,” and worshiped him (John 9:38). Let us ask the Lord today to open our eyes, so that we may see him and say the same. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus made a blind man see! He put mud on his eyes and told him to wash. The man did what Jesus told him, and he could see! Then he said, “Lord, I believe.” Jesus is the light of the world. Let us always do what Jesus says, and we will see how good he is.

homily: Dear friends, today the Gospel brings us to the dinner table. Some Pharisees and scribes notice that the disciples of Jesus eat without washing their hands first. For them it was a matter of tradition, and a good tradition. But Jesus uses the occasion to teach something deeper.

He quotes Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me” (Mark 7:6). It is possible to say all the prayers, to keep all the customs, and still have a heart that is far from God. And then Jesus says, “You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition” (Mark 7:8).

He gives an example. God said: “Honor your father and your mother.” But some people said, ‘What I would have given to my parents is Corban, it is dedicated to God,’ and so they gave nothing to their old parents. They looked pious, but they made void the word of God (Mark 7:10–13).

Brothers and sisters, this is very close to our life. A donation to the church is a good thing. A big feast is a good thing. But if our old father or mother sits alone in the back room, if no one has time to talk to them, then something is wrong. Today is the day we remember grandparents and the elderly. The first reading reminds us: “Honor your father and your mother… so that it may go well with you” (Deuteronomy 5:16).

Isaiah shows us what happens when people forget God and each other: “Manasseh devoured Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh” (Isaiah 9:21). Brother turns against brother. Let us ask where in our families there are such quarrels, and let us be the first to make peace.

And Saint Paul tells us how to live: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10:17). Not in our family name, our money or our good works, but in the Lord. This week, let us honour our parents, keep our hearts clean, and boast only in him. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus said: honour your father and your mother. That means your grandparents too! Some grown-ups said they were too busy because they were giving to God, and Jesus said that was wrong. This week, give your grandparents a hug, tell them a story, or draw them a picture. That is a way of loving God, too!

homily: Dear friends, in today's reading Saint Paul says something very brave: “We do not lose heart.” He was tired, criticised and misunderstood. Yet he says: God has been merciful to me, and so I will not give up.

Then he tells us how he works. “We refuse to practice cunning or to falsify God’s word; but by the open statement of the truth we commend ourselves to the conscience of everyone in the sight of God” (2 Corinthians 4:2). A good preacher, and a good parent and a good friend, has nothing to hide. And he adds: “We do not proclaim ourselves; we proclaim Jesus Christ as Lord” (2 Corinthians 4:5).

Why? Because the light is Jesus. “It is the God who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). God does not shine from a distance; he shines from a face, the face of his Son.

In the Gospel Jesus is sad and strong at the same time. Some teachers who should have opened the door of God's kingdom closed it, and played clever games with words and oaths. Jesus tells them: God hears every word. Whoever swears by the altar swears by God, and whoever swears by heaven swears by God's throne (Matthew 23:20–22). We do not need clever games. We need honest hearts.
So let us do one small thing today: keep one promise we have delayed. Let our Yes be Yes and our No be No (Matthew 5:37). Then the light of Christ's face will shine through our words. Amen.
kids: Children, Saint Paul says: Jesus is the light! Light helps us to see, and light helps others to find the way. You can carry a little of that light when you tell the truth, even when it is hard.
Jesus does not like clever tricks with promises. When you say Yes, mean Yes! When you say No, mean No! And remember: God hears every word you say.

homily: Dear friends, today the Church remembers the Seventy Disciples of Jesus. We do not know their names, and that is part of the message. Jesus did not send only the Twelve; he sent seventy others. The mission is for all who are baptised, and that means you and me.

“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Luke 10:2). Jesus sends them two by two, with peace on their lips: “Peace to this house!” They did not have much to take with them. They had a message, a companion and a promise.

The promise is in the other readings. God says through Isaiah, “I will open rivers on the bare heights, and fountains in the midst of the valleys” (Isaiah 41:18). Wherever the Gospel arrives, dry hearts open like wells in the rains. And Paul says, “If God is for us, who is against us?” and “nothing in all creation will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:31, 39). Today is the First Friday: let us bring our fears to the open heart of Jesus.

Then Jesus tells us the price and the pay. The price: love him above all, and take up the cross. The pay: not gold, but welcome. “Whoever welcomes you welcomes me,” and a cup of cold water given in his name will not lose its reward (Matthew 10:40, 42).

Our own prayer at the Qurbana comes from Mar Addai and Mar Mari, disciples whom our tradition counts among the Seventy. Today let us be like them: let us pray for labourers, let us welcome the stranger, and let us carry the peace of Christ to one house. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus sent seventy friends to tell people about God, two by two. They said, ‘Peace to this house!’ You can do that too: be a friend who brings peace.
Jesus also said that even a glass of cold water given to someone in his name is a great gift. This week give a glass of water, a smile and a kind word to someone who is tired or sad!

homily: Dear friends, today is the first Monday of Kaitha, the season of summer and harvest. Our readings begin the season with two serious questions. The first is from Saint Paul, and the second is from Jesus.

Paul says to the Corinthians: “When you come together, it is not really to eat the Lord’s supper” (1 Corinthians 11:20). Why? Because each one ate his own food. One person was hungry and another was drunk. They came to the table of the Lord, and they humiliated the poor. “Do you not have homes to eat and drink in?” Paul asks. He is angry because he loves the poor.

Then Paul reminds them of what the Lord did on the night before he died. He took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said, “This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” The cup is the new covenant in his blood. As often as we eat this bread and drink this cup, we proclaim the Lord's death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). Because we eat one bread, we are one body. We cannot be one at the altar and strangers at the door.

In the Gospel Jesus tells a short story. A father says to his two sons, “Go and work in the vineyard today.” One says, “I will not,” but later he changes his mind and goes. The other says, “I go, sir,” and does not go. Which one did the will of the father (Matthew 21:28–31)? Jesus does not praise the No; he praises the going. Words are not enough: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father” (Matthew 7:21).

Today let us ask ourselves: Where have I said Yes to God, and have not done it? Where have I said No, and can I still change my mind? It is never too late to turn back. And let us do something today: make peace with someone before Sunday's Qurbana, and do the one task we have been saying Later to. “Son, go and work in the vineyard today.” Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus tells a story about two sons. The father asked them to work in the vineyard. One said, ‘No!’ but later he went. The other said, ‘Yes!’ but he did not go.
Which boy did what his father wanted? The one who went! Jesus wants us to say Yes with our hands. Today, do one thing you have been putting off, and help someone at home without being asked!

homily: Dear friends, today is the first Tuesday of Kaitha, and two Bible readings speak to us about gifts: what God has given and what we do with it.

Saint Paul tells the Corinthians: “Be infants in evil, but in thinking be adults” (1 Corinthians 14:20). Be innocent about evil, and clear and wise in your judgement. He also asks what a stranger sees when he walks into our church. If all is noise and show, he will say, “They are out of their mind.” But if the word of God is spoken so that it can be understood, the stranger will fall on his knees and say, “God is really among you” (1 Corinthians 14:25). That is what our worship is for.

In the Gospel a nobleman goes away and gives ten servants ten pounds each: “Do business with these until I come back” (Luke 19:13). When he returns, two servants have used the money and are praised: “Well done, good slave! Because you have been trustworthy in a very small thing...” (Luke 19:17). The third buried it in a cloth. Why? “I was afraid of you.” He thought his master was harsh, and fear made him do nothing.

Many of us have buried something: a talent for singing, for teaching, for kindness, for prayer; time we could give to the parish or to a sick neighbour. God is not a harsh master. He is the giver of every gift, and he wants it to be used. “Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). It is not the size of the gift that counts but the faithfulness.

Today the Church also remembers Saint Maria Goretti. She was a poor girl of eleven who refused to do wrong and was badly hurt for it. Before she died she forgave the one who hurt her. Later he repented. She was a child in age, but in her choices she was strong and clear: an “infant in evil” and an adult in judgement. Let us ask her to pray for our children and young people. And let us not bury our gifts, but use them, until the Lord comes. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus tells a story about a master who gave his servants money and went away. Two servants used it well. One was afraid and hid it. Jesus wants us to use the gifts God has given us: singing, helping, kind words, drawing, praying.

Today we also remember Saint Maria Goretti. She was a girl who loved Jesus very much and always chose what was right, and when someone hurt her badly, she forgave him. Ask her to help you to be brave and kind, and to forgive.

homily: Dear friends, in today's Gospel some people ask Jesus: “If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.” Jesus answers that he has already told them by his works. The problem was not that they had not heard; it was that they were not ready to listen.

Then Jesus says something very beautiful: “My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27). Three things: they hear, he knows them, they follow. This is the whole of the Christian life. Listening in prayer, being known and loved by the Lord, and walking behind him.

Saint Paul tells Timothy, “Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of the eternal life” (1 Timothy 6:12). The fight is not with people. It is the daily struggle to stay faithful: to be gentle when we want to shout, to be honest when it costs us, to pray when we are tired.

Many voices call us today: the phone, advertisements, fear, our own pride. But the sheep who spend time with the Shepherd know his voice. Let us read the Gospel every day and say the family prayer together, and we will know which voice to follow.
And the Lord promises: “No one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). We may be weak, but his hand is strong. Let us hold to him in this season of Kaitha, and he will bring us home. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus is the Good Shepherd, and you are his little sheep! A shepherd knows each sheep by name, and the sheep know his voice. Speak with Jesus every morning and every night, and you will learn his voice. Then, when someone asks you to do something wrong, you will hear Jesus in your heart say: ‘Come this way, little sheep.’ And nobody can take you out of his hand!

homily: Dear friends, Saint Paul tells the Corinthians how to pray: “I will pray with the spirit, but I will pray with the mind also” (1 Corinthians 14:15). Prayer needs both the heart and the head. When we only feel, we may not know what we are saying. When we only think, our prayer may become dry.

He also speaks about the Amen. When the priest gives thanks to God at the altar, the people answer Amen. That small word means: yes, this is true, and this is my prayer too. But for the people to say Amen, they must understand. Our Qurbana is celebrated in our own language so that every Amen may be real.

Paul says that in church he would rather speak five words that teach others than ten thousand that no one can follow (1 Corinthians 14:19). The measure of everything in the Church is whether it builds up. This is a good thought at the start of Kaitha, the season of growth.

In the Gospel Jesus is in the Temple, and the argument is hard. Some people insult him. Jesus does not insult them. He says: “I honor my Father.” Then he says something wonderful: “Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). He uses the name that God told Moses at the burning bush. He is God's Son, and he is God.
They picked up stones. But we pick up our Amen. Let us say it this week with understanding, at the Qurbana and in every prayer, and keep his word. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know what Amen means? It means: yes, this is true, and I agree! When the priest prays at Holy Qurbana, we all say Amen. Say it with your heart, not only with your mouth! And Jesus told us a great secret: he was there even before Abraham, long, long ago. Jesus is God's Son, and he is always with us.

homily: Dear friends, today the Church of the East remembers Mar Yakob, a bishop of Nisibis who lived about seventeen hundred years ago. He was a man of prayer, a teacher of the Scriptures, and the teacher of the young Ephrem, who became one of the greatest poets of our tradition. Our Qurbana, with its prayer of Addai and Mari, comes from this same Church.

The first reading is God's promise to Jacob: “Do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God” (Isaiah 41:10). God does not say this to the strong. He says it to a little people, even to the “worm Jacob”. He chooses the small and holds them with his right hand.

In Acts, people burned their books of magic in public. The name of Jesus is not a charm. We do not trust amulets, horoscopes or lucky days; we trust the Lord himself. If there is any such thing in our house, today is a good day to put it away.
Saint Paul tells us that our weapons are not the world's weapons. They are prayer, the word of God and love, and they are used for building up and not for tearing down (2 Corinthians 10:4, 8).

And Jesus says: “Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows” (Luke 12:7). Not one is forgotten before God. If we acknowledge him before others, he will acknowledge us before the angels, and the Holy Spirit will teach us what to say. Let us carry this courage into the week. Amen.
kids: Children, today we remember Mar Yakob, a bishop who loved to pray and to teach children. One of the boys he taught, Ephrem, grew up to write beautiful songs for God. Jesus tells us not to be afraid, because God knows every little sparrow, and he knows you even better. So when you are afraid of the dark, of exams or of storms, say: ‘Jesus, you are with me.’

homily: Dear friends, in today's Gospel four friends carry a paralysed man to Jesus. The house is full, so they climb up, make a hole in the roof, and let their friend down. We do not know their names. But Mark says: “When Jesus saw their faith” (Mark 2:5). Faith can carry another person.

And what does Jesus say to the man? He does not first say, ‘Walk.’ He says, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” The man had come for his legs, but Jesus gave him what he needed most. Only God can forgive sins, and Jesus does it, and proves it by making the man walk.

This forgiveness is given to us in the sacrament of Reconciliation. If we have been away for a long time, today's Gospel tells us that there is no hole in the roof too hard to make. The Lord is waiting.

Saint Paul tells the Corinthians that we are “the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16). God lives in us. So we refuse everything that is not worthy of his dwelling: lies, cheating, impurity, idols. At the same time we respect and love our neighbours of every faith.
On this Saturday, let us ask Mary, the Mother of Jesus, to teach us to be like the four friends: to carry others to her Son. Let us name one person today and carry them in prayer. Amen.
kids: Children, do you remember the four friends who made a hole in the roof? They loved their friend so much that they did not give up. Jesus saw how much they believed and made the man walk. You can also carry your friends to Jesus: when a friend is sick or sad, say a prayer for him. And remember, Jesus lives in you like in a little church, so be kind and clean in your words and deeds.

homily: Dear friends, today the Apostle James says: “Blessed is anyone who endures temptation” (James 1:12). Every one of us has trials, in health, in the family, in work. If we stay faithful, we will receive “the crown of life”. But James also says something we must never forget: God does not tempt anyone. When we fall, we must not say, ‘God tempted me.’

James shows us how sin grows: first a desire, then a consent, then the act, and then the habit, and finally death. So we must stop it at the first step. When a bad thought comes, say a short prayer, and turn. And against the birth that ends in death, God gives us another birth: “he gave us birth by the word of truth” (James 1:18). We are his first fruits.

James also tells us that every good gift comes from above, from the Father of lights, who never changes (James 1:17). In these days of monsoon, when the sky changes every hour, it is good to remember that our Father does not change. Let us thank him each evening for three gifts.

In the Gospel Jesus says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father” (Matthew 7:21). It is not enough to say the right words. We must do what he says.

Two houses, one rain. Everyone who hears his words and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on rock (Matthew 7:24). In 2018 Kerala saw what the flood does to a house with no foundation. Let us build on the rock this week by doing one thing that the Lord has said. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus told a story about two houses. The wise man built his house on rock, and the foolish man on sand. When the rain and the floods came, the house on the rock did not fall! When you listen to Jesus and do what he says, you are building on rock. Be kind, tell the truth, say your prayers, and help at home. Then, when something hard comes, you will stand strong, just like the house on the rock.

homily: Dear friends, James begins today with a question we all know: where do our quarrels come from? He answers like a good doctor. They come from cravings that make war inside us (James 4:1). We want something, we do not get it, and we turn on those nearest to us.

Think of the quarrels we have seen: over a boundary, a share of the land, a seat in a committee, a word that was never forgiven. James says that friendship with the world is enmity with God. By the world he means the way of living in which everything is measured by what I have and what people say of me.

But God is not a rival to our joy. He loves us with a jealous love, and he gives more grace to the humble (James 4:6). So James gives us the way back: submit to God, resist the devil, and the devil will flee.

Jesus shows us what that grace looks like. “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke 6:20). Not will be: is. The one who has God has everything, and has no need to fight over scraps. And he warns us: “Woe to you when all speak well of you” (Luke 6:26). It is easy to live for applause.
This week let us make one peace. Let us ask God for what we truly need, share a little of what we have, and be glad that the kingdom belongs to the poor and the humble. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus said: blessed are the poor, for the kingdom of God is theirs. That means God loves people who have little, and he wants us to share with them. When you quarrel with your brother or sister, say sorry first. That is how people become friends of God!

homily: Dear friends, Paul tells us today, “We do not lose heart.” Whoever has watched a parent grow old, or has felt the weight of years, understands how much those words are worth. Our outer nature is wasting away, he says, but our inner nature is being renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16).

Why does Paul speak with such confidence? Because he knows that the One who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also (2 Corinthians 4:14). Our troubles are real, but they are slight compared with the glory being prepared. We look not at what can be seen, but at what cannot be seen.

Paul was a tentmaker, and he says that our earthly body is like a tent. When it is folded up, God has a building ready, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens (2 Corinthians 5:1). That is why we stand at the grave of our dear ones with hope.

In the Gospel Jesus says, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). A seed in a tin is safe and useless. A seed in the wet earth looks lost and becomes a field. Jesus himself is that grain, and so are all who give their lives for others.

This week let us find one place where we can let a seed fall: a sharp word we keep back, an hour we give to someone old or sick, a quarrel we end. He who serves Jesus must follow him, and where he is, there will his servant be also (John 12:26). Amen.
kids: Children, a seed looks lost when the farmer puts it in the mud, but then it becomes a green plant with many grains! Jesus said that is how love works. When we give something up for someone else, God makes something beautiful grow from it.

homily: Dear friends, today the Church looks at a mountain: Mount Carmel. After three years of drought, the prophet Elijah went to the top of Carmel, bowed to the ground and prayed for rain. His servant looked toward the sea seven times. Six times there was nothing. At the seventh: “Look, a little cloud no bigger than a person’s hand is rising out of the sea” (1 Kings 18:44).

That little cloud is a picture of hope for everyone who has prayed and waited. And the Carmelite tradition sees in it a picture of Mary: small, humble, and bringing in her womb the Rain that makes the earth bloom, Jesus our Saviour. Today is the feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, and in Kerala so many of us belong to her family: the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate, the Sisters of the Congregation of the Mother of Carmel, and thousands of families who wear her scapular.

But what does she teach us? A woman in the crowd praises Jesus' mother, and Jesus answers, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!” (Luke 11:28). He is not putting his mother down. He is telling us why she is blessed: she heard the word of God and did it. “Let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). The scapular is not a charm. It is a sign that we want to live as she lived.

Paul adds that God is “the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction” (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). When we have been comforted, we are to comfort.

And today the Church also thanks God for Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai, who carried the Gospel to the East. The Qurbana we celebrate on most Sundays uses their prayer. This week let us pray again a prayer we had given up, let us keep one line of the Gospel, and let us comfort one person. Our Lady of Mount Carmel, pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, a servant looked at the sea seven times, and at last he saw a tiny cloud, and then the big rain came! Our Lady of Mount Carmel teaches us not to stop praying and to listen to Jesus. And Mar Mari and Mar Addai traveled far to tell people about Jesus. We can tell our friends about him too!

homily: Dear friends, today the readings put two tables before us. In the first, James asks: “Do you with your acts of favoritism really believe in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ?” (James 2:1). A person with gold rings comes into the assembly, and we give him the best seat. A poor person in dirty clothes comes in, and we say, “Stand there.”

James says: this is not the Lord's way. God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom (James 2:5). The law that rules the Christian assembly is the royal law: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (James 2:8). In our churches nobody should be placed higher or lower because of his clothes or his money.

In the Gospel, Jesus tells of a man who gave a great dinner and invited many. “Come; for everything is ready now.” But they all made excuses (Luke 14:17–18): a field, oxen, a wedding. These are all good things. But when God calls, they cannot be put first.

Then the master sends his servant to the streets and lanes to bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame. The servant says, “there is still room” (Luke 14:22). That is the heart of God: there is always room for one more. We should be the same.

This week let us look at our excuses, and let us look at the person nobody notices. Let us greet that person, sit with him, and invite him. And let us answer the Lord's call: “Come; for everything is ready now.” Amen.
kids: Children, God invited everybody to a great feast, even those whom nobody invited. When someone is alone at school or in the church, you can say, “Come and sit with us. There is still room!”

homily: Dear friends, today's Epistle asks a simple question: what is your faith worth if nobody can see it? Saint James says: “For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is also dead” (James 2:26).

He gives two examples. Abraham believed God, and then he obeyed God even when it was very hard. Rahab was a stranger in Jericho, yet she believed in the God of Israel and she risked her life to save two messengers. Both were justified; both had a faith that acted.

We are saved by the grace of God that we receive in faith, and that faith is alive when it shows itself in love. The believer does not earn God's love, but the one who has received it cannot keep it locked inside.

In the Gospel Jesus grieves over Jerusalem: “How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). We know this picture from our own courtyards. Jesus is the one who would gather us; all that is asked of us is to be willing.
This week let us ask: where is my faith only words? Let us do one good deed that costs us something, and let us run under the Lord's wings each evening. Amen.
kids: Children, have you seen a mother hen when a kite flies over? She spreads her wings and all the chicks hurry underneath. Jesus said he wants to gather us like that, and be our safe place. And what do we do? We can run to him in prayer, and we can open the door to someone who needs help, like Rahab. That is faith that works!

homily: Dear friends, Saint James asks today: who among you is wise? He answers: the one who shows by a good life that his works are done with gentleness (James 3:13). Wisdom is not what we know; it is how we live.

James names two wisdoms. The wisdom of the world is full of envy and selfish ambition, and wherever it rules there is disorder. The wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, willing to yield, full of mercy. Which one do we practise at home, in the parish and in our village?

In the Gospel Jesus returns to Nazareth. At first people are amazed, but then they say: “Is not this Joseph's son?” They cannot see God's work in someone they know so well. Then, when Jesus says that God cared for a widow in Sidon and for Naaman the Syrian, they are filled with rage. They envy the mercy shown to others.
That can happen to us too. We can overlook the grace that comes through the people closest to us, and we can be unhappy when God blesses someone else.

Let us ask for the wisdom from above. “A harvest of righteousness is sown in peace for those who make peace” (James 3:18). This week let us be peacemakers: let us rejoice with others and thank God for the people at home. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus came back to his own town, but the people there said: he is only Joseph's son! They did not see who he really was. Let us look carefully at the people at home, because God does wonderful things through them. And when a friend gets a prize, let us clap for them and be happy. That is God's wisdom!

homily: Dear friends, today Saint Paul speaks of something wonderful: “So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!” (2 Corinthians 5:17). Christ died for all, so that we may live for him.

God has done the first thing: in Christ he reconciled the world to himself, not counting our sins against us (2 Corinthians 5:19). Now he gives this work to us. We are his ambassadors. God makes his appeal through us: “be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20).

In the Gospel Jesus walks along the lake and sees fishermen at work. He says: “Follow me and I will make you fish for people.” And immediately they left their nets and followed him (Mark 1:17–18). They were ordinary men with ordinary jobs, and the Lord gave them a great mission.

Each of us has a net we are holding: a habit, a grudge, a fear, a comfort. And each of us has a person whom we have not forgiven. The Lord calls us to leave the net and to make the first move toward peace.
This week let us go to the sacrament of reconciliation, and let us ask someone's pardon, or give ours. Then we shall be what Paul says we are: God's ambassadors. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus called four fishermen and they came at once! They left their nets and their boats. Jesus calls you too, to be his friend and helper. You can be his messenger of peace: when two friends quarrel, you can help them make up. Say sorry first, and forgive quickly. That is what an ambassador of Jesus does!

homily: Dear friends, today the Church remembers Saint Mary Magdalene. The Lord healed her of great darkness, and she followed him to the end. She stood near the cross with Mary his mother, and on Easter morning, while it was still dark, she came to the tomb (John 20:1).

She found the tomb empty and she wept. And then someone said her name: “Mary!” (John 20:16). That is all it took. She knew his voice. The Good Shepherd knows each sheep by name, and he knows you by your name.

Then Jesus gave her work: “go to my brothers and say to them...” (John 20:17). “Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord’” (John 20:18). The apostles at first thought it an idle tale, but this woman was the first witness of the Resurrection. That is why the Church calls her the apostle of the apostles.

Saint Paul asks, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans 8:35). Not hardship, not death, not the darkness. Mary did not let go of her love at the cross, and she was the first to see the risen Lord.
This week let us stay near the Lord when it is dark, listen for him calling our name, and tell at least one person what he has done for us. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know the friend of Jesus who cried at the empty tomb? It was Mary Magdalene. She missed Jesus so much! Then Jesus called her name, “Mary!”, and she knew it was him. She ran to tell everyone: “I have seen the Lord!” Jesus knows your name too. Tell someone this week about how good Jesus is!

homily: Dear friends, today Saint Paul kneels and prays for us: “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, as you are being rooted and grounded in love” (Ephesians 3:17). That prayer is also for you and for your family.
